CLAUDE.content:
Contexto del proyecto — SOLE Voltaje

Este archivo es la memoria compartida del proyecto para agentes de IA (Claude, Gemini, etc.).
actualízalo cuando cambie la estructura, los flujos o las convenciones del repositorio.


¿Qué es SOLE Voltaje?
Jardín digital de conocimiento práctico para comunidades rurales y semiurbanas de Colombia y Latinoamérica con baja conectividad. Enseña a personas —muchas con baja escolaridad, en zonas remotas— cómo mejorar su conectividad, conseguir equipos, convocar a su comunidad y usar internet en grupo.

URL producción: voltaje.solecolombia.org
Rama producción: voltaje
Stack: Quartz 4.6 (static site generator) + GitHub Pages
Idiomas: es/ (principal), en/, pt/ (traducidos con Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite)
Organización GitHub: sole-colombia


Estructura del repositorio
Ver ROADMAP.md en la raíz del repositorio para el estado detallado de la arquitectura y fases activas (PWA, Tauri, Offline).

├── content/                   ← Working directory principal
│   ├── es/solve/              ← Soluciones en español
│   ├── es/inspire/            ← Inspiraciones en español
│   ├── es/glossary/           ← Conceptos/glosario en español
│   ├── es/disconnected/       ← Contenido desconectado
│   ├── en/                    ← Traducciones inglés (generadas)
│   ├── pt/                    ← Traducciones portugués (generadas)
│   ├── assets/                ← Imágenes (.webp preferido)
│   ├── templates/             ← Plantillas de contenido

│   └── .gemini/               ← Configuración agentes Gemini
│       ├── GEMINI.md          ← Memoria para Gemini CLI

├── docs/

├── glossary_tags.tsv          ← Tags y metadatos de conceptos/glosario
└── ROADMAP.md                 ← Única fuente de verdad (Fases B/C)


Tipos de contenido
1. Soluciones (es/solve/solv-*.md)
Paso a paso concreto para construir, instalar o arreglar algo.
Frontmatter obligatorio:
title: "¿Cómo hacer X?"
resumen: "Una oración que diga qué logra el lector. Max 15 palabras."
date: AAAA-MM-DD
tags:
  - "Electricidad"        # Electricidad | Señal | Dispositivos | Espacio | Personas
permite:
  - "Compartir"           # Conseguir | Mejorar | Compartir | Medir
dificultad: "Muy Fácil"   # Muy Fácil | Fácil | Medio | Complejo
costo: "Gratis"           # Gratis | < USD 25 | USD 25 - 50 | > USD 50 | Gasto mensual
ayudantes: "Sin ayudantes" # Sin ayudantes | 1 persona | 2-3 personas | Más de 3 personas
tarda: "Minutos"          # Minutos | Horas | Días | Semanas
autor: "SOLE Colombia"
draft: false
Estructura del cuerpo:

Saludo según perfil de voz (sin encabezado)
## ¿Qué es [título]?
## ¿Para qué sirve?
## Antes de empezar...
## ¿Qué necesitas?
## ¿Cómo hacerlo? — pasos con formato > ### Paso N → [Acción]
## Recomendaciones
## ¿Cómo saber si esta solución funciona?
## Otros internets posibles
## Soluciones relacionadas
## Referencias
## Historial de cambios

2. Inspiraciones (es/inspire/insp-*.md)
Preguntas grandes, historias y reflexiones sobre conectividad comunitaria.
Frontmatter obligatorio:
title: "¿Pregunta grande?"
resumen: "..."
date: AAAA-MM-DD
tags:
  - "historias-potentes"  # o "vamos-a-romper", "te-ha-pasado", etc.
autor: "SOLE Colombia"
draft: false
3. Conceptos/Glosario (es/glossary/conc-*.md)
Definiciones de términos técnicos adaptadas para audiencias no técnicas.
4. Desconectados (es/disconnected/disc-*.md)
Recursos para comunidades sin acceso a internet.

Reglas de Markdown / Quartz

Nunca H1 en el cuerpo. Quartz lo genera desde title.
Wikilinks con flecha: [[es/solve/solv-nombre|Texto visible →]]
Imágenes con alt text: ![Descripción de acción](assets/images/carpeta/archivo.webp)
Pasos siempre dentro de blockquote: > ### Paso N → [Acción]
Callouts como blockquotes: > *Consejo: ...* > *Atención: ...* > *Ánimo: ...* > *Vas bien: ...* > *Para pensar: ...*
No archivos extra en content/ (no .txt, .csv, .json — solo .md y assets)
No comentarios HTML con metadatos en .md
Separadores --- entre secciones ##


Agentes disponibles
Cacharrera Editora (voltaje-editor)

Versión activa: v2.8
Archivo: content/.gemini/skills/voltaje-editor/SKILL.md
Rol: Creación y revisión de soluciones, inspiraciones y notas
NO es agente de código — solo trabaja con contenido editorial
Invocar en Gemini: @voltaje-editor
Invocar en Claude: a través del skill voltaje-editor

Agente de Frontmatter

Archivo: docs/editorial/PROMPT_AGENTE_FRONTMATTER_SOLUCIONES.md
Rol: Auditoría y análisis de frontmatter, criterios de dificultad, nivel editorial

en/disconnected/index.title: Disconnected
en/disconnected/index.summary: A quick guide to keep things running without relying on the network.
en/disconnected/index.content:
How to connect the “disconnected”?
This is one of the big questions that inspired the creation of the platform you’re on right now: SOLE Voltaje ⚡⚡

But… how can the 2.6 billion people who don’t have Internet access connect to a connectivity platform without being connected? 🤔

This is the big question that inspired the creation of the tool you have in your hands: The Disconnected (El Desconectado).

In 2024, the SOLE Colombia team designed a tool so that anyone, anywhere in the world, regardless of their prior knowledge, could understand —in a practical and fun way— how the Internet works without having the Internet.
The tool is a deck of cards that invites you to navigate Internet concepts and connectivity solutions in a dynamic and simple way. With The Disconnected, you can:

Learn key Internet concepts (for example, what megabytes are, what types of mobile signals exist, what a server is, etc.).
Identify how good your signal is for accessing the Internet (a mini-diagnostic).
Discover and evaluate the connectivity solution(s) that work best in specific contexts.

The cool thing about this deck is that, like everything in Voltaje, it’s a tool built day by day in community. That means we will keep adjusting it based on the lessons and contributions from the communities we work with and from people like you who decide to use it.
Here is a quick summary of how it works 👇🏽

About The Disconnected
This tool consists of three types of cards:

Tinkering cards (Cartas cacharreras)
Navigation cards (Cartas navegadoras)
Connection cards (Cartas conectivas)

There is no specific order, so you can start with any of the three types. Here’s what you can do with each one 👇🏽

Tinkering cards: How’s your signal?


To understand how the Internet works wherever you are, you can start by “tinkering” with the signal you have. But, what signal do you have? How does it work? We have two cards that will help you answer these questions in practice: how to tinker with your mobile signal? or how to tinker with your WiFi signal?
Starting from this first distinction, you can identify how the Internet signal reaches any device! Just flip over either of the two cards and follow the instructions to start navigating.


Navigation cards: What would you like more of?


These cards will help you navigate the Internet while you learn about the importance of asking Big Questions. You will also learn about how the Internet travels, how fast it is, what signal you have, how to make the most of it, and much more. You can use these cards in a thousand ways. We’ll share one of the many possible dynamics:


Choose 2 cards at random and place the “What would you like more of?” card in the middle.


Answer what you would like more of; what do you prefer… To be the Internet traveling through a cable across land and oceans, or to travel at the speed of light? You can combine the cards however you like.


Flip the card you chose and read what it says. Each card will bring you new concepts or ideas about the Internet. Some will give you specific instructions: follow them! All the cards are connected to each other. Go ahead and look for the next one, and the next, and the next. Navigate through them!


If you are with friends, family, or people from a community, you can do several rounds where everyone answers and shares what they would like more of, reading the information and solving the challenges as a team. We invite you to try all the variations you can think of!





Connection cards: What works best for connecting?


These cards present different connectivity solutions. You can open any card, follow the instructions, and identify if that solution works for what you want to learn or solve. These cards are “connective” because they will lead you to find solutions to get connected to the Internet.
Depending on your connectivity situation or your learning interests, you will find three types of cards for this category:

What are the differences between these cards? Flip them over and find out for yourself!


Recipe book of solutions: How to connect to the Internet?


In the recipe book of solutions, you will find, in summary, the solutions presented in the connection cards. Remember that you can consult the solutions in the recipe book or directly on the SOLE Voltaje platform if you need more detail to carry out the solution.


The Disconnected is inspired by diverse connectivity challenges
SOLE Voltaje, and The Disconnected in particular, were designed for people with diverse connectivity challenges. After a survey conducted in 2020 by SOLE Colombia, we discovered that half of the people we interact with do not have Internet for one or more of the following reasons:

There is no signal: In the places where they live, there is no mobile or cable coverage. In some places, especially in scattered rural areas, there are public schools with satellite connectivity provided by the government, but its quality and consistency are poor.
The signal is bad: In other spots, the signal is intermittent, which makes it impossible to make video calls or watch videos. Generally, this forces people to travel across the territory to find a better connection point.
They don’t have the money to pay for it: Even if there is a signal available, the service represents a very high cost for the personal or family budget.
They don’t know what the Internet is for: Although many people mention the previous reasons, their answers suggest that there is also a lack of knowledge about the potential of the Internet, as priority is given to paying for other services like satellite television. In many communities, there is a belief that the Internet is limited to Facebook and WhatsApp, since those are the applications that are usually included for free in mobile plans.


Do you want to take The Disconnected to a truly disconnected context?
If you live in a place with very little or no Internet connection, or you know or work with a community or group of people in these conditions, you can use The Disconnected to navigate the Internet without being connected.

Enter your email in the form below to receive the download link for the digital version (ready for you to print yourself).
If you want to have the printed version (the one you see in the photos), write to us at hola@solecolombia.org and we will get it to you.

en/glossary/conc-2g-net.title: 2G Network
en/glossary/conc-2g-net.summary: The tech that bridged the gap from analog to digital.
en/glossary/conc-2g-net.content:
The 2G (Second Generation) network is the mobile technology that marked the shift from analog to digital, making encrypted voice calls and text messages (SMS) a reality. It handles basic voice and text communication, while also supporting some limited data services like email and slow-speed internet access. It was the bedrock for the global expansion of mobile telephony and the foundation for the tech that followed, even if its data speeds are a bit sluggish by today’s standards.
What is the 2G network?

Digitalizing communications: 2G was the first generation to embrace digital tech for mobile comms, leaving those old analog systems in the rearview mirror.
GSM Technology: It’s built on the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM).
Core services: Its bread and butter is voice calls and sending/receiving text messages (SMS).

What’s it good for?

Voice calls: It let us make encrypted voice calls with much better clarity than the analog days.
SMS Messaging: It made sending and receiving text messages possible, which completely changed how we stay in touch.
Limited data services: With the introduction of services like GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) →, it cracked the door open for basic data, allowing for very limited internet access and email.
Coverage: It’s still a champ because it provides solid coverage in rural or mountainous areas where the fancy new networks haven’t reached yet.
IoT devices (Internet of Things): It’s still kicking in some machine-to-machine (M2M) communication gear and GPS tracking devices.

Its legacy and future

Foundation for the future: 2G laid the groundwork for advanced tech like 3G and 4G by proving just how efficient digital systems could be.
Gradual sunset: Because its data speeds are pretty pokey compared to the new kids on the block, most carriers are shutting down and replacing 2G networks to repurpose those frequencies for more efficient tech like 4G and 5G.

en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.title: 3G/4G Antenna
en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.summary: A little gadget to get you hooked up to 3G or 4G networks.
en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.content:
A 3/4G antenna, also known as an LTE antenna, is a handy little device that helps you get online using 3G and 4G mobile networks. These antennas act like a bridge, grabbing and sending radio signals so your smartphones, tablets, and modems can talk to the cell towers, which helps smooth out your connection and give it a bit more pep.
A few more details:

How it works: Think of 3/4G antennas as the go-between for your gadgets and the cell towers, making that wireless magic happen.
Types of antennas: You’ve got a couple of main flavors: directional antennas, which are like a flashlight beam—focused in one direction for extra reach—and omnidirectional ones, which are more like a lantern, spreading the signal all around.
Boosting your signal: If you’re stuck in a dead zone or just have spotty service indoors, hooking up a 3/4G antenna can give your signal the boost it needs to get things moving.
Aiming matters: Getting the angle right is key. You’ll want to point that antenna toward the nearest cell tower to get the best possible reception.
Hooking it up: These antennas usually connect to your gear using coaxial cables → and SMA connectors, or you might need an adapter if you’re plugging into a MIFI router →.
MIMO technology: Some 4G antennas use MIMO (Multiple Input Multiple Output) tech. It’s basically using multiple antennas at once to make your connection faster and more reliable.
Not the same as WiFi: Keep in mind, these aren’t the same as WiFi antennas →. While WiFi runs on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, 4G antennas work on specific frequency bands set by your carrier.
Rural life: If you’re out in the sticks where the signal is a bit shy, an outdoor antenna can be a real lifesaver for getting a decent internet connection.

en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.title: Wise Assistant (Local AI)
en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.summary: A consultant program that lives on your server and helps you crunch your own data.
en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.content:
The Wise Helper is a special Artificial Intelligence program that lives and works right inside your own computer or servidor →. Unlike other AIs, this one doesn’t need the internet because everything it knows comes from the files and “digital books” you keep in its memory.
In our tech kitchen:

It’s an Expert Consultant.
It’s not the one doing the heavy lifting (that’s the Procesador o Cocinero →‘s job), but rather the one who analyzes the recipes and gives you advice.
Internal reading: The helper doesn’t go out into the street looking for answers; it reads the manuals, guides, and documents you have in the pantry (Almacenamiento →). That’s why it’s safe and private: what happens in the kitchen, stays in the kitchen.


The importance of the Workbench (RAM)
Even though the helper is very smart, it has a limitation: to think and answer, it needs to spread all the information out on the Workbench (Memoria RAM →).

If you have plenty of RAM (a big workbench), the helper can read many pages at once and answer you quickly.
If you have very little RAM (a small workbench), the helper has to keep opening and closing folders constantly, which makes it take a long time to give you an answer.


In short: The helper is only as agile as the space you give it to work on the bench and how many sous-chefs are helping it out.


What is it for?

Analyzing your own data: You can ask it to summarize meeting minutes or help you find a date in a long document.
Educational support: It helps students understand difficult concepts by explaining them in simple words.
Translation and writing: It helps translate texts from one language to another or write formal letters for the community.


Related concepts

Posibilidades de IA Local →
Memoria RAM →
Procesador (CPU) →

en/glossary/conc-antenna.title: Antenna
en/glossary/conc-antenna.summary: A handy gadget for catching and sending waves.
en/glossary/conc-antenna.content:
In a nutshell, an antenna is just a gadget designed to send and/or catch electromagnetic waves.
About antennas


Transmitting: Antennas beam electromagnetic waves out into space, letting us talk to each other from afar. Nasa


Receiving: They can also grab those electromagnetic waves right out of the air, turning them into electrical signals that a receiver can make sense of. Pilares invisibles de la comunicacion inalambrica


Types of antennas: There’s a whole bunch of them out there, like satellite dishes, dipoles, and Yagi antennas →, each one built with its own special quirks for different jobs. Tipos de antenas


Applications: Antennas are the backbone of radio, TV, mobile communications →, wireless networks →, and a whole heap of other tech that relies on electromagnetic waves. Museo de telecomunicaciones Vicente Miralles Segarra




References

Nasa
Wikipedia

en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.title: Bandwidth
en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.summary: The maximum amount of data that can zip through your network at once.
en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.content:
Bandwidth is the capacity of a network connection to carry data. It’s usually measured in Megabits per second (Mbps).
In our tech kitchen:

Think of it as the width of the hallway leading to the kitchen.
If the hallway is narrow, only one person can pass through at a time with their plate; if there are too many folks, they get bunched up, and everyone arrives late to the table.
If the hallway is wide, plenty of people can come and go with lots of food at the same time, nice and smooth.


Don’t mix it up with speed
A lot of folks think bandwidth is speed, but really, it’s capacity. A wide hallway doesn’t make you walk any faster, but it does let more people walk together without bumping into each other. The more bandwidth your community has, the more neighbors can use the server at the same time without things getting sluggish.

Related concepts

WiFi Signal →
Local Network →
How to measure bandwidth? →

en/glossary/conc-canva.title: Canva
en/glossary/conc-canva.summary: An online graphic design platform for everyone, easy-peasy.
en/glossary/conc-canva.content:
Canva is a free online graphic design platform that lets anyone—whether you’ve got design chops or you’re just starting out—whip up all sorts of professional-looking designs.
It’s got a straightforward, easy-to-use interface packed with a whole toolbox of templates, images, fonts, and graphic elements. It makes putting together presentations, social media posts, infographics, cards, resumes, and a whole lot more feel like a breeze.

en/glossary/conc-client.title: Client
en/glossary/conc-client.summary: The folks interacting with the servers.
en/glossary/conc-client.content:
In computing, a client is a piece of hardware or software that taps into a service or resource provided by a server →.
The term can refer to either a physical device (like a computer or smartphone) or a software program (like a web browser) used to chat with a server. (Source: Brave)
More on “clients”


The client’s role: The client sends requests to the server to get at the data, services, or resources it’s hosting. (Source: IONOS)


Client-server interaction: In a client-server setup, the client kicks off the conversation, and the server → answers those requests. (Source: IONOS)


Examples:

A web browser like Google Chrome or Mozilla Firefox is a client that asks a server for web pages. (Source: Brave)
An email program that connects to a server to send and fetch messages is another classic example. (Source: Linube)
A mobile device accessing a cloud app is yet another type of client. (Source: TechTarget)

Types of clients:

Fat clients (or heavy clients): These have their own storage space and can run apps on their own, without needing the server for every little thing. (Source: Slideshare)
Thin clients: These rely heavily on the server to run apps and store data; they’re basically just a window into the server’s work. (Source: Slideshare)

Why do they matter?
Clients let folks access a whole world of services and resources from afar, making it a breeze to interact with distributed systems and networks. (Source: Oracle)

en/glossary/conc-coaxial-cable.title: Coaxial Cable
en/glossary/conc-coaxial-cable.content:
Coaxial cable is the go-to wire for carrying high-frequency electrical signals.
It’s got two concentric conductors:

The center one, called the core: this is the workhorse that carries the information.
The outer one, looking like a tube, called the mesh, shield, or braid: this acts as the ground reference and handles the current return.

Sandwiched between the two, there’s an insulating dielectric layer, and the quality of the cable mostly depends on how good this stuff is.
The whole setup is usually wrapped up in a protective insulating jacket (also known as the outer sheath).

💡 Parts of an RG-59 coaxial cable (for signals). See also: Cable RG6 →
A: Protective plastic jacket (thermoplastic elastomer)
B: Copper mesh (shielded conductor made of aluminum braid coated in copper)
C: Insulation (foam dielectric)
D: Center conductor or copper core (copper-clad steel).
References:
A coaxial cable consists of electronic signals that make up the information Wikipedia.gov

en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.title: CMD Command Prompt
en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.summary: Chatting with the computer... but in its own language.
en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.content:
In the Windows world, CMD, or Command Prompt, is a command-line interface that lets you chat directly with the operating system → using text commands.
It’s a handy tool for running commands, managing files, troubleshooting hiccups, and automating those repetitive tasks.
The Command Prompt (CMD) is basically:

A command interpreter: CMD takes the commands you type and translates them into actions the operating system can understand and carry out.
An alternative to the graphical interface: Even though Windows has a fancy visual interface, CMD offers a faster, more efficient way to get things done, especially for power users or when you need to automate processes.
A troubleshooting sidekick: CMD lets you run commands to diagnose and fix system issues, like network glitches or configuration headaches.
A foundation for scripts: CMD is the bedrock for creating and running scripts, which helps you automate those complex, repetitive chores.

In short, CMD is an essential tool for managing and tinkering with Windows systems, offering a powerful and flexible way to interact with the operating system through text commands.

en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.title: Processor (CPU)
en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.summary: The brain of the rig, in charge of running every single instruction.
en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.content:
The Processor or CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the component that crunches the numbers and makes the decisions in your rig.
In our tech kitchen:

The Processor is The Chef.
It’s the one who grabs the ingredients from the counter (RAM Memory →), reads the recipe (the program), and whips up the final dish.
The chef’s speed (measured in Gigahertz or GHz) determines how fast the information gets processed or how quickly they can cook things up.


Why does it matter?
A chef can have “extra arms” (called Cores). If it has 4 cores, it’s like having 4 chefs working at the same time on different dishes. That’s what lets your computer multitask without getting stuck.

Related concepts

Memoria RAM →
Hardware →
Sistema Operativo →

en/glossary/conc-daemon.title: Daemon (background service or program)
en/glossary/conc-daemon.summary: Programs running quietly in the background, doing the heavy lifting.
en/glossary/conc-daemon.content:
A service, resident program, or daemon is a special kind of program that runs in the background, rather than being directly controlled by you. These programs stick around in the system, meaning they can run persistently or even restart themselves if you try to “kill” the process, depending on how the daemon is set up and the system’s own rules. The name comes from the backronym Daemon (Disk And Execution Monitor).
Daemons usually have a few tell-tale signs:

They don’t have a direct “interface” for you to interact with, neither graphical nor text-based.
They don’t use standard input/output to report errors or log what they’re doing. Instead, they use system files in specific spots (/var/log/ in most modern UNIX systems) or rely on other specialized daemons like syslogd to handle the logging.

For example, a machine hosting an HTTP server → will use an HTTP daemon to keep the service running so visitors can access the web. Another classic example is a “chronological” daemon like cron, which quietly handles scheduled tasks like system maintenance in the background.

en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.title: DHCP Protocol
en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.summary: The system that automatically assigns an IP address to every gadget that connects to the network.
en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.content:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is the service in charge of handing out IP addresses automatically.
In our tech workshop:

DHCP is The Receptionist.
When someone walks into the workshop (connects to the WiFi), the Receptionist greets them and says: “Welcome! Today, you’ll go by number 15 (IP 192.168.1.15).”
Thanks to the Receptionist, you don’t have to fiddle with any manual settings on your phone; they make sure everyone has a name and a seat at the table.


Why is it useful?
DHCP allows devices to request and receive an IP address from a DHCP server, simplifying network management and preventing IP address conflicts. (Sources: Akamai and Arsys)
Imagine 20 people show up to a community meeting with their phones. Without a Receptionist (DHCP), you’d have to go one by one, assigning numbers so no one overlaps. DHCP handles that in milliseconds.

Related concepts

IP Address →
Local Network →

en/glossary/conc-dns.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
en/glossary/conc-dns.summary: The system that translates easy-to-remember names into IP addresses.
en/glossary/conc-dns.content:
DNS is like a massive address book that links a domain name (like google.com) to a numerical address (IP →). (Sources: Cloudflare and Wikipedia)
In our tech kitchen:

DNS is like Nicknames.
Instead of telling the delivery driver to go to “House 192.168.1.15,” we just tell them to head over to “David’s place” or the “Community Kitchen.”
This nickname system is way easier for us folks to remember, but the system knows exactly which numerical address belongs to each nickname.


How does it work?
When you type a domain name into your browser, it sends a request to a DNS server. The server looks up the matching IP address and sends it back to your browser so it can connect to the web server hosting the site.
On your Pocket Server →, we set up a local nickname like solevoltaje.local. That way, any neighbor who connects to your WiFi just has to type that name into their browser to get into the “Community Kitchen,” without having to memorize any tricky numbers.

Related concepts

IP Address →
Nginx Web Server →
Local Network →

en/glossary/conc-dnsmasq.title: DNS Redirector and Lightweight DHCP Server
en/glossary/conc-dnsmasq.content:
Dnsmasq is a piece of software that handles DNS caching (DNS), acts as a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol server (DHCP →), manages router advertisements, and handles network booting for small networks—all built as free software.
Dnsmasq is light on system resources, runs happily on Linux, BSD, Android, and macOS, and comes bundled with most Linux distributions.
Because of this, it’s tucked away inside many home routers → and all sorts of Internet of Things gadgets, and it’s even part of Android.
If you’re itching to learn more, you can check out Wikipedia.

en/glossary/conc-docker-container.title: Docker Containers
en/glossary/conc-docker-container.summary: A portable, pre-equipped kitchen that works the same anywhere you plug it in.
en/glossary/conc-docker-container.content:
Docker is a technology that lets you “package” an application along with everything it needs to run (like languages, databases, and settings) inside a box called a Container.
In our kitchen analogy:

Docker is a fully-equipped portable kitchen.
Imagine you want to open a restaurant in another village. Instead of hauling bricks, pots, and hiring a plumber, you just bring a container that already has the stove installed, the pots in place, and the recipes ready to go. You just plug it in, and you’re set!
This ensures that if an application (like a digital library) works on my computer, it will work exactly the same on your Raspberry Pi or the school server.


What’s it for?
In community projects, Docker is a godsend because it lets you share complex systems (like a file server or a local AI) “hand-to-hand.” You just pass over the “container,” and the other person doesn’t have to wrestle with tricky installations; everything fires up on the first try.

Related concepts

Server →
Pocket Server →

en/glossary/conc-domain-name.title: Domain Name
en/glossary/conc-domain-name.summary: Like your home address, but for a website on the internet.
en/glossary/conc-domain-name.content:
A domain name is a unique, easy-to-remember address used to get to a website or an internet service.
Think of it like the mailing address for a website, but instead of a bunch of numbers, it uses text. For example, “solecolombia.org” is a domain name. It lets folks visit websites and services without having to memorize those complicated, clunky IP addresses →. (Source: Google Help)
In more technical terms, a domain name is just a way to translate a numerical IP address (like 192.0.2.1) into a string of text that’s easy to type and remember, like “example.com”. This translation magic is handled by the Domain Name System (DNS) →, which acts like a phonebook that matches domain names to their corresponding IP addresses.
Here are a few key things to keep in mind about domain names:

User-friendly: Domain names make it a whole lot easier for people to find and visit websites, since they’re way simpler to remember and type than IP addresses.
Online identity: A domain name is basically the digital identity of a website or service. It’s what users will type into their browser to pay your site a visit.
Ownership and registration: Domain names are registered through authorized registrars and you pay a yearly fee to keep them under your belt.
Domain parts: A domain name usually has two main parts: the name itself (e.g., “solecolombia”) and the extension or top-level domain (e.g., “.org”).

A domain name is an essential tool for navigating the internet, letting users get to websites and services easily and efficiently, while also serving as a site’s calling card on the web.

en/glossary/conc-edge-connection.title: EDGE Connection
en/glossary/conc-edge-connection.content:
The EDGE connection, when we talk about mobile phone tech, can refer to two things: either the “Enhanced Data rates for GSM of Evolution” (EDGE) technology—a 2G network that acted as a bridge to 3G to offer basic internet—or the concept of “Edge Computing,” a method of processing data right near its source to speed up high-speed apps and services on connected devices, like the Internet of Things (IoT).
It’s an evolution of GPRS → that boosts data transfer speeds on 2G mobile networks →, serving as a stepping stone toward 3G networks.
It allows for a faster data connection than standard 2G, which was just enough for basic tasks like video calls, sending messages, and web browsing before 3G networks came along. That little “E” symbol on your phone is the sign that you’re hooked into this network.

en/glossary/conc-ethernet.title: Ethernet cable connection
en/glossary/conc-ethernet.content:
An Ethernet connection is a technology that lets you hook up electronic devices to a local area network (LAN) → or a wide area network (WAN) using a cable. Its main job is moving data between gadgets, whether you’re sharing files or just getting online.
In a bit more detail:

Hardwired connection: Ethernet uses cables, usually RJ45 ones, to get devices talking to each other. There are different types of Ethernet cables, sorted by how fast they move data and their network frequency. Ethernet gives you faster speeds and a steadier connection than wireless setups like Wi-Fi →, plus it’s safer and easier on the wallet.
Connects your gear: Ethernet is the go-to for linking up all sorts of devices, from computers and routers to game consoles, smart TVs, and more. It’s the bread and butter for connecting things in one spot, like your home or office.
Moves data: Through those Ethernet cables, devices can swap data packets back and forth, making communication and file sharing possible.
Versus Wi-Fi: While Wi-Fi is definitely more convenient, Ethernet is the way to go if you want top-notch speed, stability, and security.

In short, an Ethernet connection is a fundamental piece of tech for wired data networks, giving you a reliable and efficient way to link up your devices and share information.

en/glossary/conc-firewall.title: Firewall: The Bouncer for your Network
en/glossary/conc-firewall.summary: A security system that keeps an eye on who's coming in and going out of your digital turf.
en/glossary/conc-firewall.content:
A Firewall is a security tool that monitors network traffic and decides whether to let information through or block it based on a set of rules.
In our tech kitchen:

The Firewall is The Bouncer.
It stands at the kitchen door, keeping an eye on every ingredient and every person trying to get in.
If someone tries to bring in something rotten (a virus) or sneak in uninvited (an attack), the bouncer shuts the door on them to protect the cook and the guests.


Why does it matter?
In a community network, the Firewall ensures that outsiders can’t access neighbors’ private information or mess with how the Pocket Server → runs. It’s like having a smart lock on your kitchen door.

Related concepts

Server →
Local Network →
SSH Protocol →

en/glossary/conc-firmware.title: Firmware
en/glossary/conc-firmware.summary: The low-level software baked right into your device's chips.
en/glossary/conc-firmware.content:
Firmware is a type of computer program that provides low-level control for a device’s specific hardware. It sits right “in the middle” between the hardware and the software.
In our tech kitchen:

Firmware is The Stove’s Manual.
It’s the factory-baked instructions that tell the stove how to ignite when you turn the knob, or tell the router how its lights should blink.


Why does it matter?
Sometimes, gear needs a “firmware update.” It’s like the manufacturer sending over a new page for that stove manual so it uses less gas or runs safer. Keeping it up to date helps your pocket server stay nice and steady.

Related concepts

Hardware →
Operating System →

en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.title: USB Flash Drive
en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.summary: Think of it as a tiny, portable trunk to haul your data wherever you go.
en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.content:
The USB Flash Drive (also known as a “thumb drive” or “pen drive”) is a handy little storage gadget that plugs right into your computer via a USB port →.
In our kitchen analogy:

The USB drive is like a lunchbox or a small container.
It’s perfect for carrying a portion of your meal (your files) from one kitchen (computer) to another, without having to haul the whole pantry (Hard Drive →) along with you.


A bit of history
USB drives popped up in the late 90s and took over for floppy disks and CDs. Back then, if you wanted to save just one song or a document, you needed a noisy, square disk that broke if you even looked at it wrong.
The USB drive changed the game because it’s small, tough, and doesn’t need batteries or extra cables. Its capacity has grown leaps and bounds: nowadays, a drive the size of your finger can hold thousands of books or hundreds of movies.

What’s it good for?

Carrying files: Documents, photos, or music.
Backing up info: Keeping a spare copy safe outside your computer.
Installing software: It’s often used to install an Operating System → (like Windows or Linux) on a new machine.


A word of advice…

Heads up: USB drives are super useful but easy to lose. Never keep sensitive info (like passwords) on them without protection. They’re also one of the most common ways viruses hop from computer to computer; make sure to scan them regularly.


Related concepts

USB Connection →
Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
SD Memory →

en/glossary/conc-gprs.title: GPRS (General Packet Radio Service)
en/glossary/conc-gprs.content:
GPRS was a key piece of tech that brought the concept of packet-switched data to mobile networks, laying the groundwork for the mobile data services we take for granted today. It’s still a handy tool for applications where you don’t need blazing-fast speeds.

General Packet Radio Service: Think of it as breaking information down into little “packets” of data, which are sent independently across the network.
GPRS is a data communication protocol that runs on top of second-generation (2G) mobile networks →, acting as a nice little upgrade to GSM technology.
Instead of hogging a dedicated, continuous channel for data (like GSM did), GPRS only grabs network resources when it’s actually sending data, making it a whole lot more efficient.

What’s it good for?

Internet Access and Mobile Data: It let folks connect to the internet from their mobile devices, even if the speeds were a bit modest.
Multimedia Messaging (MMS) and Email: It made sending and receiving messages more complex than simple SMS a breeze.
Location Services: It was used to provide location tracking right through the mobile network.
Security Alarms: GPRS is still pulling its weight in alarm systems, allowing for the secure transmission of alarm signals without needing to rely on a landline.

en/glossary/conc-hardware.title: Hardware
en/glossary/conc-hardware.summary: The physical guts of your rig, everything you can actually get your hands on.
en/glossary/conc-hardware.content:
Hardware refers to all the physical components of a computer system. It’s the metal, plastic, and circuitry that give the machine its body.
In our tech kitchen:

Hardware is the Utensils and the Furniture.
The pot (the computer), the burners (the processor), the countertop (the RAM), and the shelves (the hard drive).
Without hardware, the software (Operating System →) wouldn’t have anywhere to “cook” anything.


Why does care matter?
Just like a pot that gets burnt or bent stops working right, if hardware gets knocked around, wet, or overheated, the system will fail even if the recipes (the software) are perfect. Keeping your hardware clean and cool is the secret sauce to making your pocket server last for years.

Related concepts

Software (Operating System) →
Processor (CPU) →
RAM Memory →

en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.title: Hostapd Daemon
en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.summary: Turn your computer into a Wi-Fi hotspot.
en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.content:
A Hostapd (host access point daemon) is a user-space daemon that lets your network interface card (NIC) act as a wireless access point (AP) and an authentication server.
Basically, it turns your computer into a router Wi-Fi →, letting other gadgets hop onto the internet through it.
In a bit more detail:

Access Point (AP): Hostapd sets up a wireless network that other devices can connect to, just like a standard router.
Authentication Server: It handles the handshake for users trying to join the network, making sure only the devices you’ve given the green light can get in.
IEEE 802.11: Hostapd runs the IEEE 802.11 protocol, the bread and butter of wireless networking, covering things like access point management, authentication (WPA/WPA2), and secure network access.
Implementations: There are a few versions of hostapd out there, like the one by Jouni Malinen (the go-to one), OpenBSD, and Devicescape.
Linux and FreeBSD: Hostapd plays nice with Linux (Host AP, madwifi, and mac80211-based drivers) and FreeBSD (net80211).
Common Use: You’ll mostly see it used on gear like Raspberry Pi to whip up Wi-Fi hotspots or in wireless security testing rigs.

en/glossary/conc-hspa-technology.title: HSPA Technology (High-Speed Packet Access)
en/glossary/conc-hspa-technology.summary: A real boost for your 3G network.
en/glossary/conc-hspa-technology.content:
HSPA stands for “High-Speed Packet Access” and it’s basically a turbo-boost for 3G mobile networks. It ramps up the speed and efficiency of data transfers, both for downloading (HSDPA) and uploading (HSUPA).
It’s there to let mobile devices hop onto the internet at speeds way faster than basic 3G, making it easier to use data-heavy services on smartphones → and tablets, especially in those spots where 4G or 5G just hasn’t reached yet.
What is HSPA?

HSPA is a third-generation (3G) technology that soups up UMTS and WCDMA networks by adding HSDPA for downloads and HSUPA for uploads.
HSDPA (High-Speed Downlink Packet Access): This kicks up your download speeds, so you can browse faster and grab those big files without waiting forever.
HSUPA (High-Speed Uplink Packet Access): This boosts your upload speeds, making it a breeze to share photos, videos, and other hefty files to the network.

What’s HSPA good for?

Faster data speeds: HSPA offers significantly higher data speeds compared to the original 3G networks, giving you an experience that feels a lot like a DSL connection.
Better network efficiency: It uses clever tricks like advanced modulation and makes better use of the spectrum to move data around more efficiently.
Access to data services: It lets your mobile devices tap into high-speed services like web browsing, video streaming, and app downloads, keeping things running smooth.
Handling multiple tasks at once: With 3G and HSPA, your phone can juggle voice calls and data services at the same time without breaking a sweat.
Staying connected in tricky spots: Even with 4G and 5G around, HSPA is still a reliable workhorse. It’s crucial for keeping you connected in rural areas or when 4G is feeling a bit sluggish or crowded.

en/glossary/conc-imei-code.title: IMEI Code
en/glossary/conc-imei-code.content:
The IMEI is a unique 15-digit code that identifies every mobile phone worldwide. It stands for “International Mobile Equipment Identity” and acts just like a digital ID card for your device, letting carriers tell one phone apart from another on their networks. (Source: BBVA)

Unique ID: The IMEI is a one-of-a-kind serial number for every phone, making sure yours stands out from the crowd. (Source: Enacom)
Network info: Carriers use it to spot your device when it hops onto their network, which is how they track, lock, or unlock your phone. (Source:BBVA)
Safety and control: The IMEI is your go-to for reporting a phone as lost or stolen. Once it’s flagged, it gets blocked, so nobody else can use it with a different SIM card. (Source:BBC)
How to find it? You can dig up your IMEI by dialing *#06# on your keypad, checking your device settings, looking at the original box, or even peeking under the battery if it’s removable. (Source:T-Mobile)
Handy info: Beyond security, the IMEI is great for pulling up details about your device, like the make, model, and where it was born.


  
  

  📄 See video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video is a great companion to the article, breaking down what the IMEI code is and why it's the key to identifying your mobile phone globally. Follow this guide to get the lowdown on how this unique 15-digit identifier keeps your device secure and accounted for.
  


It’s not the same as a SIM: Unlike the SIM card →, which you can swap between phones, the IMEI is permanently tied to the device itself.

en/glossary/conc-information-system.title: Information System (IS)
en/glossary/conc-information-system.summary: Physical and logical bits and pieces that let us swap data around.
en/glossary/conc-information-system.content:
We define a computer system as the bunch of physical and logical parts that work together to take in, store, and process data, then spit it back out as useful results. The blueprint of a computer system covers everything that has a tangible side (hardware →) and a logical side (software →).
Nowadays, computer systems are the backbone of how we organize ourselves, acting as a powerful tool for swapping information and building networks that make distance pretty much irrelevant.
Components of a computer system
The basic nuts and bolts that make up every computer system are:

Hardware: This covers all the physical bits of the system—basically, anything you can actually touch. If we’re talking about a computer, these would be things like the screen, the keyboard, or the mouse.
Software: This is the logical side of the system, the intangible stuff. It’s the whole collection of programs, including data, instructions, apps, and so on, that let us talk to the hardware to get things done.
Computer personnel: Anyone who interacts with the system in some way, whether they’re the folks building the software, the programmers, or just regular users like you and me.

Characteristics of a computer system
Some key traits that define a computer system are:

They’re built to process, store, fetch, and receive information.
They provide a friendly interface so folks can use and manage them easily.
They make automating tasks a breeze, since the programming is set up to handle jobs on its own.
Their main goal is to offer us better, easier ways to live our lives.

Classifying computer systems
We can sort computer systems based on:

Processing volume: Depending on how much data they can chew through and manage.
Usage: That is, what the system is actually being used for—whether it’s for simple, specific tasks or handling a massive pile of variables.
Function: Depending on whether it’s designed for specific jobs within a workflow. It might be programmed to offer suggestions for decision-making or to make a decision itself based on the data it’s gathered.
Grouping: Whether they’re standalone systems or part of a bigger web of interconnected machines in private, local, or wide-area networks, and so on.

Now that we’ve got a handle on what computer systems are, let’s look at some practical applications—in other words, what a computer system is actually good for in the real world. (Source: Universidad Isabel I)

en/glossary/conc-interface.title: Interface
en/glossary/conc-interface.summary: The handshake or connection point between two systems.
en/glossary/conc-interface.content:
Broadly speaking, an interface is a point of contact or connection between two systems, components, or entities that lets them talk to each other and swap information.
It can be physical, like the connection between a keyboard and a computer, or logical, like how a program chats with the operating system →.
Types of interfaces:

User Interface (UI): This is how you, the user, interact with a system—whether it’s a program, a website, or a gadget. It covers all the visual and functional bits that let you get things done and move around the system. (Source: Wikipedia)
Application Programming Interface (API): This defines how different software programs or components can talk to each other, letting them tap into each other’s functions and data. (Source: Microsoft)
Network Interface: This is the connection point between devices on a network, like a Network Interface Card (NIC) that hooks a computer up to a network. (Source: Microsoft)
Brain-Computer Interface (BCI): This is some cutting-edge tech that allows for direct communication between the brain and an external device, like a prosthetic limb. (Source: Wikipedia)

In short, an interface makes it easy for different parts to interact and trade info, whether they’re physical, logical, or conceptual.
Wireless interfaces
A wireless interface is a mechanism that lets electronic devices talk to each other without needing physical cables, using radio waves or other wireless tech. It’s what lets you connect to computer networks, like Wi-Fi, or chat between nearby devices, like with Bluetooth.
A closer look:

Cable-free communication: Unlike wired interfaces that need physical connections like Ethernet or USB cables, wireless interfaces use radio waves or other tech to beam data back and forth. (Source: Mastervolt)
Common types: The most common examples of wireless interfaces you’ll run into are Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), Bluetooth, and NFC. (Source: Fibermall)
How they work: These interfaces are usually built into Wireless Network Interface Cards (WNICs) or adapters, which plug into devices and let them communicate with other gear or networks via radio waves. (Source: Quora)
Applications: Wireless interfaces are the backbone of mobile connectivity for laptops, smartphones, and tablets, and for setting up Wireless Local Area Networks (WLAN or Wi-Fi). (Source: Cisco)
Security: Wireless interfaces usually come with security features, like WPA3, to keep the data being sent safe and sound. (Source: Fibermall)
Operating modes: Some wireless network cards can act as Access Points (AP) so other devices can connect to them, or as clients that hop onto a network through an access point. (Source: Vyos)

en/glossary/conc-ip-address.title: IP Address
en/glossary/conc-ip-address.summary: The unique number that identifies every gadget connected to a network.
en/glossary/conc-ip-address.content:
An IP Address (Internet Protocol) is just a string of numbers that identifies a device (computer, phone, printer) on a network.
Think of it like this in our tech kitchen:

The IP is the House Address.
For data to get where it needs to go, every piece of gear needs a unique address. For example, on your local network, those addresses usually start with 192.168.1....
Without this address, the Delivery Guy (Nginx) → wouldn’t know which screen to drop the info off at.


Local IP vs. Public IP

Local IP: This is your device’s address inside your home or neck of the woods. It’s like the room number inside a hotel.
Public IP: This is your network’s address to the outside world (the big internet). It’s like the hotel’s main street address in the city.


Related Concepts

DHCP Protocol →
Nginx Web Server →

en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.title: JavaScript Language
en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.summary: The dynamic waiter that makes everything on your screen move and shine.
en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.content:
JavaScript (JS) is the language that breathes life into what you see on your browser or phone.
In our tech kitchen:

JavaScript is the dynamic waiter.
While HTML sets the table and CSS picks the tablecloth color, JavaScript is the one that makes the menu change when you swipe, lets you know your order is ready, or lets you chat with others without refreshing the page.
Unlike PHP or Python, which usually work “inside” the kitchen (the server), JavaScript usually works “out front” with the customer (on your phone).


Why does it matter?
Without JavaScript, the internet would just be a series of static pages like old newspapers. Thanks to JS, we can have applications on the local server that feel fast and modern, allowing the community to interact smoothly.

Related concepts

PHP Language →
Python Language →

en/glossary/conc-latency.title: Latency
en/glossary/conc-latency.summary: The time it takes for a data packet to travel across the network.
en/glossary/conc-latency.content:
Latency is the exact time it takes for a data packet to travel across a network.
Think of it as the time that passes from the moment your browser sends out a request for information until the requested answer finally arrives back at your doorstep.
The lower the latency, the snappier and better your internet connection will feel.
To measure latency, we look at two main things: the ping →, which is a unit of measurement expressed in milliseconds (ms), and lag, which is what we call it when that delay gets out of hand.
You can check both of these with a speed test.
What is ping?
Ping is the yardstick we use to measure latency. Before we dive deeper, do you know what latency actually is? In plain English, latency is the time it takes for a data packet to travel through the network. In other words, it’s the exact time elapsed from when your device makes a request to the server until you get a response back.
Now, ping is the metric used to measure that latency, and it’s expressed in milliseconds (or “ms” for short). The rule of thumb here is: the lower the ping, the better. Ideally, you want your ping to stay under 100 ms. Once you’re down around 65 ms, your connection is solid enough that you shouldn’t have any trouble hopping on a video call. If you’re a gamer, though, you’ll want that ping to be around 20 ms so you don’t deal with any annoying delay or lag.
What is lag?
Lag is that frustrating, excessive delay that pops up in real-time communications. It can happen because of high network latency, or maybe your device just doesn’t have enough processing power to keep up with the service you’re using. It could be your computer, or it could be your internet connection acting up.
Lag shows its face in different ways depending on what you’re doing. For example, in videos, the image quality usually takes a hit; your music might start sounding choppy or distorted; and, the classic gamer nightmare: the delay between pressing a button and seeing your character actually perform the action.

en/glossary/conc-linux-system.title: Linux System
en/glossary/conc-linux-system.summary: A free and powerful OS, perfect for spinning up community servers.
en/glossary/conc-linux-system.content:
Linux is an open-source operating system, which means its original “recipe” is public, and anyone can peek at it, copy it, or make it even better.
In our tech workshop:

Linux is a Modular and Free Kitchen.
Unlike other kitchens where you can’t change a thing, in Linux, you can rearrange the countertops, repaint the walls, and even invent whole new ways of cooking.
It’s famous for being rock-solid and secure: once you fire up a Linux stove, it can run for years without ever needing to be turned off.


Why do we use it at Voltaje?
We use Linux because it doesn’t charge us a dime to use it, it respects our privacy, and it runs like a charm on old gear that other systems would just toss in the trash. It’s the solid ground we build our Pocket Internet → on.

Related Concepts

Operating System →
Giving an old computer a second life →
Terminal →

en/glossary/conc-local-network.title: LAN (Local Area Network)
en/glossary/conc-local-network.summary: Computer networks that don't necessarily need to be hooked up to the Internet.
en/glossary/conc-local-network.content:
A local network, or LAN (Local Area Network), is basically a bunch of gadgets (like computers, phones, printers, you name it) all hooked up together in a small spot, like your house, an office, or a building.
These networks let your devices swap things like files, printers, and even share a single internet connection. (Source: Cloudflare)
Main features of a LAN:

Limited range: LANs are built for small, cozy spaces. (Source: NinjaOne)
Connecting nearby gear: Devices link up using cables → or wireless connections → within a specific physical area. (Source: Share.google)
Sharing resources: Devices on a LAN can easily access and share files, printers, and other goodies. (Source: Servicios UNS)
Shared internet: A LAN lets you split one internet connection among several devices. (Source: Cloudflare)
Control and security: LANs make it easier to keep an eye on security and manage who gets to access what. (Source: AWS)
Speed: LANs usually zip data around much faster than those big, sprawling networks. (Source: Coltecno)

Examples of LANs:

A home network connecting your computers, smartphones, and other gadgets around the house.
An office network linking up employees’ computers and the office printer.
A school network connecting computers for both students and teachers.

(Source:OliviaWireless)
In short, a LAN is just a computer network that lets devices talk to each other and share resources in a local area. (Source:Share.google)

en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.title: 4G or LTE Connection
en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.summary: A mobile comms standard to surf the web at full speed.
en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.content:
LTE, which stands for Long Term Evolution, is the global standard for wireless communication that powers fourth-generation (4G) mobile networks. It brings much faster data transfer speeds and lower latency → compared to the old 3G days. Its main job is to get you high-speed internet on your mobile devices, making things like video streaming, quick downloads, and IoT (Internet of Things) gadgets run smooth as butter.
What’s LTE good for?


Web browsing and streaming: Lets you load websites, videos, and music faster and without that annoying buffering.


Crystal-clear calls: The Voz sobre LTE (VoLTE) tech lets you make voice calls over the LTE data network, which makes the sound quality way better and connects your calls in a snap.


Better mobile communication: Makes sending instant messages and hopping on video calls way more efficient.


Expanding IoT applications: LTE is the backbone for connecting a whole bunch of devices—like smartwatches, sensors, and home automation systems—to the internet.


Working from anywhere: It gives you the speed and stability you need for video conferences and cloud platforms, so you can get your work done from just about anywhere.


Standardization and evolution:
LTE is a long-term standard that’s still the foundation for 5G networks. It keeps evolving with versions like LTE-Advanced (LTE-A) to push even faster speeds and better performance.

en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.title: MiFi Modem
en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.summary: A portable gadget to whip up a WiFi network using mobile data.
en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.content:
A MiFi modem, also known as a portable WiFi router, is a handy little gadget that lets you set up a local WiFi network using a mobile data connection, like 4G or 5G, so all your devices can hop onto the internet wirelessly. Think of it as a pocket-sized WiFi hotspot you can take just about anywhere. (Source: Verizon)
The MiFi sets up a high-speed broadband connection that can be shared by up to ten users at once. You can hook it up to all sorts of WiFi-enabled gear: desktops, laptops, tablets, mobile phones, cameras, game consoles, and MP3 players. In many cases, like with an Apple iPad, it can save you from needing a separate data plan for the device itself, so you don’t have to shell out for an extra service.
What’s more, some of these devices can even double as a USB flash drive since they come with internal storage, and some can even be expanded with memory cards.
When you’re ready to use it, your devices connect to the MiFi network just like any other WiFi. The speeds you’ll get depend on your service plan and the type of network (like 3G or 4G) it’s latching onto. (Source: Wikipedia)

en/glossary/conc-network-agents.title: Network Agents
en/glossary/conc-network-agents.summary: Little helper programs that get computers talking to each other on their own.
en/glossary/conc-network-agents.content:
Network Agents are little programs or services (like hostapd or dnsmasq) that handle the automated chores to keep the network humming along.
In our tech kitchen:

They’re the Sous-Chefs.
While the head cook is busy prepping the meal, these helpers take care of the nitty-gritty: letting folks know the kitchen is open, handing out tickets at the door, or making sure the tables are wiped down and ready for guests.


Which agents do we use?
In your Pocket Server →, we use agents like hostapd to whip up the WiFi signal and dnsmasq so everyone gets an IP address automatically. Without them, the network admin would have to do all the heavy lifting by hand.

Related concepts

DHCP Protocol →
WiFi Signal →
How to build your Pocket Server? →

en/glossary/conc-nginx.title: Nginx Web Server (The Dispatcher)
en/glossary/conc-nginx.summary: The guy in charge of taking orders and handing out the goods to whoever asks for them.
en/glossary/conc-nginx.content:
Nginx (pronounced “en-yin-ex”) is a piece of software called a “Web Server.” Its main job is to take requests from browsers (like Chrome or Firefox) and answer back by sending over the files they’re asking for.
In our tech kitchen:

Nginx is the Delivery Rider.
When someone types an address on their phone, the Rider runs to the kitchen, grabs the prepared dish (the webpage or file), and zips it over to their screen.
It’s lightning-fast and can handle hundreds of folks at the same time without breaking a sweat.


Nicknames and Addresses
Since real addresses are long, clunky numbers that are hard to remember (called IPs), we use the DNS → system to give our delivery rider some nicknames.
Instead of telling the neighbors to look for the rider at “Street 192.168.1.15,” we tell them: “Look for solevoltaje.local.” It’s a friendly name that everyone can learn easily, just like how we use nicknames for delivery apps or for our buddies in the neighborhood.

Related Concepts

Servidor →
DNS (Apodos de Red) →
¿Cómo instalar Nginx? →

en/glossary/conc-operating-system.title: Operating System
en/glossary/conc-operating-system.summary: An Operating System (OS) is the main program that manages all the hardware and software on a computer or phone.
en/glossary/conc-operating-system.content:
An Operating System (OS) is the main program that manages all the hardware and software on a computer or phone.
In our tech kitchen:

The Operating System is the Kitchen Layout and Rulebook.
It defines where the countertops go (RAM), how to access the pantry (Hard Drive), and who has permission to use the knives (security).
It’s in charge of making sure the cook (processor) doesn’t get flustered and knows which order to prep first.


Different kitchen styles
Every operating system has its own way of organizing things:

Windows: It’s like a pre-fab, super popular kitchen. Everything comes in its place and it’s easy for most folks to use, but sometimes it can be clunky and hard to customize.
macOS (Apple): It’s a designer kitchen—very sleek and smooth—but it only works in the houses (devices) they build themselves.
Linux: This is a kitchen you can build and tweak exactly how you like it. It’s the foundation for almost all the Servidores → in the world.

Carpetas y Rutas →
Hardware →

en/glossary/conc-paquetes-internet.title: Internet Packets
en/glossary/conc-paquetes-internet.summary: The tiny chunks of data that make up everything traveling across the web, from a simple WhatsApp text to a full-blown video.
en/glossary/conc-paquetes-internet.content:
When you send a WhatsApp message, watch a YouTube video, or open a webpage, your device doesn’t send or receive that information all at once, like a solid block. It breaks it down into tiny little pieces called packets, sends them one by one (or a few at a time), and once they reach their destination, it puts them back together in order.

Why are they called “packets”?
Think of it like sending a really long letter by mail. Instead of stuffing it into one giant envelope, you cut it into a hundred pages and send each page in its own separate envelope. Each envelope has a label: “Page 34 of 100, going to address X, coming from address Y.” When they arrive, the recipient just puts all the pages in order and reads the whole letter.
That’s exactly what your router does with data: it chops it into packets, sends them across the network, and the receiving device reassembles them.

What’s inside each packet?
Every packet has two parts:

Header: The control info — where it’s coming from, where it’s going, what number it is in the sequence, and how to check that it arrived in one piece.
Payload: The actual content — those bytes of the video, the message, or the image.


What happens if a packet gets lost?
On the internet, packets don’t always make it. Sometimes one gets lost along the way because the network was congested or the signal dropped for a split second. The communication protocol (usually TCP) notices that a packet is missing and automatically asks for it to be resent. That’s why sometimes a download “stutters” for a moment and then keeps going—it was just waiting for a lost packet to catch up.

How do we measure packet loss?
Packet loss is expressed as a percentage. If you send 100 packets and only 97 arrive, you’ve got 3% loss.

























LossPerceived effect0–1%No noticeable issues1–5%Small stutters in video or voice5–10%Frequent cutouts in video callsOver 10%Very unstable connection, hard to use
In a radio enlace →, the CCQ metric tells you exactly how well those packets are arriving: a CCQ of 90% or higher means almost everything is getting through just fine.

Everything travels in packets
It doesn’t matter if it’s an HD video, a text message, a voice call, or a photo—everything gets turned into packets before it travels across the network. The only difference is how many packets there are: a high-definition video might have millions; a text message, just a few.

Router →
Señal WiFi →

en/glossary/conc-php-language.title: PHP Language
en/glossary/conc-php-language.summary: The specialized sidekick for reading and running your server's recipes.
en/glossary/conc-php-language.content:
PHP is a programming language designed specifically for building websites and applications that run on a Server →.
In our community kitchen:

PHP is a specialized sous-chef.
While HTML is like the printed menu (which never changes), PHP is the helper who knows that if a customer orders “stew,” they need to head to the pantry, grab the ingredients, and whip it up on the spot.
Thanks to PHP, the server can show different things to each person (for example, displaying your username or your personal files).


Why does it matter?
PHP is the engine behind famous tools like WordPress, Wikipedia (MediaWiki), or Facebook. In a local community network, installing PHP lets your server stop being just a simple list of files and turns it into an interactive platform where folks can post their own stories or manage their documents.

Related concepts

How to build your own Pocket Server? →
Server →
JavaScript Language →

en/glossary/conc-ping-program.title: Ping utility
en/glossary/conc-ping-program.summary: A handy tool to check the connection speed between two gadgets.
en/glossary/conc-ping-program.content:
The ping program is a network diagnostic tool used to check connectivity and latency between two devices.
Essentially, ping sends a data packet to a target device and measures how long it takes to get a reply back. This time, measured in milliseconds, is known as latency → or ping, and it’s a great way to gauge how solid your connection is.
How does it work?

The ping command sends an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) packet to the target device.
The target device, if it’s online, replies with an ICMP echo packet.
The ping tool measures how long it takes for that reply to arrive and shows it as “Round Trip Time” (RTT) in milliseconds.
Plus, ping can tell you if there’s any packet loss, which just means some of those packets didn’t make it to their destination.

What’s it used for?

Checking connectivity: Making sure a device is actually online and talking back on the network.
Measuring latency: Figuring out the quality of your connection, which is super important for online gaming and video calls.
Troubleshooting network issues: Spotting connectivity problems, packet loss, or high latency.

In short, ping is an essential tool for diagnosing and checking the quality of the network connection between two devices.

en/glossary/conc-python-language.title: Python Language
en/glossary/conc-python-language.summary: The versatile Swiss Army knife that can whip up anything from a simple script to full-blown AI.
en/glossary/conc-python-language.content:
Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world because it’s easy to read and can handle just about anything you throw at it.
In our tech workshop:

Python is the Head Chef.
It’s famous because its recipes read almost like plain English.
It can do it all: from automatically organizing your shopping list to training a “wise assistant” (Local Artificial Intelligence →).
It’s the go-to language for building AI Agents that can live right inside your pocket server.


What’s it good for?
In a community setting, Python is the perfect tool for automating tasks, analyzing weather or crop data, or running language models that help summarize important info without needing to be connected to the internet.

Related concepts

PHP Language →
JavaScript Language →
Local AI Possibilities →

en/glossary/conc-radio-enlace.title: Wireless Link
en/glossary/conc-radio-enlace.summary: A wireless internet bridge that hooks up two distant spots using directional antennas.
en/glossary/conc-radio-enlace.content:
A radio link (also called a microwave link or point-to-point link) is a system that transmits information between two distant spots using directed radio waves, just like an invisible beam of light traveling from one antenna to the other.

How does it work?
Picture two folks shouting at each other in an open field. If you cup your hands around your mouth to aim your voice, your shout carries a lot further than if you just yell in every direction. The antennas in a radio link do exactly that: they focus all that signal energy into a single beam to reach much further.
A radio link needs two antennas pointing straight at each other, with the path between them clear of any obstacles (trees, buildings, hills). We call that line of sight.

How it differs from regular WiFi






























Home WiFiRadio LinkCoverage20–50 meters1–50 kilometersDirectionAll directionsJust between two pointsUseConnecting phones and computers at homeConnecting two networks or remote communitiesAntennaSmall, omnidirectionalLarge, directional

Types of radio links

Point-to-Point (PtP): One antenna on Hill A and another on Hill B. It’s the most common and the most powerful setup.
Point-to-Multipoint (PtMP): One central antenna that beams the signal out to several “client” antennas in different spots. It works like the sun shining down on several communities at once.


Most common frequencies
In many places, the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands are unlicensed (no permit needed). They’re the same frequencies your home WiFi uses, but directional antennas turn them into long-range tools:

2.4 GHz: Reaches up to 5–8 km. Handles rain and light vegetation better. More budget-friendly.
5 GHz: Reaches up to 3–25 km. Higher speeds. Needs a clearer path. (Depends on the antenna’s size and power).


What’s it used for in rural communities?

Bringing internet from a spot that has a signal to a village that doesn’t.
Connecting one organization’s office to another several kilometers away.
Building a community network where the cost of the service is shared among several families.


Key terms

RSSI: Tells you how strong the signal is arriving. Measured in dBm. The sweet spot: between -45 and -65 dBm.
CCQ: Measures connection quality as a percentage. Anything above 90% is solid.
Fresnel Zone: The “bubble” of space that needs to be clear around the radio beam so the signal doesn’t get degraded.
PoE (Power over Ethernet): A system that powers the antenna through the same network cable.
dBi: The unit that measures gain (focusing power) of an antenna. The higher the dBi, the further it reaches.
