WiFi Signal →
Router →
4G Antenna →
Yagi Antenna →

en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.title: RAM Memory
en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.summary: It's your computer's immediate workspace, just like a kitchen countertop.
en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.content:
RAM (Random Access Memory) is the place where your computer keeps the information it’s using right this second.
To make it easy to picture, imagine your computer is a kitchen:

The RAM is your countertop.
The bigger the countertop, the more ingredients (programs) you can have out and ready to chop without things falling on the floor or getting cluttered.
The processor is the cook, grabbing whatever they need from the counter.


How does it work?
When you open a program (like your browser or a document), the computer pulls it out of the “pantry” (the hard drive) and sets it on the “counter” (the RAM).
The catch is that RAM is a kitchen hand with a short-term memory: it’s incredibly fast at handing you what you need, but the moment you turn off the stove (the computer), it wipes the counter clean and forgets everything that was there. That’s why, if you don’t “save” your work to the hard drive, it’s gone for good.

Why does it matter?
If you’ve got plenty of RAM, you can have a bunch of pots on the stove and chop several ingredients all at once. If you’re running low, the cook has to keep putting things back in the pantry and pulling them out again every time they’re needed, which makes the whole lunch (your work) take a lot longer.

Related concepts

Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
Operating System →
Swap Memory →

en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.title: Raspberry Pi
en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.summary: A tiny, low-cost computer perfect for tinkering, learning, and building your own projects.
en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.content:
What is it?
A Raspberry Pi is a credit-card-sized computer that you can tinker with and set up however you like.
Out of the box, it doesn’t come with a keyboard, mouse, or monitor, but you can hook those up—and plenty of other peripherals—without breaking a sweat.
Its “hard drive” is a MicroSD → card, where you’ll install a version of Linux → optimized for these little boards. This gives you a super portable computer that sips electricity and can handle just about anything you’d normally do on a desktop PC.
How to power up your Raspberry Pi?
To get your Raspberry Pi running, you need to plug it into a power source.
The most common way is using a USB to microUSB or USB-C cable (depending on your model) plugged into a USB power adapter. Just make sure that adapter is putting out the right voltage and current for your specific Pi model.
Steps:

Find the power port: Older models, like the Raspberry Pi 3 and earlier, use a microUSB port, while the newer ones, like the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5, use USB-C.
Plug in the power adapter: Connect your USB power adapter to the wall outlet and then plug the corresponding USB cable into your Raspberry Pi.
Check the power: If everything is hooked up right, your Raspberry Pi should fire up. Most models have little indicator lights to let you know it’s getting juice.

Keep in mind:

Voltage and current: The Raspberry Pi needs a 5V power supply. The current you need depends on the model, but for something like a Raspberry Pi 4, we generally recommend between 2.5A and 3A. (Source: Bret).
Phone chargers: While some phone chargers might do the trick, it’s always better to use a power adapter specifically designed for the Raspberry Pi. It keeps things running smoothly and saves you from power-related headaches.
USB Hubs: If you’re planning to plug a bunch of USB gadgets into your Pi, think about using a powered USB hub so you don’t starve the board of power.
Batteries: If you’re looking to run your Pi off a battery, make sure you use a DC/DC converter to step the battery voltage up to 5V.
Raspberry Pi Pico: You can power the Raspberry Pi Pico with an external battery pack connected via a microUSB to USB cable.

en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.title: RG6 Cable
en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.summary: A type of coaxial cable used for TV and internet signals.
en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.content:
An RG6 cable is a type of coaxial cable → mainly used for piping cable TV, satellite, and internet signals, along with some high-definition video setups.
It’s well-regarded for its ability to handle higher frequencies and keep signal loss to a minimum, making it a solid go-to for both indoor and outdoor jobs.
Key features:

Center conductor: Usually, an RG6 cable sports a copper center conductor, sometimes copper-clad steel.
Dielectric insulation: An insulating material that keeps the center conductor separated from the shielding mesh.
Shielding: RG6 cable packs a layer of shielding to protect the signal from electromagnetic interference (EMI) and noise. It can be single, double (foil and braid), or quad-shielded.
Impedance: Typically 75 ohms, which is the standard impedance for most video and TV applications.
Applications: It’s used to hook up antennas, cable boxes, satellite dishes, and to carry internet and TV signals.
Advantages: It offers better signal quality and less signal loss compared to other coaxial cables like the RG59, especially for high-frequency and long-distance runs.

In short, the RG6 cable is a versatile, high-performance coaxial cable, perfect for transmitting video and data signals across different setups and distances.

en/glossary/conc-router.title: Router
en/glossary/conc-router.summary: The gadget that manages the traffic flow in your network.
en/glossary/conc-router.content:
A Router is a device that connects different networks and decides which path data should take to reach its destination.
In our tech kitchen:

The Router is The Expediter.
Its job is to take the dishes coming out of the kitchen and know exactly which table (phone or computer) they need to go to, without them getting cold or lost along the way.
If two people order stew at the same time, the expediter makes sure each one gets theirs correctly.


How does it help the community?
The router allows many neighbors to connect to the same Local Network → at the same time. By acting as the “Expediter,” it manages the traffic so everyone has a smooth experience, sharing the Bandwidth → fairly.

Related concepts

Local Network →
WiFi Signal →
DHCP Protocol →

en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.title: SD Memory Card
en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.summary: A tiny card to stash your photos, videos, and files on your gadgets.
en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.content:
A MicroSD card is a tiny, portable storage device.
Sometimes folks just call them SD cards, but it’s better to get the names right based on their size: SD (the big ones), MiniSD (the middle ones), and MicroSD (the little guys).
It’s handy to know the class of the memory card, as that tells you how fast it reads and writes data. Generally, it’s a good idea to stick with Class 10 cards to make sure you’ve got decent speed and your devices won’t choke when they’re trying to get to your saved files.

en/glossary/conc-server.title: Server
en/glossary/conc-server.summary: A beast of a machine that dishes out services and data to other rigs.
en/glossary/conc-server.content:
A server is a type of computer or computing system built to dish out services, resources, or information to other gadgets or folks over a network →.
Think of it as the middleman that takes requests and passes them along to other machines or individual users. These services can include storing files, wrangling databases, hosting websites, and a whole lot more.
At its heart, a server is just a beefy computer designed to handle heaps of data and tackle complex tasks efficiently for a bunch of users all at once.
Some common examples of servers you’ll run into:

Web servers: They store and serve up web pages.
Mail servers: They handle the heavy lifting of sending and receiving emails.
Database servers: They store and manage big ol’ piles of data.
File servers: They let you store and share files with everyone.
Application servers: They run apps for multiple users.

Depending on what they’re up to, we can break them down into:

Test servers: A test server, sometimes called a staging or pre-production server, is a separate sandbox used to test and kick the tires on apps or websites before they go live on a production server (the one the real users see). The big difference is the goal: the test server is for thorough tinkering, while the production server is for the real deal.
Production server: Its whole job is to serve up apps and websites to the end users who are actually interacting with them. It holds the real user data and the live, running application. It’s open to the public or a specific group of users.

Servers are the backbone of the internet and business networks, keeping the conversation going and letting information flow between different devices and users.

en/glossary/conc-simcard.title: SIM Card
en/glossary/conc-simcard.summary: That tiny smart card that hooks your phone up to the mobile network.
en/glossary/conc-simcard.content:
A SIM card, or Subscriber Identity Module, is a little removable card you pop into smartphones → and other gadgets to identify them on a cellular network and get them hooked up to services like calls, texts, and data.
Think of it as a digital key that lets your device talk to your carrier’s network and proves you’re the one holding the phone.
What does a SIM card actually do?

Identification: The SIM holds unique info about you, like your phone number and the details of your service plan.
Authentication: It lets your device securely handshake with your carrier’s network.
Service Access: It unlocks the ability to make calls, send texts, and use mobile data.
Storage: It can also stash contacts, SMS messages, and other bits of user data.

How have SIM cards evolved over the years?

Original SIM: About the size of a credit card.
MiniSIM: A bit smaller than the original.
MicroSIM: More compact than the MiniSIM, famously used in devices like the iPhone 4.
NanoSIM: The tiniest one, used in most modern smartphones.
eSIM: A SIM built right into the device, letting you switch carriers without ever needing to swap out a physical card.

en/glossary/conc-smartphone.title: Smartphone
en/glossary/conc-smartphone.summary: A smart gadget with internet access and a bunch of apps to keep you connected.
en/glossary/conc-smartphone.content:
A mobile phone, or cell phone as we often call it, is a handy portable electronic device that lets you make and receive calls wirelessly, hooking into a mobile network.
Beyond just the basics of calling and texting, modern mobile phones—especially smartphones—are like Swiss Army knives, packing in internet access, apps, cameras, media players, and a whole lot more.

Mobile communication: The bread and butter of a mobile phone is letting you chat with folks from afar over a wireless network.
Portability: What makes these gadgets special is that you can carry them anywhere and use them on the go, as long as you’ve got a signal.
Extra features: Smartphones, in particular, are loaded with extras: web browsing, music and video playback, snapping photos and videos, and running all sorts of apps.
Mobile networks: Mobile phones connect to mobile communication networks →, which use base stations to bounce radio signals around and keep devices talking to each other.
Evolution: Mobile phones have come a long way from simple call-only bricks to the multi-talented smartphones we use today, thanks to tech breakthroughs like shrinking down components, better networks, and smarter software and apps.

en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.title: SSH Protocol
en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.summary: A secure way to remote into your server and tinker with it from another machine.
en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.content:
SSH (Secure Shell) is a protocol that lets you access and manage a computer or server remotely through an encrypted, secure connection.
In our tech kitchen:

SSH is The Master Key.
It lets the kitchen manager slip in through the back door without having to be there in person.
Most importantly, this key travels inside a sealed envelope (encrypted); nobody along the way can see what the manager is doing or swipe the password.


What’s it for?
In our Pocket Server →, we use SSH to install software, organize folders, or fix hiccups right from our own chair, using the Terminal →. It’s the go-to tool for tinkerers working from afar.

Related concepts

Terminal →
Server →
Firewall →

en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.title: SSID Identifier
en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.summary: The public name that identifies a WiFi wireless network.
en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.content:
The SSID, or Service Set Identifier, is the name that identifies a Wi-Fi network →.
It’s the name you see when you’re scanning for available wireless networks on your gear, like your phone or laptop. It lets folks tell one Wi-Fi network apart from another in the area so they can hook up to the right one. (Source: Lenovo)
To put it plainly, the SSID is just the name of a Wi-Fi network, like “Juan’s Place” or “Starbucks_Wi-Fi.” Your devices use the SSID to sniff out and connect to the right network. Just keep in mind that the SSID doesn’t provide security on its own; network security is handled by protocols like WPA2 or WPA3. (Source: Kaspersky)
In short, the SSID is the handle that identifies a Wi-Fi network and makes it easy for everyone to connect to the network they’re looking for. (Source: Fortinet)

en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.title: Storage (Hard Drive & SSD)
en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.summary: The spot where you stash all your data so it doesn't vanish when you pull the plug.
en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.content:
Storage is the part of the computer responsible for keeping your files, photos, programs, and the operating system safe and sound permanently.
If we stick with the kitchen analogy:

Storage is your pantry or a big warehouse outside the house.
That’s where you keep the sacks of food (your files) so they stay put even when you’re done cooking.
When you need something to cook with, you grab it from the pantry and put it on the countertop (the RAM Memory →).


Types of storage
As technology moves forward, we’ve gone from slow-but-huge “pantries” to lightning-fast “refrigerators.”
HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
This is the traditional hard drive. It works with spinning platters and a needle that physically “reads” the information. Think of it like a huge, cheap warehouse, but a bit slow. It’s still the best bet for storing massive amounts of files (like in Servers →) because you get a lot of space for not much money.
SSD (Solid State Drive)
This is the solid-state drive. It doesn’t have any moving parts; it uses chips (just like USB drives). It’s way faster than an HDD. Imagine the pantry is now right next to the countertop, making it super easy to grab what you need. Your computer boots up in seconds!
NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express)
This is the latest evolution of the SSD. They’re tiny and plug directly into the computer’s “brain.” It’s like having an automated system that puts the ingredients right into the cook’s hand instantly.

The real world and technology
Technology was designed by mimicking how we humans organize ourselves. Networks, for example, are like water pipes: information flows from one place to another. Servers are like community warehouses where we all store things (the cloud). Understanding these concepts helps us see that the digital world is just a translation of what we already know how to do in the kitchen or the workshop.

Related concepts

RAM Memory →
Server →
SD Memory →

en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.title: SWAP Memory
en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.summary: Disk space that gives your RAM a hand when things get crowded.
en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.content:
SWAP memory, also known as swap space or virtual memory, is a section of the hard drive → that an operating system → uses as if it were RAM memory → when the physical RAM is running low.
Think of it as an extension of your RAM. It lets the system shuffle less-used data from the RAM over to the hard drive, freeing up space in the RAM for the tasks that actually need to get moving right now. (Source: Aprendo Linux)
In simpler terms, swap memory is like a temporary storage shed on your hard drive that the OS uses when it’s run out of room in the main workshop (the RAM). When a program gets greedy for more memory, the OS can move the stuff you aren’t currently using into the swap space, clearing out the RAM so you can keep your programs running smoothly.
Why do we use it?

Preventing memory crashes: When the RAM is packed to the brim, the OS can lean on the swap to keep your apps from freezing up or acting wonky.
Running more programs: Swap memory lets you juggle more programs at once than your physical RAM would normally allow.
Hibernation: On some systems, swap memory is the go-to spot for saving the system’s state when you put it into hibernation.

How does it work?

RAM running low: When the RAM gets full, the OS spots the data that hasn’t been touched in a while.
Moving to swap: That “dusty” data gets moved from the RAM to the swap space on the hard drive.
Freeing up RAM: Now that the RAM has some breathing room, it can handle other processes that need immediate attention.
Accessing the swap: When you finally need that data back, the OS pulls it from the swap and loads it back into the RAM, often shuffling other less-used data out to make room.

Pros and cons:

Pros: Lets you run more programs and keeps things from crashing when your RAM is maxed out.
Cons: Accessing swap memory (on the hard drive) is a whole lot slower than accessing RAM. If you rely on it too much, your system is going to feel sluggish.

Swap memory is a handy tool for managing resources, especially if you’re working with a machine that doesn’t have a ton of RAM. Just keep in mind: it’s a lifesaver, but if you lean on it too hard, your system’s performance is going to take a hit.

en/glossary/conc-system-folders.title: Folders and Paths
en/glossary/conc-system-folders.summary: The filing and labeling system to keep your files from getting lost in the machine.
en/glossary/conc-system-folders.content:
Folders (or directories) and Paths are just how the operating system keeps things tidy so nothing gets lost in the shuffle.
In our tech kitchen:

Think of it as the Shelving and Jar System.
A Path is the exact address of where you stashed something. For example: Pantry > Top Shelf > Salt Jar.
On your computer, a path looks like this: /home/usuario/documentos/foto.jpg.


How are they organized?
Every system has its own “way of tidying up”:

On Windows: Everything starts with a letter, usually the C: trunk. (Ex: C:\Usuarios\David\Fotos).
On Linux: No letters here. Everything sprouts from a common root called / (slash). Think of it like a big tree where every branch is a folder. (Always picture it as a tree).
The server folder: By convention, the stuff the world can see on your server usually lives in a folder called /var/www/. It’s like the kitchen counter!


Related concepts

Sistema Operativo →
Sistema Linux →
Servidor de Bolsillo →

en/glossary/conc-terminal.title: Terminal or console
en/glossary/conc-terminal.summary: A handy tool to boss your computer around using text commands.
en/glossary/conc-terminal.content:
In computing, a terminal or console is basically the gadget you use to hook up to a computer. In more technical terms, it’s a text-based user interface that lets you chat with an operating system → or an application.
Back in the day, this meant an actual physical rig with a keyboard and a monitor. Nowadays, it usually refers to a piece of software that mimics that old-school setup—a program that lets us talk directly to our operating system without needing all those fancy graphical interfaces.
Let’s break it down a bit more:

Terminal: This is the interface where you run commands, wrangle applications, and see the output in a text environment. These days, it’s mostly used to describe the software program that emulates a physical terminal, letting you interact with the OS through commands.
Console: Traditionally, a console was a physical piece of hardware—like a keyboard and monitor plugged straight into the computer. Nowadays, the term can also refer to the terminal interface used to manage and configure systems, and it’s also used for the management interfaces of cloud services.
Difference between console and terminal: Even though folks often use the terms interchangeably, the console can refer to the physical hardware, while the terminal is the software emulating that hardware. In practice, both terms are used to describe the command-line interface where we type in our instructions for the system.

In short, both the terminal and the console are interfaces that let you communicate with the operating system, whether it’s through a physical device (historically) or a software program (these days).

References

Terminal on Wikipedia

en/glossary/conc-umts.title: UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System)
en/glossary/conc-umts.summary: A third-generation tech for mobile data transmission.
en/glossary/conc-umts.content:
UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System) is a third-generation (3G) mobile technology that brought us high-speed internet and multimedia services, stepping up as the successor to GSM (2G) →.
Its main job is to deliver broadband wireless communications with faster download and upload speeds than the old networks, making web browsing, video calls, and multimedia apps run a whole lot smoother.
(Source: 1NCE)
What’s UMTS good for?

Mobile broadband internet: It lets you connect devices to the internet at speeds way faster than what we had back in the 2G days.
Multimedia services: It handles high-speed data transmission, which is the secret sauce for bandwidth-hungry apps like video calls, downloading media, and zippy web browsing.
Better quality and capacity: It offers a much cleaner connection, almost like a landline, and lets more folks hop on the network at the same time without it getting clogged up.
A bridge to 4G/LTE: Even though it’s 3G tech, upgrades like HSPA (High Speed Packet Access) and HSPA+ pushed its limits closer to 4G (LTE) territory, giving that old infrastructure a longer lease on life.
Plays nice with all sorts of gear: It supports a wider range of gadgets and apps, including those “Internet of Things” (IoT) devices that are always thirsty for data.

Key features of UMTS


CDMA tech: It uses W-CDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) to push data at high speeds across a wider radio frequency band.


Network parts: It’s made up of the Radio Access Network (UTRAN), the Core Network (CN), and the User Equipment (UE).


Improvements over GSM:
It started off offering speeds up to 2 Mbps, but with those HSPA and HSPA+ upgrades, it climbed up to 42 Mbps or more—leaving those old GSM networks in the dust.


Referencias | References

WirelessLogic
Avance Digital
Emnify
ScienceDirect

en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.title: USB Connection
en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.summary: The universal language for hooking up and powering your gadgets.
en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.content:
The USB (Universal Serial Bus) is the standard that lets almost any electronic gadget talk to another. Think of it as a smart outlet that doesn’t just pass power, but also information (photos, music, documents).
Following our kitchen analogy:

The USB port is like a wall outlet, but one that works for the blender, the radio, and even for charging your phone.
Back in the day, every appliance brand had its own weird plug; USB came along so everyone could use the same one.


The history of standards
At first, USB was a mess: there was USB-A (the big rectangular one), micro-USB (the one on old phones), and mini-USB. Each one had a different shape, and you never had the cable you actually needed.
Brands wanted you to buy their specific cables, which created tons of electronic waste (cables that are now useless).

The power of the people and USB-C
USB-C is that small, rounded connector that you can plug in either way (it doesn’t have a “right side up” or “upside down”). What makes it special isn’t just the tech, but how it became the standard:

Grassroots movements: Groups of people, consumer organizations, and movements like “Right to Repair” put pressure on governments.
Laws for the planet: In places like the European Union, laws were created to force all brands (even the stubborn ones) to use a single universal charger: USB-C.
Result: Thanks to people coming together to demand less waste and more convenience, today we can use one single cable for our laptop, phone, and headphones. A huge win for the collective over the market!


What’s it for?

Power: Charging your devices.
Data: Moving files between a Memoria USB → and your computer.
Connecting tools: Keyboards, mice, cameras, and even fans.


Related concepts

Memoria USB →
Almacenamiento (Disco Duro y SSD) →
Hardware →

en/glossary/conc-username.title: Username
en/glossary/conc-username.summary: A username is a unique string of characters that identifies you in a computer system, like a social network, a website, or an app.
en/glossary/conc-username.content:
A username is a unique string of characters that identifies you in a computer system, like a social network, a website, or an app.
Think of it as your digital handle; you use it to log in and get into your account, usually paired with a password to prove it’s really you. (Source: Dashlane)
In a nutshell, a username:

Identifies you uniquely: It’s how the system tells one person from another, keeping things organized and making sure you get the right permissions.
Is your key to log in: It’s how you introduce yourself to the system so you can access your account and all your stuff.
Can be public or private: In some places, your username is out there for everyone to see, while in others, it’s kept under wraps.
Has to be one-of-a-kind: No two folks can have the same username in the same system—otherwise, things would get messy fast.
Can be alphanumeric: Usually, it’s a mix of letters and numbers, though some systems let you throw in special characters like underscores or dots.
Is not your password: Your password is the secret lock that keeps your account safe, while your username is just your public ID tag.

en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.title: WhatsApp
en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.summary: A messaging app for sending texts, voice notes, and making calls.
en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.content:
WhatsApp is an instant messaging and calling app owned by Meta. It lets you send messages, hop on voice or video calls, and share files, all over the internet.
It’s a go-to tool for both personal chats and getting business done.
You can use it to send text, voice notes, and videos, make voice and video calls, and share things like photos, documents, locations, and contacts.
While most folks know it for keeping in touch with friends and family, there’s a version built for business called WhatsApp Business. It’s handy for chatting with customers, managing sales, and offering support.
Heads up! WhatsApp is usually included in most mobile data plans, but keep an eye out—you might still see extra charges for data usage or downloads that aren’t covered by your specific plan.
It works on different sistemas operativos →, like Android and iOS, and there’s a web version too.
The app keeps your personal chats, calls, and media safe with end-to-end encryption. That’s just a fancy way of saying that only you and the person you’re talking to can see what’s being shared.
WhatsApp’s interface is straightforward and easy to get the hang of, making it a breeze to connect with people, especially those already in your contact list.

en/glossary/conc-wifi.title: WiFi Signal
en/glossary/conc-wifi.summary: It's the wireless connection that lets data fly through the air.
en/glossary/conc-wifi.content:
WiFi (or Wireless Fidelity) is a technology that lets you connect devices to a network without needing cables, using radio waves instead.
In our tech kitchen:

WiFi is like The Kitchen Aroma.
When the servidor → has the info ready, it “wafts” it through the air, just like the smell of a good hearty stew.
Your phone or computer is like the “nose” that catches that scent and connects to grab the goods.
If you wander too far away or there are thick walls in the way, the aroma (the signal) gets weaker until it fades away completely.


How to boost the aroma?
To make sure the WiFi reaches every corner of your community, it’s important to place the Router → up high and clear of obstacles—just like you’d set a steaming pot near an open window so the smell invites everyone in.

Related concepts

Router →
Red Local →
Ancho de Banda →

en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.title: Yagi-Uda Antenna
en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.summary: A directional antenna built to pull in signals from way out there.
en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.content:
A Yagi antenna → is a type of directional antenna, famous for its high gain and ability to focus a signal in one specific direction.
Think of it as having a main backbone called the boom (or active element) and a bunch of shorter bits, called directors and reflectors, lined up along it.
How does it work?

Active element: This is the heart of the operation. It’s the one hooked up directly to your transmitter or receiver, where the main signal gets sent or picked up.
Directors: These are the shorter rods sitting in front of the active element, pointing toward where you want your signal to go. They help “aim” the signal, boosting the antenna’s gain.
Reflector: This one is longer than the active element and sits behind it. It acts like a mirror for radio waves, bouncing them forward to concentrate the signal where you need it and cutting down on interference from behind. That’s what gives the antenna its punch.

Key features:

Directivity: Yagi antennas are laser-focused. They’re much better at sending or grabbing signals when you know exactly where the source is.
Gain: Gain is basically how well the antenna squeezes the signal into a tight beam. Yagis have high gain, which is why they’re great for reaching out over long distances.
Size: The size depends on the frequency you’re working with, but generally, they’re a lot more compact and manageable than big parabolic dishes.

What are they good for?

TV and radio reception: You’ve probably seen these on rooftops. They’re the go-to for pulling in a clear signal, especially if you’re out in the sticks where coverage is spotty.
Wireless comms: They’re solid for point-to-point or point-to-multipoint links where you need a dedicated, directional connection.
Ham radio: Radio enthusiasts love Yagis for long-distance chatting and radio contests.
Radar systems: In some military and radar setups, Yagis are used to focus and steer those radar beams.

In short, the Yagi antenna is a trusty tool in any tinkerer’s kit for boosting signal reception and transmission, thanks to its knack for being highly directional and packing a lot of gain.

en/inspire/insp-big-questions.title: Everything Starts with a Big Question
en/inspire/insp-big-questions.summary: An experience to spark curiosity and learn as a group.
en/inspire/insp-big-questions.content:
Download this solution to use it offline
This is an experience designed to spark curiosity in anyone, anywhere, and get them using the Internet in groups to learn.
If you like it, you can download SOLE Voltaje Offline and take it to places with little or no connectivity. Enjoy!
So, how can I know something I don’t know?
Let us tell you a little story about how we learn.
[Taken from SOLE Colombia (2019) A conversation with Sugata Mitra]

  
  

Taken from SOLE Colombia (2019) A conversation with Sugata Mitra


Read the transcript
Historically, if you wanted to know something, the traditional way was to find someone who knew it and ask them. That’s not very practical because you can’t always find the person in question or you can’t go see them, so it used to take a long time to learn things. All of this changed thanks to writing. People could write down what they knew, and if you wanted to know it, you could find it and read it.
But some people opposed writing. Surprisingly, the most famous opponent of writing was Socrates, the Greek philosopher. His objection was that you can read what someone has written, but you can’t ask them questions, and sometimes it’s not easy to find what has been written either. That problem was solved with libraries, where many people’s writings are kept in one place, but even that had a problem because, first of all, you have to find the library and go to it. Second, if you are reading something and have a question, you have no one to ask.
This started to change thanks to the Internet. Now, you can find what anyone writes at any time, and while you’re reading, if you have a question, (usually) you can find someone to ask. So, the two problems Socrates had—namely: 1) where do I find the writings and 2) who do I ask if I have a doubt—seem to have been solved thanks to the Internet.
To this, we must add one last thing: if reading is done with many people together, everyone can ask each other. Therefore, a group of learners can build a very inexpensive learning space with little material available where they have a computer, the Internet, and can ask each other questions. In other words, it turns out to be very easy to create a self-learning environment, and that is what we call a Self-Organized Learning Environment, or SOLE.
The idea is very simple and powerful: it is possible for learners to create their own learning environment using the Internet!


So, if you wanted to know the answer to something you don’t know, how would you do it?
Think of anyone, like you, young or old, anywhere in the world who wants to answer a question they’ve always had and never been able to solve: their possibilities for learning, from the oldest to the most recent, could be:

Step 1 → Ask someone who knows: Oral tradition

Look for someone around you who knows the answer to your Big Question. It could be a friend, your parents or grandparents, a teacher, or a neighbor.
If they don’t have the answer, ask them who might, and travel together with this question to ask that other person.
This is how most ancestral knowledge is passed down, even today.

Step 2 → Look in writings: Textual transmission

Where are there writings on the topic of that question? At home, at a neighbor’s house, at school, at the public library, or somewhere in the nearest town?
Go and look for them together. Like in the story of libraries, knowledge can be passed down in writing, and librarians or teachers might know which books your answer could be in.
Imagine… This is how we’ve learned since writing was invented, and it has gradually become more equitable as public education becomes universal. However, there are still many people who do not have access to it.
Did you find the answer?


Yes!
Great! And did any new questions come up? Go back to asking someone who knows, or go back to looking in writings that you have within reach.


No.
Then where else can we find it? I suppose if you are reading this, it might sound obvious that you can search on the Internet. Just keep in mind that, in 2024, half the people in the world DO NOT have access to the Internet.



Step 3 → Search on the Internet: Digital interconnection

Doing a search on the Internet is like having the biggest library in the world in your pocket. Google or any other search engine where you type your Big Question is like the librarian who searches through all the texts, videos, audios, and other content on the Internet and offers them to you so you can explore them.
However, I don’t know if you know, but searching on the Internet on your own is difficult. There are many answers to your Big Question; some are better than others, but there are also many wrong ones. There are even lies written by people or even machines, like those called Artificial Intelligence (AI). Learning to judge that sea of information in order to learn is quite an art. The same thing happens when you ask someone who knows or look in writings.
The best way to overcome this is to doubt, be curious, and ask new questions. This is what scientists and artists do; they don’t just settle for the first thing they learn. Although sometimes learning alone—being self-taught—is demanding, regardless of whether you have access to all the information.

Step 4 → Search on the Internet in a group: SOLEing

At SOLE Colombia, we have discovered that many people who don’t have access to good education can learn to learn almost anything using the Internet in a group because they can doubt, be curious, and ask new questions together. It’s like being self-taught, but in a group, which is not only easier, more fun, and more powerful than using the Internet alone, but it also proposes a new way of being together. We call this SOLEing.

WHAT IS SOLE?
SOLE (Self-Organized Learning Environments) is a disruptive learning methodology that empowers communities to develop autonomy, collaboration, deep learning, and, most importantly, to solve real-life problems!
A SOLE session is simple. You need a space with people, a few computers with Internet access, and Big Questions. In a SOLE session, learners self-organize to find answers to the questions using the Internet, without the need for a teacher.
WHAT IS THE GRANNY CLOUD?
Along with SOLE is the concept of the Granny. Research has shown that limited intervention from an untrained facilitator can promote thriving learning processes. A Granny’s role consists of sparking curiosity, asking questions, listening carefully, and providing a warm environment. The Granny Cloud is a network of volunteers from all professions and walks of life who connect remotely with SOLEs to co-facilitate and offer participants the opportunity to experience worlds very far from their own.
And what if you don’t have the Internet?
If you don’t have the Internet, you will always be able to know more using the first options, even if they have the difficulties that Sugata Mitra mentions in the video.
However, at SOLE Colombia
In SOLE Voltaje, we have the idea that using the Internet in a group to learn is a way to have new, healthy human relationships that will allow us not only to change the way we learn and dialogue but also the way we create the world we want together. Even more, it will change the shape of the Internet to be more inclusive, diverse, and equitable. But for this, it is important that everyone can access the Internet.

en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.title: How to build memory in a SOLE Lab?
en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.summary: Purpose: To nimbly gather the history of the Boca de Camarones SOLE Lab from the perspective of each group of collaborators (Boca de Camarones Community, SOLE Colombia, and the Internet Society Foundation).
en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.content:
Purpose: To nimbly gather the history of the Boca de Camarones SOLE Lab from the perspective of each group of collaborators (Boca de Camarones Community, SOLE Colombia, and the Internet Society Foundation).
Instructions
In groups, tell the life story of the SOLE Lab. On colored panels, draw:

1st panel: The beginning. Why did the idea or need arise?
Last panel: What is the SOLE Lab today, and how does it feel to have it?
Intermediate panels: Milestones or key moments in the SOLE Lab’s history.


Step 1 → How do our SOLE Lab stories connect?

On a canvas, we’ll organize the drawings, connecting the stories with yarn.

Step 2 → How does my life story connect with the SOLE Lab’s history?

Developing the device

The experiences narrated below are the result of what each group shared about their time with the SOLE LAB. To avoid twisting their words, we use ““ to quote exactly what the person said. In other parts of the text, we paraphrase, aiming to stay true to what was expressed throughout the session.
We use the word milestone to refer to those events or happenings that are significant to the person telling the story.

Boca de Camarones Community
Elainer:
Milestone 1: “The SOLE LAB started back when I worked at the Puntos Vive Digital.” Elainer was an ICT manager. Once that project ended for him, the idea of having a SOLE LAB popped up.
Milestone 2: He remembers running a SOLE about what internet connection actually is.
Milestone 3: When he heard the story of the SOLE LAB, he realized it could be the starting point for sharing with the community. One event he remembers with joy is the SOLE Festival.
Milestone 4: “For my work, I had to do a webinar. I remembered what I learned in SOLE and I was able to do it. The grandmother helped me lose my fear of screens.”
Milestone 5: Elainer mentions that it’s not just SOLEs happening in that space. The SOLE LAB has been used as a point of interest for tourists. Tourists rest and connect to the internet; plus, they get told the story of the space.
Caril:
Milestone 6: Caril tells us everything she learned about shrimp thanks to a SOLE. “Thanks to a great question, we learned about shrimp: what does a shrimp eat?”
Marcelo and Ana María:
Milestone 7: The two of them organized a SOLE with the kids. They say it was very exciting for the community.

Marcelo works with the kids in the community and has ideas that could generate economic sustainability, like using video games or offering the connection space to foreigners.
Marcelo remembers when the materials for building the SOLE LAB started arriving and everything that process entailed. For his part, he remembers how rewarding it was to help with the construction and see it finished.
Ana María takes care of the space, the garden, and the SOLE LAB. Ana María mentions that they have managed and held bingos and other activities of interest to the community.

Internet Society Foundation
Gustavo
Milestone 1: “Everyone should have internet access.” That’s why ISOC grants exist, where they care about the internet being used in a communal and open way. That’s why the SOLE LAB is a space of great interest to him and the mission of his work.
Milestone 2: For Gustavo, the SOLE LAB is a way to connect the internet and people.
Milestone 3: For him, the SOLE LAB should have a flag showing it’s a space for democratizing knowledge.
Milestone 4: “We think differently, but our stories connect.”
SOLE COLOMBIA
Milestone 1 [2015]: Sanjay wondered what a library of the future with internet, mediated by the SOLE methodology, would look like.
Milestone 2 [2017]: They met Elainer and got to know the Puntos Vive Digital, where he worked.
Milestone 3 [2018]: The first version of the SOLE LAB was made in La Sevillana.
Milestone 4 [2021]: The first SOLE LAB was funded through the Internet Society call for proposals.
Milestone 5 [2022]: Sanjay and Belén traveled to Boca de Camarones and started managing the design and construction of the first SOLE LAB.
Milestone 6 [2023]: “Now the first SOLE LAB in Boca de Camarones is a reality. It exists, it works, and we want it to be sustainable for the community.”
Findings and learnings

All the SOLE LAB stories connect people, histories, and affections. It’s interesting how people’s tastes and passions are boosted within the community and in SOLE.
Running a SOLE LAB involves synergy and the meeting of several common wills.
The stories go beyond the SOLE LAB; in other words, this space becomes a pretext for living and coexisting in new ways.
Having been part of the project generates pride and dignity.

en/inspire/insp-fish-game.title: Resources for one, resources for all
en/inspire/insp-fish-game.summary: We learned to play to reflect on how we use common goods.
en/inspire/insp-fish-game.content:
Did you know you can use games to build community agreements? 💭
In the Fish Game, we learn through a simple but powerful experience: the more we fish for ourselves, the fewer fish are left for everyone else. But when we work together, we can make sure there’s enough for everyone.
This game is a metaphor for real life. The fish aren’t just fish. 🌱 They represent the resources we share: internet, land, food, even the air we breathe!
Think of it this way: imagine sharing an internet plan with your neighbors. If we all use it mindfully, we can make it go further and benefit the whole community. But if we only look out for our own interests, the resource runs dry fast and hurts everyone. Are you ready to make agreements with your community?

en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.title: How to change the world from your living room? Meet the Granny Cloud
en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.summary: Discover how to support learning with a loving touch.
en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
What is The Granny Cloud?
The Granny Cloud is a concept born alongside the SOLE idea. It captures the spirit of those folks who support learning with a loving gaze—the ones who nudge us to learn in subtle ways, offering warm encouragement, asking just the right questions, and marveling at our discoveries.
These are people who have a blast learning, are naturally curious, and truly enjoy interacting with learners. Sugata Mitra called this perspective “the Granny gaze.” Suneeta Kulkarni, his research partner, formed The Granny Cloud, and at SOLE Colombia, we’ve picked up that torch and legacy to build La Nube de Abuelitas (The Granny Cloud) in Spanish.
Who makes it up?
We are volunteers—men and women—from all over the globe. We have Grannies in Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Mexico, Colombia, the United States, Peru, Chile, Vietnam… you can find Grannies just about anywhere!
There is a Granny Cloud Coordinator who manages the sessions, handles scheduling, and keeps everyone in the loop about who will be attending each session that requests a Granny.
Every year, right when projects kick off, new Grannies join the fold. They discover their own motivation, and we train them in the methodology so they can “SOLE” and enjoy this incredibly rewarding role.
How can you become a Granny?
All you need to be a Granny is a desire to connect with communities learning through the SOLE Methodology. Need some tools? You can download the Granny Manual and find stories about our Grannies on the SOLE Colombia website. You can also request to join The Granny Cloud via this form, and we’ll get in touch to tell you all about it.
Keep an eye on our social media and other platforms (take a peek at our website) to find out when the next costurero (gathering) is called and what the schedules are for upcoming SOLEs. Don’t miss out!

en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.title: Grandma's Cloud: what happens when the connection drops
en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.summary: Communication and presence don't need a lot of bells and whistles.
en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
There’s a question I get asked a lot when I tell people what an Abuelita does in a SOLE: what happens if there’s no connection? The answer is easy to say, but not so easy to grasp. I always say: you just make it work! And people look at me wondering, “but if it’s a video call and there’s no connection, what’s the point of being a SOLE Abuelita?”
What really happens is that you realize communication and presence don’t need a lot of bells and whistles to actually happen.
Obviously, if the SOLE has a super solid connection, everything flows organically. People chat, we hear everyone, we can interact easily, we talk and do amazing searches… it feels easy, pleasant, and by the end, your heart feels full and happy.
When those conditions aren’t met and the connection is rough—the image is pixelated, the sound is choppy, we can’t even hear the Big Question, or the video chat doesn’t even seem to work in real-time—frustration sets in. We don’t get what’s going on, we feel like hanging up and getting on with our day because this makes no sense at all… This feeling multiplies if it’s one of our first connections, if we’ve just started in the Abuelita Cloud.
At the same time, on the other side, there’s a community that can’t hear us either, they see us as a blur, there are many of them, the computer screen where the Abuelita is projected is tiny, the sound coming out of the speaker is way too low. Maybe it’s hot, or it’s right after lunch. In the Tuning Visits, for example, it’s the first time communities are doing a SOLE, and they don’t quite get what’s happening, how they’re going to find answers via Internet, how to use the computer, what they’re supposed to do at each moment, or who that person is trying to talk to them from who-knows-where.
From experience, I tell you: the power of the Internet is like the power of water… it seeps through anywhere! It seeps through everywhere! And that’s when a message, somehow, from the other side of the world tells you, “I’m with you, that question you’re asking is fantastic, I’m searching and I found (…) congrats on that research, I’ll see you for the next SOLE!” And that’s when the room fills with joy, letting us all know that we came here to learn, that we are TOGETHER. And that TOGETHER takes on a much bigger and more powerful meaning.
From here, we thank all those who didn’t give up, those who sent a question or an answer via WhatsApp, those who voted later on, all those who followed the game, minute by minute… THANK YOU to everyone!

en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.title: Q&A: The ins and outs of being a 'Granny'
en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.summary: We're clearing up the common head-scratchers about the Granny experience.
en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
What’s the minimum time commitment for the sessions?
Consistency is the secret sauce of learning. We know life happens and responsibilities shift, so we understand that some Abuelitas might not be able to stick around indefinitely. If you can’t commit to a regular schedule or a long stretch, just let us know what you can manage. It could be dropping into a session every now and then, or just touching base with the coordination team or other Abuelitas to help us brainstorm ways to tackle the challenges ahead.
How does seeing the “privilege gap” between your environment and theirs affect us?
Feel free to share your reality and your world with others—we all grow, get inspired, and open up new possibilities when we connect with different walks of life.
This experience touches us all in the same way. You, too, will discover and learn from other worlds. You, too, will be enriched by this journey. Let this experience and these people into your life!
What happens to the children or adults when the experience with the Abuelita ends?
It’s a question many have asked, and it’s a valid concern. Even if some experiences are shorter than expected, the impact on the children and the people involved sticks around. Read our SOLE stories to see what people say about the Abuelitas Cloud in the communities where we’ve supported SOLE sessions, and let yourself be moved by the magic.
What should I do if the media contacts me to talk about or film my interaction as part of the Abuelitas Cloud?
If we’re interacting with children, we have to look out for their best interests and make sure they aren’t exposed inappropriately. Before speaking to the media or taking photos or videos of anyone, please get in touch with the SOLE Colombia team.
How is the Abuelitas Cloud funded?
As we’ve mentioned, the Abuelitas are volunteers, and thanks to that, many children, young people, and adults have been able to connect and share experiences. We want to keep it that way, though we might explore new ways to sustain the relationship with the Abuelitas down the road.
And if I can’t be an Abuelita, can I help in another way?
There are always opportunities to join this global movement to transform the future of learning. At SOLE Colombia, we’re open to finding the best way for you to get involved. You can check out the roles de la Comunidad SOLE Colombia and find where you feel most at home. Let us know what interests you or if you have a proposal!
If you still have unanswered questions, write to us at hola@solecolombia.org—we’re just a message away.

en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.title: Ever wondered how the internet, power, or mobile signal actually reaches you?
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.summary: Discover the journey of information from the source straight to your doorstep.
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.content:
Every day we check messages on our phones, flip on a light, or take a phone call.
It all feels like everyday stuff, but 150 years ago, it was pure magic when cities like Bogotá—down in Colombia—saw the miracle of electric light for the very first time.
[Así llegó la luz a Bogotá](www.senalmemoria.co/piezas/luz-llego-bogota#:~:text=Bogotá fue la primera ciudad,inconvenientes de ahí en adelante)
Or take Myanmar, over in Asia—they didn’t get their first taste of the Internet until 2012.

en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.title: How does the Internet actually work?
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.summary: Get the lowdown on how data travels across the web.
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
Think about when you go to a restaurant and order a cup of coffee. You, as the client, ask or consult the waiter, who goes to the kitchen, comes back a while later, and serves you that cup of coffee, just like a good server. You might not know exactly how they brewed it, but you know it’s a cup of coffee when you take a sip. The Internet works pretty much the same way. Let’s take a look.

  
  SOLE Colombia, 2024.

When you hop on the internet and have a question, what you’re doing is consulting it from a smartphone or computer, communicating with a bunch of other computers owned by people or companies that store exactly what you’re looking for.
The information you want to consult could be a webpage, a video, a photo, a video call, a file, or a message. These are just some of the formats for digital files that get sent over the internet.
The phone, computer, or tablet you use to connect to the internet is called the client.
The computer where the information you’re looking for is stored is called the server.
How does information travel across the Internet?
For the information sent by a server to reach your home, neighborhood, village, or community, the client you’re using connects to the Internet. Let’s say, for example, your cell phone is somewhere in Colombia and the answer is sitting on a server in Europe. This is the grand adventure your question goes on.

  
  How does your question travel across the Internet? SOLE Colombia, 2024.

Your phone connects via electromagnetic or wireless waves to a cell tower (or several). Your question travels as zeros “0” and ones “1” to one of those towers and heads down a cable that runs underground to some central hub. Then, it gets redirected to a port where that cable connects to a submarine cable. This cable runs under the ocean to the other continent, then comes back up to another cable hub that carries your question to the place where the server with your answer is located. The server receives your question and responds with the stored information—also in zeros “0” and ones “1”—and it gets sent back along that same route to your phone. And all of that happens in a matter of milliseconds! Pretty incredible, don’t you think?
Diver installing a submarine cable

  
  Taken from Erbauer 2. Klasse Christopher Farmer, from Taylorsville.

Internal structure of a submarine cable

  
  Taken from: youtu.be/k1SMnnddpvI

Global map of submarine Internet cables

  
  Global map of submarine Internet cables. Data by Greg Mahlknecht, map by OpenStreetMap contributors (CC BY-SA 2.0).

Keep in mind that these submarine cables are what allow us to transmit data so that telecommunication services can exist. The reason information travels so fast is that these cables are made of fiber optics—basically, glass. This means the information, those zeros “0” and ones “1,” is sent as light, and light is the fastest thing in the entire universe.
Isn’t it wild what we humans have come up with?

So, let’s head back to the start: when was the last time you used the Internet as a group? Maybe that memory—sharing a search, a screen, a question—is the beginning of another possible Internet. The Library of the Future is just that: proof that other Internets are possible, and that we’re already building them.

Recharge Your SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca.
That’s what we’re building with the Library of the Future: an ecosystem where access isn’t the finish line, but the starting point. A space where the network doesn’t just connect devices, but also stories, doubts, and hunches—a space to connect and ask questions without fear.
In the SOLE Labs, we’ve seen how something shifts when a community gathers around a screen. Kids, young people, and elders asking questions together. The Internet stops being a stream of information we consume in solitude and becomes shared territory. In a group, questions arise that don’t pop up when we’re alone. Memories mix, curiosity wakes up, collective projects are born. Using the Internet as a group is, in itself, a radical act because it defies speed, noise, and the instruction to accept things without questioning.

Plug in your SOLE Lab in Dominguillo, Cauca.
The Internet has turned into a personal space for consumption; “being connected” doesn’t really mean being connected to others or connecting with others. And that’s what changes when we use the internet as a group.

SOLE Festival in Boca de Camarones, La Guajira.
Today, nearly three billion people around the world remain disconnected. And that digital exclusion cuts across bodies, languages, and landscapes. It’s not just a technical problem: it’s a silent way of saying who counts and who doesn’t. But that’s not all—those of us who do have access to the Internet tend to use it not to connect, but to isolate ourselves further from those around us. We use it to order food, to keep up with other people’s lives, to buy things, to read about what interests us. We rarely use it to cook with others, to see others, to swap knowledge, to create together.
Maybe you don’t remember. Because most of the time, we connect alone: in front of a cellphone, a laptop, or a tablet. The experience of the Internet has become intimate, individual, and often passive. We accept answers that appear without us asking, we navigate algorithms that predict what we want before we even say it. But something is lost when we use the Internet in solitude: the chance to look each other in the eye while we search, to ask questions out loud, to invent together.
When was the last time you used the Internet as a group?
While millions remain without Internet, those of us who have access use it each on our own. What if the future of the Internet was using it as a group?

en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.title: How does a message travel from your phone to your friends'?
en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.summary: Discover how the Internet signal actually gets around.
en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
The Internet signal travels through physical infrastructure like fiber optic and copper cables, as well as radio waves (Wi-Fi) and, to a lesser extent, via satellite or mobile networks (4G/5G). Data gets turned into electrical or light pulses (bits) that zip along these paths to their destination, using routers and other gear to send and receive the info.
Guided Media (wired):

Fiber optic: Sends data as pulses of light through thin strands of glass.
Copper (Coaxial and twisted pair): Uses metal wires to carry electrical signals, like in those old-school ADSL connections.
Submarine cables: The lion’s share of global Internet traffic travels through fiber optic cables laid deep under the ocean.

Wireless Media (no wires):

Wi-Fi: Uses radio waves to hook up your gadgets (like your phone or computer) to a router.
Mobile networks (3G, 4G, 5G): Signals are beamed through antennas and cell towers to give you Internet access on the go.
Satellite: Sends and receives signals to and from a satellite orbiting up in space.

How does the magic happen?

Step 1 → Conversion to bits: When you send something (like an email), your computer turns it into pulses of electricity or light (bits).
Step 2 → Transmission: These bits travel through the physical infrastructure (cables, air, or space) to a piece of network gear.
Step 3 → Routing: Routers and other network equipment steer these bits along the most efficient path to where they need to go.
Step 4 → Reception: At the receiving end, the bits are turned back into the original info you can actually see or use.

(Source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medio_de_transmisi%C3%B3n)

Gigabytes (GB) are the amount of data you can use to browse, chat, listen to music, watch videos, and more. When you’re offered an internet plan in GB, they’re giving you a set amount of internet data you can burn through.
1 GB = 1000 MB (megabytes)
Ever wonder how much mileage you can get out of a Giga?

You can watch a 30-minute HD (high definition) video
You can listen to 200 songs
You can hop on 4 hours of video calls
You can visit 600 webpages
You can send 350,000 text messages

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.title: How did they boost the Internet in Cáceres, Antioquia?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.summary: Five community leaders level up Internet access in their neighborhood.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.content:
In the community of Altos del Tigre, in the municipality of Cáceres, five community leaders are making the near-impossible a reality: improving access to Internet in their neighborhood.
Yadiris Vaquero, Luz Cenith Acevedo, Kenia Yepes, Blanca Ofir Moreno, and David Ojeda, SOLE Ambassadors for their community, have been working hard for a long time to make sure having Internet stops being a hidden treasure in their territory. Because let’s be real, in Cáceres, just like in many places around Colombia, a stable connection has always been a luxury.
This year, however, something shifted. Starting with the Tuning Visits back in May, the Ambassadors and other community members took the opportunity to learn together how this whole Internet thing actually works and why, specifically in Cáceres, getting a signal was such a tall order. The answer? Basically, because there aren’t any cell towers for miles around, and the telecommunications infrastructure is pretty much non-existent.
But that didn’t discourage them. Quite the opposite—they rolled up their sleeves and got to work. They assessed the situation, hunted for solutions, and with the program’s support, they managed to find the perfect fit: a Jangala device. This small but mighty gadget makes it possible to connect communities in hard-to-reach areas, and for the folks in Cáceres, it was like opening a door to a whole new world.

    This video complements the article about the initiative by five community leaders in Altos del Tigre, Cáceres, to improve Internet access. It shows the work done by these individuals to bring connectivity to their community.

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
So, thanks to the Jangala and the hard work of the SOLE Ambassadors—and all the community members who pitched in to get this solution up and running—Cáceres now has Internet at a community access point.

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article about the initiative by five community leaders in Altos del Tigre, Cáceres, to improve Internet access. It shows the work done by the community to overcome connectivity challenges in their territory.

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article about the initiative by five community leaders in Altos del Tigre, Cáceres, to improve Internet access in their community. The audiovisual material documents the efforts and the impact of this local project.
  


Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
And for many, this achievement means so much more than just “getting connected”: it’s a chance to learn, to stay informed, and to keep up with the world. Kids, young people, and adults can now access information, participate in SOLE sessions, and, as they put it, “solve those big questions that used to seem like they were from another planet.”
Listen to what one of the local tinkerers has to say—he was the one who jumped in to help set up the Jangala antenna with the whole SOLE crew:

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article on how five community leaders from Altos del Tigre, in Cáceres, Antioquia, are managing to improve Internet access in their community. Through this testimonial, the positive impact of this initiative for the local residents is shown.
  


Arnulfo, Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
The work of Yadiris, Luz Cenith, Kenia, Blanca Ofir, and David Ojeda has marked a real turning point in Cáceres. Today, thanks to their dedication and the Jangala, the community doesn’t just have Internet; they are transforming how they use it—discovering, sharing, and creating all sorts of new possibilities for their community.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.title: How did the Internet get a boost in Chalán, Montes de María?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.summary: The story of how connectivity got fixed up in Chalán.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.content:
Chalán is a municipality in the Sucre department of Colombia. Out in these parts, rural villages like Monte Bello, Rancho Rojo, and Alemania are using the Internet in a unique way: they’re hooking up as a group to tackle big questions, get homework done, watch movies, or just share their stories with the world.
Since 2023, Yulieth Farasica has been a SOLE Ambassador, sparking a real change in her community by leading collaborative learning sessions. On top of that, this year she helped us install, teach, and promote shared Internet access in her village, Alemania. Now, the neighboring villages can get online too, making it easier to stay in touch and get the information they need.
Listen to Yulieth tell her story about the lessons learned from connecting the community:

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the story about improving connectivity in Chalán, Sucre. It shows how residents of villages like Monte Bello and Rancho Rojo use Internet access collectively to learn and share as a community.
  


That’s how Alemania has become a hub for folks from Monte Bello, Rancho Rojo, and other nearby communities. People are traveling over just to use this connection, which was set up and got running thanks to everyone pitching in.

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the story of how the communities of Chalán, Sucre, have transformed their access to connectivity. It shows how residents of villages like Monte Bello and Rancho Rojo use the Internet collectively to learn and share as a group.
  


We’ve now got six ambassadors trained in the SOLE methodology who’ve learned how the Internet works and how to use their Jangala to share it with others!
Yulieth, Astrid, Yuranis, Johana, Celia, Maryuris, and Yolanda are changing the world. Thanks to their hard work, more children, young people, adults, and elders in Chalán have Internet access today. From neighboring villages like Monte Bello and Rancho Rojo, people are coming to the Alemania village to get connected and be part of this network that they’ve built and sustained themselves.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.title: How did the Internet get better in Colosó, Montes de María?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.summary: La Estación and the La Esmeralda Indigenous Cabildo are just a 15-minute motorbike ride from each other.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.content:
La Estación and the La Esmeralda Indigenous Cabildo are just a 15-minute motorbike ride from each other. Both are neighboring communities in the Colombian municipality of Colosó, in the department of Sucre. Until recently, neither of these communities had a public space to access the Internet as a group. However, since 2023, they’ve taken the plunge and started using the connectivity solutions we installed together in their territory to boost Self-Organized Learning.
No one is better suited than Mónica Vega, one of La Estación’s star Ambassadors, to share the story of how these communities are transforming their access to information, connection, and education. Ready to hear her out? Don’t forget to turn up the volume!

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article on improving connectivity in the municipality of Colosó, Sucre. It shows the positive impact that the arrival of the internet has had on communities like La Estación and the La Esmeralda Indigenous Cabildo.
  


Mónica Vega, during Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Did you hear her? It’s incredible how her community has used Jangala and the connection to the Internet to strengthen the bonds between its members. But Mónica’s story doesn’t end there. This year, she decided to visit her neighboring community, La Esmeralda, to motivate more people to tinker with the technology.
Even though Jangala wasn’t the right fit for this community, Mónica and Gabriel, being the excellent “tinkerers” they are, rolled up their sleeves and didn’t let anything stop them. Together, we explored other connectivity options, and finally, with Mónica’s help, we installed an omnidirectional antenna and a router. Now, the Ambassadors of La Esmeralda are empowering their neighbors to use the Internet as a group.

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article on improving connectivity in the municipality of Colosó, Sucre. It shows the positive impact that the arrival of the internet has had on communities like La Estación and the La Esmeralda Indigenous Cabildo.
  


Gabriel, during Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
What’s more, the community has created its own website to tell the whole world about their products, traditions, services, territory, history, and customs. Community Internet is now in their hands!

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.title: How did the Internet get better in Dominguillo, Cauca?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.summary: The story of how connectivity got a boost in Dominguillo.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.content:
In 2023, the community of Dominguillo started experiencing an unexpected transformation, all thanks to a new window of connection. It all kicked off when, through the Hilando Vidas y Esperanza program by USAID, implemented by the IOM, a device called Jangala arrived at the local public school library. This little piece of kit allowed for stable Internet access for the first time, which quickly became an invaluable resource for everyone.
Here’s Luis Miguel Mina—or Lucho, as we all know him—introducing the Jangala, or “Jang,” as they decided to call it. He’s one of the SOLE Ambassadors we trained in 2023:

Franki, Lucho, and Mateo at the Inspiration Workshops in Dominguillo, Cauca (2023).
Inspiration Workshops, Dominguillo, Cauca (2023).
The device was set up in the library to facilitate SOLE sessions (Self-Organized Learning Environments), a method that invites participants to learn autonomously and collaboratively through Big Questions. With these tools up and running, the folks in Dominguillo didn’t just explore topics of interest; they started digging into questions about their own culture and traditions, bringing the community together around shared knowledge and rediscovering their roots through the Internet.
Listen to Luis Miguel Mina and Nancy Campo talk about this experience:

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article on digital transformation in Dominguillo, Cauca. It shows how the arrival of new connectivity devices, thanks to the *Hilando Vidas y Esperanza* program, improved internet access in the community.
  


Luis Miguel Mina and Nancy Campo
SOLE Ambassadors at the SOLE Festivals in Dominguillo, Santander de Quilichao (2023).
However, as time went on, the community could no longer use the school library for their SOLE sessions. By then, the impact of this connection had been so profound that the people of Dominguillo didn’t want to give it up. Convinced of the importance of having a community space for learning and connectivity, they sought support to create their own connection hub: the Dominguillo SOLE Lab.
And… guess what? Together, we worked on developing the SOLE Lab, a public space where chairs, tables, and computers were set up, and Internet access was restored. With the SOLE Lab, the residents of Dominguillo got back the chance to connect with the world, continue their SOLE sessions, and explore new ways of learning.

Dominguillo SOLE Lab, Cauca (2024).

Learning and community work at the SOLE Lab, Dominguillo (2024).

Children and youth participating in SOLE sessions, Dominguillo (2024).

Connectivity and global communication from Dominguillo, Cauca (2024).
Thanks to this effort, Dominguillo didn’t just improve its Internet connection; it strengthened the community bond. Now, the SOLE Lab is a meeting point where residents keep learning and sharing their knowledge.

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article on digital transformation in Dominguillo, Cauca. It shows the positive impact that the arrival of a new connectivity device, facilitated by the *Hilando Vidas y Esperanza* program, had on the community's life.
