en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.title: How did the Internet get a boost in San Juan Nepomuceno, Montes de María?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.summary: The story of how connectivity got fixed up in San Juan Nepomuceno.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.content:
The following snippets are a collection of testimonials, images, and scenes showing how using group Internet in the municipality of San Juan Nepomuceno is transforming access to the network for neighboring communities, such as San José del Peñón and La Haya.
First Stop




SOLE Festivals, Montes de María, (2024).
To get to San José del Peñón, you have to cross seven rivers, cross your fingers that the rain doesn’t play a nasty trick on you, and marvel at the majestic beauty of this land. It’s no coincidence that, upon arrival, a large sign proudly welcomes you: “San José del Peñón, magical, fertile, and powerful land.”
The geography of San José del Peñón, with its mountains and dense vegetation, prevents signals from nearby towers from reaching the village. Installing a community connectivity solution was a challenge that required the effort of the entire community. With collective support and hard work, we managed to install our Rural KIT against all odds: a Yagi antenna and a router that now make it possible for the community to gather periodically to do SOLE.

  
  

Gabriel, Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).

  
  

Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Rafael Antonio García, a natural-born tinkerer in his community, tells us in his own words what the process was like to install the antenna: Turn up the volume to hear his story!

  
  

Rafael Antonio in Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
You don’t need to be an expert or have experience building networks, antennas, or cables to tinker. Like Don Rafael Antonio, you too can get encouraged to collaborate with others to create a common good.
Currently, the community of San José del Peñón, along with its neighbors, has continued doing SOLE on their own, using group Internet to research Big Questions like: Why does water make things wet? Why don’t humans use 100% of our brains? Why is there fresh water and salt water? Why are babies born without teeth?

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).
That’s not all; the San José del Peñón community also created their own website, where they can upload their products and services, share their traditions, games, and everything they want to show the world about their community. Take a look!
SOLE: San José del Peñón

Second Stop:
Since 2023, we have built a super close relationship with the community of La Haya. This year, one of the SOLE Ambassadors from there joined as a SOLE Explorer to help us bring a connectivity solution she was already familiar with to San José del Peñón. Mariana Fernández was our indispensable support in training new ambassadors in her municipality and managing to install the connectivity solution in this new SOLE community.
Turn up the volume to hear in her own words what this experience was like, and how using group internet has transformed her territory:

  
  

Mariana Fernández, Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Thanks to community collaboration and the implementation of solutions like the Rural KIT, today San José del Peñón and La Haya have community access to Internet, facilitating both learning and cultural exchange in the Montes de María.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.title: How did the Internet get better in Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in Nuevo México.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.content:
Care, a will for change, and reconciliation? That’s what’s happening in the Nuevo México village, the Nasa Kiwe Tekh Kxsaw community located in Santander de Quilichao.

Community research on connectivity, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).

Community analysis process of Internet access, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
Using the SOLE methodology, the community asked themselves: what happens to our bodies when we get a hug? Mostly women, using the internet and computers as a group. Laughing, chatting, researching via the internet, and figuring out things they’d never talked about before, or things they’d always just assumed. Sharing their feelings and creating new knowledge. Together.

Hands-on tinkering and learning at the SOLE Lab, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
How the internet works was the topic of our workshop: submarine cables that carry the Internet signal along the ocean floor to the community, how to use it together, and what we can do with that great red that connects us globally.
We installed a Jangala and an omnidirectional antena in a space where the community regularly meets to make decisions.

Implementation of the Jangala device for community connectivity, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
Currently, the Nasa Kiwe Tekh Kxsaw community continues to ask themselves Big Questions using the Internet and technology as a group. Let them tell you about it themselves 👇🏽

  
  

  📄 See video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article by showing the connectivity improvement process in the Nuevo México village, Santander de Quilichao. Through images, it highlights the community effort and the positive impact of internet access on this population.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.title: How did the Internet get a tune-up in Piendamó, Cauca?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.summary: The Hilando Vidas y Esperanza (Weaving Lives and Hope) program by USAID and IOM brought SOLE Colombia to El Agrado.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.content:
The Hilando Vidas y Esperanza (Weaving Lives and Hope) program by USAID and IOM brought SOLE Colombia to El Agrado. Together, we’ve been working to bridge the digital divide, bringing Internet access to isolated communities, giving connection a real purpose: using the Internet together to learn in a self-organized and autonomous way. Since 2023, Piendamó, Cauca, has been the star of this story of change.
Alexander García, the Tinkerer Building Bridges
It was in El Agrado that we met Alexander García, a young community leader with a curious and committed spirit. From the start, Alexander was enthusiastic about technology and, especially, the Internet. With SOLE’s support, we installed a connectivity solution and a few computers in the community hall, which soon became the hub for learning and gathering for his neighbors.

Collective explanation about connectivity and the Internet, Piendamó, Cauca (2023).

Practical demonstration of using the Internet during SOLE Festivals, Piendamó (2023).

Children and youth exploring the Internet during SOLE activities, Piendamó (2023).

The Journey to the Misak Pisicatau Reserve
Alexander’s curiosity about how routers, antennas, and networks actually work quickly turned him into an expert. In a matter of months, he went from someone who didn’t care much about tech to a real “tinkerer.” This newfound skill has turned him into a bridge between his community and neighboring ones, sharing what he knows with everyone else.
In 2024, Alexander joined us on a new mission: bringing Internet to a neighboring indigenous community in the Misak Pisicatau Reserve. Upon arrival, we ran speed and signal tests, and it was Alexander who quickly figured out that no antenna could get a stable connection in that mountainous terrain.

  
  

SOLE Tuning Visits, Piendamó, (2024)
The good news is that the Reserve already had a stable satellite Internet connection, so we just had to install a router to fine-tune it. Listen to him talk about the moment we installed that router like a pro!

  
  

Tuning Visits, Piendamó, (2024).
With his technical skills and passion for teaching, Alexander was the first to motivate the residents of the reserve to explore the possibilities of the Internet and join the SOLE movement. With his support, we installed computers in the community hall, and Alexander encouraged them to keep using Self-Organized Learning in their community. Thanks to his push, the Misak Pisicatau community has now created their own website, a space where they share their traditions, culture, and knowledge with the world.

Misak Piscitau Reserve, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).

Misak Piscitau Reserve, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).

Misak Piscitau Reserve, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).
This is just one of many stories that show the power of connectivity to open doors and connect worlds. We invite you to learn more about the activities this community has carried out and the projects they’ve created on their website.
SOLE: Resguardo Piscitau

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.title: How did the Internet get a boost in El Tambo, Cauca?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.summary: The story of how connectivity got fixed up in El Tambo.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.content:
Have you ever imagined a place where an entire community can get connected to Internet, learn, and create together? In El Tambo, Cauca, that dream was a shared necessity.
In this community, Internet connection in rural areas is pretty limited, and in the urban center, access is mostly private. A public space with Internet became essential so everyone could get online, work on their collective projects, and strengthen their territory.
In 2023, thanks to our partners at ADAPT Peace Building, we met the El Tambo community and their community circles: the youth circle, the water circle, and the women’s circle. These groups had been working for over a year on peacebuilding and strengthening the social fabric. From that first meeting, a deep connection was formed. The circles quickly took ownership of the SOLE methodology and saw group Internet access as a tool to reach a collective dream: a community space with an Internet connection. That’s how the spark for the SOLE Lab was lit in this community.

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).
Throughout 2024, the Ambassadors of El Tambo trained in the SOLE methodology and, together with RUTA 4 Taller, the collective work and the hands of the community brought their own SOLE Lab to life: The Second Library of the Future in Colombia!
Here is how one of the neighbors of the SOLE Lab in Barrio Obrero describes it:

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)

Plug in Your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article on improving connectivity in El Tambo, Cauca. It shows the positive impact that internet access has had on learning and collaboration in this community.
  


Plug in Your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
The SOLE Lab isn’t your average library. It’s a meeting point where kids, youth, and adults explore, create, dream, and learn together. With access to community Internet and collaborative spaces, the SOLE Lab invites the community to turn ideas into action, make collective decisions, enjoy self-organized group learning, and, why not, even watch movies.

  
  

  📄 View video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the article showing how the SOLE Lab works in El Tambo, Cauca. Through this space, it's clear how the community leverages improved connectivity to learn and create collaboratively.
  

Plug in Your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
Thanks to the SOLE Lab, the Internet connection in El Tambo improved significantly. Today, anyone can drop by and enjoy a more stable and faster connection, allowing students, families, and neighbors to get online, research, and create new ways to use the Internet together.
Now the El Tambo community can communicate and build bonds with other SOLE Lab communities and people all over the world. With every connection, bridges of collaboration are built that strengthen the sense of belonging and collective learning; each participant of the Library of the Future is part of a global network of learning and transformation.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.title: How did the Internet get a boost in Valdivia, Antioquia?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.summary: KM15 is the geographic marker on the road leading from the municipal seat to the Puerto Valdivia district.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.content:
KM15 is the geographic marker on the road leading from the municipal seat to the Puerto Valdivia district. It’s also the name of the community settled right there. Life in Km15—kilometer 15, as it sounds in Spanish—unfolds along the road that connects it to the rest of the world… or maybe not. Its geographic situation is a metaphor for its digital situation: while in many places Internet is just part of daily life, out there, it feels worlds away.
Access to community Internet was a dream for its residents. Most relied on pricey data plans on their phones or satellite Internet, options that aren’t always affordable and really limit what you can do.

  
  

After getting a taste of new ways to use the Internet through the Hilando Vidas y Esperanza program—run by USAID and implemented by IOM and SOLE Colombia—the women of KM15, who had already experienced the power of using the Internet as a group, became the driving force for change.
Their commitment to learning led them to tinker and hack their way to transforming that reality. Accompanied by SOLE Colombia, and guided by their own enthusiasm and dedication, we managed to install a Jangala device in the community hall: a space that, just like that, became the connectivity hub for Km15.

  
  


  
  

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).
The donation of several computers rounded out the toolkit these Ambassadors now use to lead SOLE sessions in their community, bringing their neighbors closer to learning, technology, and a world full of possibilities.
Today, the community hall isn’t just a meeting spot; it’s a place to share Internet and manage resources as a community.

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia (2024).

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).
The story doesn’t end there. The Ambassadors now understand how the Internet works, why it’s important to manage it, and the difference in gigabyte consumption between watching a movie or sending a message—both in terms of data usage and their own pockets. Now, they are experts at using computers and the internet as a group.

  
  

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).

  
  

The women are taking ownership of how the Internet is used in Valdivia. And you, have you ever wondered why you pay what you pay for your cell phone plan or home Internet?

en/inspire/insp-life-and-technology.title: How can technology help us weave stories?
en/inspire/insp-life-and-technology.summary: A methodology for weaving stories using a bit of tech.
en/inspire/insp-life-and-technology.content:
Implementation site: Recharge your SOLE LAB in Boca de Camarones
Implementation date:
2023/11/04
Figure 1. Photograph showing the connections participants made regarding their life experiences with technology.


Purpose: To recognize each other as part of the SOLE Lab project through our life stories in relation to technology.
Device instructions


Tell your life story through what technology has allowed you to do. To do this, select 3 milestones or relevant moments and draw them in a vignette.


How do our stories connect? We’ll use yarn to connect everyone’s stories.


Device development

The experiences narrated below are the result of what each participant shared about their life experiences with technology. To avoid misrepresentation, we use quotation marks ““ as a way to cite what the person actually said. In other parts of the text, we paraphrase the participants, trying to stay true to what was expressed throughout the session.
We use the word milestone to refer to those events or happenings that are significant to the person telling the story.
The order of the names appearing in this systematization is the order in which people connected their stories. For example: Óscar started by telling his three milestones. Later, Lizeth from SOLE Colombia followed, because she connected what she had drawn with one or several of Óscar’s milestones.
There were moments in the session where the speaker connected with the stories of several participants who had already spoken.

Óscar [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “My first TV was the first one in the community.”
Milestone 2: “When I gave presentations at school, others used a Video Beam, and I did it manually. It made me feel inferior; however, the teachers valued my posters much more because of how creative they were.”
Milestone 3: “I didn’t touch a computer until I was eleven (11). I crashed that computer and was very afraid of technology.”

Lizeth [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: Her father bought a cellphone that became the community’s cellphone.
Milestone 2: The video game machine at her parents’ shop helped her gain popularity and friends.
Milestone 3: “I filled up on floppy disks of my favorite series and learned many songs.”

Elainer [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: His first contact with computers was while studying.
Milestone 2: He worked at a Punto Vive Digital and was able to help many people.
Milestone 3: “I met SOLE Colombia and lived the experience of setting up a SOLE LAB in my community.”

Marcelo [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: He helped at the Punto Vive Digital where he worked with his brother. He says that in his childhood, he knew nothing about technology, as he hadn’t had contact with those “gadgets.”
Milestone 2: He recognizes the moment the SOLE LAB materials arrived.
Milestone 3: His first cellphone. “My first cellphone broke.”

Sebastián [audiovisual production]:

Milestone 1: “They gave me my first tape recorder. ‘Let the music play!’” he said.
Milestone 2: “They gave me my first guitar. ‘Let’s make some noise!’” he said.
Milestone 3: He talked about his first computer and how exciting it was to know everything he could do with it.

Gustavo [Internet Society Foundation]:

Milestone 1: Since he was little, he liked making magazines. When he was a kid, he started writing a blog. “This was my first job at a digital newspaper.”
Milestone 2: “My first cellphone allowed me to see the world without being afraid of the information I might find.”
Milestone 3: “Video calls allow me to connect with my sister and my nephews.”

Ana María [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “Through the internet, I connect with my friends in Aracataca.”
Milestone 2: “From age 9 to 11, I had my first MP3 player.” She says she has always liked listening to music. “I took over the remote for our first DVD player and wouldn’t lend it to my brothers.”
Milestone 3: I met Marcelo (her partner) through social media. “He lived in Santa Marta and we couldn’t see each other,” she said.

Mateo [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: He remembers his first heartbreak email. “I was writing to someone I liked, but who didn’t pay attention to me.”
Milestone 2: “My aunt gave me my first analog camera. It had a roll with 20 photos.”
Milestone 3: “My first computer broke. It was frustrating for my parents, who had gone into debt for it.”

Nicolas [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: He was calling a radio station to ask for tickets to a Soda Stereo concert. “The station answered, but the dog took the internet cable, and the call to the station was cut off.”
Milestone 2: He remembers his first video game and Game Boy.
Milestone 3: His father taught him how to ride a bike.

Caril [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “I learned to use a calculator at age 9. I didn’t know how to use it, it scared me, but I learned.”
Milestone 2: She learned to use a laptop. “The internet has been a great tool for learning how to use technology,” she said.
Milestone 3: “Thanks to SOLE, I’ve gotten into the world of networks and technology. I want to keep learning.”

SanJay [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: “I bought a sampler to make music.” It gave him a lot of happiness because he felt he could make his own music.
Milestone 2: “At 16, I won a scholarship to study in Hong Kong and bought a laptop and the movie Matrix on CD. The movie was split into two parts; my brother scratched CD 2 trying to put it in the DVD player, but it got damaged, and we couldn’t keep watching the movie.” He says it was frustrating, although now it makes him laugh.
Milestone 3: “I started making my own music.”

Paola [audiovisual production]:

Milestone 1: “They gave me my first camera. It was red. I’m nearsighted, but I learned to use it. I collected many cameras throughout my life because I like to keep the memory of moments.”
Milestone 2: “I remember my first cellphone looked like a brick.”
Milestone 3: “The internet arrived at home. This gave me the chance to connect with my friends in Uruguay.”

Findings and learnings

In the session, participants connected their stories emotionally and intuitively. There was no sense of moral or material superiority between the stories.
Having to connect with someone else’s story keeps everyone in a constant state of listening.
It’s interesting how stories about the first technological device appear—whether it’s a TV, a cellphone, a printer, etc.—and how these devices allow new relationships with other people to form.
It’s interesting how life stories in relation to technology say a lot about who we are and what we are no longer. Many stories connect with passions, tastes, or character traits of the people.
The milestones are related to happy, pleasant stories, but also to those that generate shame, pain, or nostalgia.
The importance of these devices doesn’t lie in the story itself, but in the way people connect their stories to one another.

en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.title: Socio-technical trajectory · Cacharreras Community
en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.summary: Logbook of the SOLE Voltaje development.
en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.content:
We set out to create this divergent space you’re exploring, called SOLE Voltaje: The Connectivity Solutions Guide. In this logbook, you’ll find the story of the many experiments we designed and ran to improve the user experience and interaction with our community of cacharreras (makers/tinkerers). Below, you’ll find a log organized into macro-events and micro-events, unfolding the story through the analytical lens of “socio-technical trajectories.”

Macro-events: These are the phases we designed for the development and launch of SOLE Voltaje. You can see them in the following diagram:



Micro-events: These are the specific, significant happenings that occur within each of the trajectories.
Socio-technical trajectory: A socio-technical trajectory is a process of co-constructing products, production and organizational processes, institutions, user-producer relationships, learning processes, problem-solution relationships, processes of constructing the functionality/non-functionality of a technology, rationalities, policies, and specific strategies. To understand more about socio-technical analysis, you can head over to our conceptorio.

Laying out three major controversies of interest in this trajectory, we have:

Understanding the controversy related to creating and nurturing a community of cacharreras. We found several experiments and concrete actions that managed to spark some interest and action in specific users, but in the end, it wasn’t sustainable. It seems that, given the possibilities and limitations of SOLE-Voltaje to date, considering the “Cacharrera” as a subjectivity that persists over time is very costly. It makes more sense to think of it as punctual activations that happen through deployments at events, workshops, or by chance—which won’t necessarily permeate over time. Instead, this user will enter the cacharrero logic in very limited times and spaces.
The evolution of user testing showed a broader understanding of it, allowing it to be configured in itself as a Voltaje deployment where observation and analysis are central. In other words, it seems the most appropriate way to deploy Voltaje is through user testing, because the very novelty of this guide means our understanding of appropriation is still very limited and particularized. If we don’t continue in that exercise of praxis and reflection, it will be very difficult to achieve its appropriation.
Two rhetorical and material lines were built that we haven’t synchronized yet: on one hand, SOLElab as the Library of the Future, and on the other, Voltaje: The Solutions Guide. Due to the ways we approached execution and the sheer complexity of both processes, we only managed to articulate very concrete connection points that didn’t achieve proper integration. Although this is how it stood at the time this trajectory was completed, it’s not entirely clear if integrating the two lines is the most appropriate way to allow for the understanding of the appropriation of one virtual space and the other physical space.

en/inspire/insp-sole-unal.title: What does water mean to you and your community?
en/inspire/insp-sole-unal.summary: SOLE session run by students from the National University.
en/inspire/insp-sole-unal.content:
SOLE conducted by students of the Water and Energy Observatory IV from the School of Industrial Design at the National University. April 25, 2025.

Add your answers here. Careful now! Don’t go deleting anyone else’s hard work. Feel free to add photos, videos, links…
Group 1
Authors:

Juan Hansmeier
Daniel González
Angie Ospina
Andrea Castañeda

Answer: By adapting the “self-photography” tool, we proposed “self-drawing” focused on children; where, through questions and drawings, we arrived at the required answer.

Draw your day-to-day life.
The facilitator asks different questions that, in this context, guide the child to answer “what does water mean to you?” without having to ask that question literally.
You get a drawing that holds the answer to the big question.

Group 2
Authors:
Sebastián Caraballo
Angie Varón
Cynthia Obando
Deidy Rosero
Answer:

Group 3
Authors:
Angie Caroprese
Sergio Castro
Maikol Bello
Alejandro Mateus
Answer: Mind Map as a tool.
Data discrimination based on these concepts:


Life and health (main source for drinking and cooking)


Culture and spirituality (cultural identity and celebrations)


Sustenance and economy (fishing and food)


Relationship with nature (traditional knowledge and environmental awareness)


Education and future (community water care projects)



Group 4
Authors:
David Linares
Luis Ortiz
Antonio Diaz
Gabriela Leaño
Herib Campos
What does water mean to you and your community?
We’re going to work with two tools: participatory mapping and ethnographic video.
Participatory mapping:
Participatory mapping will work to visualize and understand the social, emotional, and care dynamics regarding what water means to the community. It’s a tool for working with the community through talking circles.
1. Community activation and trust

Meeting with community leaders and key community members.
Explain the purpose and ask for permission to document with ethics and consent.

”Support tool: Talking circle + Audiovisual consent form.”
Proposed games and dynamics:
1. The river’s voice (creative icebreaker)
Objective: break the ice, introduce ourselves, connect with water.
How to play:


Each person introduces themselves by saying their name and completing this sentence:

“If I were water, I would be…” (a waterfall, a calm river, a storm, a happy little puddle, etc.)



Variant: have them do it by imitating the sound or movement of the water they chose.
2. Emotional water map (on the ground)
Objective: identify emotional bonds.
How to play:

Draw a large circle on the floor (with tape or branches) representing the territory.
The facilitator asks questions like:

“Where did you feel joy with water?”
“Where were you afraid of water?”
“Where did you learn something important with water?”


People walk around and position themselves within the map according to their answer. They can share if they want to.


Materials: dry leaves, tape, chalk, stones to mark zones.

2. Ask, feel, and draw (Participatory mapping)
Activity:


In groups, hand out a large piece of poster board with a silhouette of the territory (it can be freeform, not necessarily geographic).


Ask the question:
What does water mean to you?
Where is water present in your daily life?
Where does the water flow? Where does it stop? Where is it missing?


Draw and write:

Rivers, streams, wells, sacred sites, areas of scarcity, memories, uses, threats.
You can also use symbols, words, or emotional colors.


Materials: poster boards, markers, crayons, stickers, printed icons, colored paper.

Ethnographic video
The ethnographic video will help us identify and keep an external record of the underlying dynamics of behavior and meaning regarding water.
During the mapping:

Film the conversations while they draw.
Interview key people with open-ended questions (children, knowledge-keepers, fishers, women leaders):

What memories do you have of water?
What rituals or stories exist about water?
What has changed in the water of the territory?



Also:

Record landscapes, bodies of water, environmental sounds, daily activities (washing, boating, gathering).


Recommendation: use close-up shots of hands drawing, faces while speaking, the stroke growing on the page. That adds a lot of visual and emotional value.

en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.title: Ever wonder why videos load faster on someone else's phone?
en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.summary: We say that Internet is fast if we can get to the information we’re looking for in a jiffy.
en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.content:
We say that Internet is fast if we can get to the information we’re looking for in a jiffy.
Download megabytes (MB) are basically a measure of how quickly data travels over your internet connection. The more MB you’ve got, the faster your internet will be.
If you have:

More than 5 MB: That’s a solid speed for watching videos, listening to music, and doing all sorts of things on the internet.
Between 1 MB and 5 MB: You can manage a steady video call.
Less than 1 MB: You can still browse the internet and send text messages.

The more devices you have hooked up to the internet, the fewer download MB you’ll have to go around. That’s just because the speed gets split up among all the connected gadgets.

The photo-textual breakdown
Being a kid, being another

When I remember my childhood, I see myself taking toys apart to understand how they worked; sometimes I put them back together and they worked, other times not. I won’t forget a battery-operated police car that would pop out two officers—gringo style, with a gun in hand—out of each door as it moved. This was one of those that, thankfully, I could never put back together.
Part of my childhood was permeated by the presence of toys. Just like that police car, I remember taking my soccer ball everywhere. Even when I had the chance to see the ocean, I packed my micro-soccer ball in my luggage, and thankfully, it didn’t pop. My toys are with me.
Without knowing the world behind it, the naive instinct of a kid who only knows what their parents allow them to see let me disassemble structures, just for the sake of curiosity. I didn’t see interest behind the artifacts; I only saw smaller worlds I wanted to understand, that I wanted to open.
What can bring more joy than a toy? Sometimes just a smooth stone, thrown with the right technique, can bring free moments of enjoyment, like when we approach a lake.
Being an adult means taking care of your inner child. Just as I used to paint, play, and study, my identity increasingly returns to its multiple and rhizomatic childhood. Being a tinkerer is sometimes an identity, but now, thanks to Mate, I see it’s also a noun. Sometimes we are tinkerers, and we solve things; other times we don’t. What moves you to tinker?

Having your bag of toys

My bag of toys for the workday. 1. The bag with pockets. 2. The headphones to hear better. 3. The headphone case to protect them. 3. The hard drive to back up information. 3. Pens, cutter, and eraser. 4. The smartphone charger. 5. The toothbrush and toothpaste. 7. The USB so I don’t have to work in the cloud and can keep the information close to me. 8. The Game Boy Advance. 9. Pokémon Sapphire.
The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction
Ursula K. Le Guin
1986


Now the full essay:
pdf essay
Retrieved from: mirror.anarhija.net/es.theanarchistlibrary.org/mirror/u/uk/ursula-k-le-guin-la-teoria-de-la-bolsa-de-transporte-de-la-ficcion.pdf
The tinkering kit, the collection of toys and potions

Taking a part of the text “Making Dissent a Politics of Ourselves” by Eric Sadin, I appeal to witchcraft (the past), and witches like the powerful Isabelle Stengers, and to science fiction (the future) with psychonauts like Aldous Huxley. I invite you tomorrow to create potions together. Just like we used to do the Sabbath, this last Saturday, as a partial closing, we will do our territorial tour and try some of the potions we design tomorrow.
“In the preface to a new 1946 edition of Brave New World, Aldous Huxley writes these words, whose scope and limits are worth grasping:”

“If I were to rewrite this book now, I would offer the Savage a third alternative. Between the utopian and primitive horns of this dilemma would lie the possibility of sanity, a possibility already realized, to some extent, in a community of exiles or refugees from the brave new world, living in a kind of Reservation. In this community, the economy would be decentralist and Henry George-style, and the politics, Kropotkinian and cooperative. Science and technology would be used as if, like the Sabbath, they had been created for man, and not (as at present) that man should adapt and enslave himself to them.”

For now, I only use this fragment to invite you to create potions for humans, for our collectives, that empower them, that adapt to them, not enslave them.

Like Hermione Granger, our knick-knacks or odds and ends (magazines, markers, flowers, cables…) can support us in world-building, in our potions. Just as an example, to leave so much poetry aside, the potions can be: activity designs, lists of questions, fanzines, scents that prepare people for something, drawings, poems… anyway. Those potions depend on your skills, interests, the communities you wish to care for, and the purpose you envision for a specific time-space.

Also, like Seamus Finnigan, we can have accidents. Ultimately, we are in a perpetual learning process where we will never have guarantees of what will happen, especially when we are dream-designing alternative worlds. My only call is for care, harm-reduction, and precaution as policies. My potions seek to follow these principles by seeing the potential in oneself and in others, in the other, positioning oneself not from fear, but from trust, respect, and co-responsibility. What will be the guiding values for your potions?

en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.title: Better together, fixing things
en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.summary: Communities teaming up to boost their connectivity.
en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.content:
Is internet a headache for you? In a world where not everyone has internet and we’re feeling more isolated by the day, some communities have banded together to tackle life’s Big Questions while building connectivity networks. These networks have helped them improve their internet and strengthen their community fabric through SOLE (Self-Organized Learning Environments). These folks use community antennas, low-cost tech, and a good old-fashioned tinkerer’s spirit to roll up their sleeves, overcome barriers, and fix connectivity problems that once seemed impossible.
What if that very drive to fix connectivity issues is where the future of the internet is born? What if every connection to the internet were a vital link between life stories coming together to change the world? We don’t want to be spectators anymore; we want to be the protagonists of our own story.
SOLE Voltaje doesn’t just hand out easy answers; instead, it poses questions that spark curiosity and empower people to find their own solutions.
These communities show us that with a bit of ingenuity and grit, it’s possible to turn connectivity challenges into opportunities. We use the internet as a group because it’s safer, and because every internet connection is a connection with other people—a bond of solidarity and learning.
So, let’s celebrate these Colombian communities that are weaving a red of hope through the internet. Their work is a powerful reminder that together we can build a more connected future, where every voice counts and every story finds its place; it’s a reminder that another internet is possible. This new way of connecting is just getting started. We call this the Library of the Future.
SOLE Voltaje
When someone hits a connectivity snag, SOLE Voltaje pops up with a spark of energy: “Have you tried restarting the router? It’s like giving your connection a cup of coffee!” But their approach goes beyond simple hacks; it invites everyone to think: “Is your red clogged because everyone is watching cat videos? What if you got together with others to use the internet as a group? Maybe it’s time to reach an agreement on how we want to use the internet.”
Library of the Future
In a corner of the future, there exists a Library that doesn’t rely on books, but on the relationships between people. This is a space where knowledge isn’t stuck in one specific place, but lives in the vast red of the internet and the connections it enables between people and communities. Here, life’s Big Questions wait to be explored. This Library of the Future invites us to gather, share ideas, and learn together. In every corner, you can feel the energy of collaboration: groups of people diving into deep discussions, using technology not as a barrier, but as a bridge to understanding. The Library of the Future teaches us that through connection and dialogue, we can discover answers we never even considered.
In a world where curiosity and technology converge, the Library of the Future has found an unmatched friend: SOLE Voltaje, a solution guide designed to light the path toward knowledge. Together, they create a vibrant space where the internet isn’t just a tool, but an ally in the search for life’s Big Questions.

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.title: Test #01 SOLE Voltage
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.summary: Presentation Hi, I’m Nicolás, the cacharreo (tinkering) expert at Voltaje.
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.content:
Presentation
Hi, I’m Nicolás, the cacharreo (tinkering) expert at Voltaje. Today, we want to share the design of this User Test that we put together and ran in early 2024. We learned a ton during this process, and we’d love for you to take these ideas, make them your own, and use them to interact with your own communities.
Objective
To evaluate the functionality of three connectivity solutions currently documented on the Voltaje platform.
Solutions
The tricky technique
Installing a web server on a pocket computer.
SOLE – Voltaje · Guía de soluciones de conectividad

The easy tinker
How to boost your signal with a can?
Estimated duration: 10–15 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Guía de soluciones de conectividad

The easy technique
Restarting and sharing your phone’s internet with others.
Estimated duration: 10 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Guía de soluciones de conectividad

The tricky tinker
Building a homemade 3G antenna.
Estimated duration: 40–60 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Guía de soluciones de conectividad
Audience
Profile 1 - Doña Marlén, interested (+), skills (-)
She is over 50 years old, with a genuine interest in knowing how to use the internet to improve her way of life. She finds it difficult to use cell phones, computers, and browse the internet. She is a mother.
Profile 3 – Pepito, interested (-), knowledge (+)
He is between 14-21 years old, a student who likes using social media and playing video games. He likes having the latest tech gadgets and is well-informed about them.
Profile 2 - Paila Gorrea, interested (-), skills (+)
She is 30-40 years old, works with NGOs coordinating projects, and lives between the city and the rural communities she works with. She interacts with large funders to secure financing for NGO projects.
Profile 4 – Juanita, need (+), knowledge (-)
Methodology
We present VOLTAJE along with some categories of interest to us regarding its functionality. Then, we let the guests read and develop a solution individually, while in parallel, they share their observations regarding the presented categories. This is repeated with another solution. At the end of the solution, specific questions are asked regarding the categories of interest, and finally, an open group feedback session is held.
Observer
Your task is to be present, taking careful notes on how the user develops a solution by reading the instructions. You must be attentive to notice points of boredom and frustration.
Moderator
This is the person who presents and directs the final feedback. The other observers can participate by asking occasional questions, keeping the following recommendations in mind:

Avoid giving judgments and reflections.
Do not give opinions about the solutions.

This doesn’t mean you can’t prompt people for answers.
Since the central categories are “readability and viability,” the conversation will focus on these. The “accessibility” category might be explored in detail at a time when VOLTAJE is more advanced.
Agenda









































TimeMomentDescriptionTools9:00–9:15Welcome• Thanks for coming, welcome to SOLE• Let’s get to know each other: Name, what you do• (Optional) Tell us about a time you had an internet problem and what you did• Where are you located? Profile lines (Knowledge, skills, motivation, and need)SnacksPositional mapsPost-its9:15–9:25Exploring Voltaje• What do you know about SOLE?• (Optional) Short video about SOLE• Why are you here? (Sanjay)• Connectivity Solutions Guide• Reasons for not having internet: money, signal, knowledge• Self-management of connectivity (using internet in a group: learning, cheap, safe, fun)• You will test two prioritized solutions and give feedback• First solution: 20–30 min• Second solution: 40–60 min• We aren’t evaluating skills, but the solutions9:25–9:30Presentation of SOLE Voltaje and the exercise• How the Voltaje page is put together• Types of solutions• Meaning of icons• Structure of a solution9:30–11:00Testing the solutions• Device: cell phone or computer• Link sent via WhatsApp• Presentation of the 2 solutions and times• Build a homemade 3G antenna (40–60’)voltaje.solecolombia.org/#Construye%20una%20Antena%203G%20casera• How to boost my signal with a can (10–15’)voltaje.solecolombia.org/#%C2%BF%C3%B3mo%20mejorar%20mi%20se%C3%B1al%20con%20una%20lata%3F• Groups of 2 participants per solution• Observer per guest (takes notes)• The participant can express frustration or blockageEvaluation form11:00–13:00Group feedback• Guided conversation with questions• Listen to participant comments• Take notes in the feedback section
Observation during the test
Instructions:

Before the guest starts working on the solution, explain your role and why you are there in concrete terms.
You can hand the evaluation form to the participant once they have finished the solution or decided to stop.
Tell each participant to take their time and read each of the statements they are going to evaluate carefully.
10 minutes before finishing the test, ask the participant to stop their work and fill out the evaluation.

Observer’s role:

Foster a calm and trusting space for each participant. The observer should not judge what the participant is doing. This should be a supportive role.
Take note of the participants’ reactions and behaviors while they work on the solution; without making them uncomfortable, being invasive, or intimidating the participant.
Take note of the questions each participant has and suggest that they do/solve them as they see fit; but without over-explaining, helping, or trying to answer their doubts.

Suggested questions: How would you solve that doubt or problem? What do you think is failing in the explanation or solution that is causing you to have that doubt or problem?

Invite participants to evaluate each of the solutions calmly and honestly. The more objective and critical the participants are, the more useful the session will be.

If you have any doubts about your role as an observer during the test, take note of the doubt. You can only intervene if you see an imminent risk.
Final feedback questions
Reflection on the change in the device for profiling interest, knowledge, needs, and skills

Were there any changes in how interested you are in tinkering with gadgets?
Was there a change in how much knowledge you think you have?
Was there a change in how much skill you think you have?
How did you find the experience, how did you feel?
How did you feel?
How was the timing?
What did you find most difficult?
What did you find easiest?
What did you learn?
If you were to do this exercise again, what would you change?

Analysis tools
Possible categories (draft)
Under the umbrella of functionality, we can include different categories of interest. I propose the following, which are recommended qualities when creating instructional texts.











































































ConceptDefinitionQuestionsLegibilityThis concept refers to graphic aspects, typography, color, contrast, text distribution, layout, etc.Is the font type and size easy to read?Do the colors make it easy to read?Is the page layout appropriate?Are the images accompanying the texts sufficient or excessive?ReadabilityThis concept refers to the ease with which the text can be read, its clarity, attractiveness, completeness, timing, and comprehensibility.Are there ambiguous instructions?Are there incomplete instructions?Do you consider the grammatical tenses and the wording of the solutions appropriate for this instruction?Is the solution complete, or is a detail missing?I find it difficult to read because of the way it is written.StructuringThis concept refers to the order of the sections and, in general, the way the instruction is organized. Its internal logic and the relationship it facilitates for the reader so they don’t waste time.Do you think the structure is appropriate, or do you think it could be ordered better? Are all sections useful, or do you consider any to be unnecessary or missing?AccessibilityThis concept refers to whether the solutions contemplate multiple ways of receiving information: text, audio, video, image description, etc.Do you consider the solution accessible to different audiences?Do you consider there is any population group that would find it difficult to access the solution?Do you consider the solution is presented in a way that is accessible to beginners in the subject?

If the wording makes reading difficult. |
| Viability | This concept refers to whether the solution can be carried out, if it works; about the resources needed to do it, and if the solution is safe. | Were you able to complete the task this solution proposed to solve?
Did you find the activity dangerous at any point? |
| Traction | This concept refers to whether the solution sparks the reader’s interest in doing the solution and encourages them to continue developing related solutions. | Did the way the solution is presented encourage you to develop it?
Did the way the solution is presented encourage you to keep developing similar solutions?
Did the way the solution is presented generate interest/motivation for you to continue developing? |
| Learning | This concept refers to whether the instruction allowed you to learn new concepts that allow you to understand how the solution works. | Did you understand how the solution works?
Did you learn new concepts? |
| User test | This is an open category for participants to provide feedback on the exercise design. | |

Evaluation criteria matrix




















































































































































































































#CriterionStatement12341.1LegibilityI consider the font size and type to be appropriate for my reading.1.2The font color and contrast with the background make my reading easier.1.3The distribution and justification between texts and images facilitate reading and understanding of the texts.2.1ReadabilityThe way the texts are written makes my reading easier.2.2The texts communicate complete instructions.2.3I know all the words used.3.1StructuringThe order of the instructions is appropriate.3.2The number of images accompanying the text is sufficient.3.3The way the instructions are organized allows me to save time.4.1AccessibilityThe instructions are appropriate for beginners in the subject.4.2The instructions are presented to be used from different devices.4.3The instructions allow access to different types of audiences.The instructions allow me to develop the solution individually and in a group.5.1ViabilityThe instruction allows developing a solution that works.5.2The materials needed to develop the solution are easily accessible.5.3The instructions have any dangerous steps.6.1TractionThe way the solution is presented encourages me to develop it.6.2The way the solution is presented encourages me to learn about other related solutions.6.3The way the solution is presented invites me to know more about this topic.7.1LearningI clearly understood how the solution works.7.2I learned new concepts related to the topic.7.3I can explain to someone how to develop the solution.
Materials





















































#MaterialQty.Link1Ethernet cable (m)1Available in the office.2Fast-drying epoxy glue.5The Sintesolda brand has worked ferreco.com/inicio/6276-adhesivo-epoxico-sintesolda-rapido-transparente.html—CLQ7n5qPA_NQjMA_PR7nAZRoC2WEQAvD_BwE3Plastic cable duct (2 cm)2504Cut-resistant gloves2articulo.mercadolibre.com.co/MCO-502525366-guantes-anti-corte-proteccion-trabajo-nitrilo-industriales-_JM#position=6&search_layout=stack&type=item&tracking_id=3c36b974-e272-4bf2-b8c2-692cbf774a855Rigid pole to mount the antenna (a guadua bamboo as long as possible, 6 3 meters).36Coaxial cable (m)127Pack of plastic zip ties (10-20 cm)1
Supporting concepts
Instruction
By the term instructions, I refer to all discourses that order behavior or establish conduct, with imperatives, periphrasis of obligation, enumerations of actions, lists of facts, graphic illustrations, etc. Instructions include cooking recipes, traffic codes, contest rules, appliance user manuals, medication leaflets, employment contracts, or DIY guides. These types of texts govern our lives.
Criteria
Instructions should be:

For everyone. For beginners, who know nothing, and for experts, who verify details or solve problems.
Complete and precise: They must cover everything: all functions, all steps, all conditions, or all characteristics of the object or task.
Appropriate. It is convenient to organize them to “serve” the reader. There are no universal structures or a canonical order. They shouldn’t waste time.
Manageable. Besides being understood, each instruction must be operational. The reader must grasp it with one reading and must be able to execute it without difficulty.
Neutral. Without emotion, courtesy, irony, or humor.
Safe. Confusing instructions can cause accidents.
Comfortable: It is convenient to foresee how the instructions will be used and adapt them to the situation.






























Legibility criteriaExplanation1.1. SizeThe font size should be at least 14 pt.1.2. TextsThe texts should be justified.1.3. ContrastThe contrast should be opposite and facilitate reading.1.4. LayoutThe distribution between texts and images facilitates reading and understanding of the texts.1.5. TypographyThe course uses an accessible typography. Example: Verdana or Trebuchet.

































Readability criteriaExplanation2.1. WordingThe wording of the solution facilitates the understanding of the texts.2.2. ComprehensionThe instructions are easy to understand, regardless of the use of technical language.2.3. MotivationThe wording of the text stimulates and motivates progress in the development of the solution.2.4. Duration and course timesThe times for carrying out the solution are consistent with the instructions.2.5. StructureThe solution instructions are complete2.6.The solutions are missing details to explain
Recommendations
Below are other tips for writing instructions and recommendations:
Give each group of instructions a title. This can be the objective (installing a program on the PC), the final product (project budget), or the topic (office etiquette rules). The title allows referring to the instructions in other parts of the text.
Choose the most appropriate terms. These must be precise and also simple so that the reader can understand them. Also, ambiguous and confusing formulations should be avoided.
Select the appropriate verb form. It is better to use the imperative verb mode, which expresses a command or exhortation, using the “you” (e.g., avoid the terms) treatment. This way, we address the reader directly. The imperative is clearer than impersonality (e.g., “it is answered”) or the infinitive (e.g., “to answer”). Regarding the treatment (formal or informal), the Writing Manual points out that this will depend on the degree of formality of the text.

Start with the verb. Starting each instruction with the verb makes the writing clearer. The first thing the reader sees, at the beginning of each line, is what they must do.
Avoid negations, whenever possible. These are harder to understand than affirmations. It is better to formulate instructions affirmatively, if feasible.
Eliminate repetitions. Reiterating indications should be avoided. It is better to summarize them.
Homogeneity. It is advisable to maintain the chosen writing style in all instructions. For example, it is a mistake to start with a noun -as here, with homogeneity- if a conjugated verb is used in the rest of the instructions. It would be better to say “Write homogeneous instructions.”

Characteristics of an instructional text

The sequence of activities is presented in a correct and understandable chronological order, numbering them and using connectors that help the understanding of actions to achieve a result.
Graphic marks such as numbers, asterisks, or dashes are used to differentiate or sequence the series of steps.
It can be accompanied by graphics, illustrations, and/or drawings, depending on the type of instructional text to be developed.
It presents clear, precise, and linear language. It must be understood by anyone.

Guidelines for writing an instructional text

Determine the intention of the text.
Describe the physical resources and functions that make up the action to be performed.
Organize the writing into two parts, headed by a subtitle that identifies its content.
Number each of the steps.
Respect the chronological sequence of the process steps in the writing.
Use verbs in the infinitive, imperative, or 3rd person.
Use chronological connectors: to start, in the first place, in the second place, finally,
then, after, so, starting from, before, next, immediately, etc.
Add some warnings and precautions that the user should keep in mind.
Use appropriate language according to the activity.
Write with clear and simple sentences.

Instructions on how to climb a staircase
Julio Cortázar*

No one will have failed to notice that frequently the floor folds in such a way that one part rises at a right angle to the plane of the floor, and then the next part is placed parallel to this plane, to give way to a new perpendicular, a behavior that repeats in a spiral or broken line up to extremely variable heights. By crouching down and placing the left hand on one of the vertical parts, and the right on the corresponding horizontal one, one is in momentary possession of a step. Each of these steps, formed as seen by two elements, is situated a little higher and further forward than the previous one, a principle that gives meaning to the staircase, since any other combination would produce forms perhaps more beautiful or picturesque, but incapable of moving one from a ground floor to a first floor.
Staircases are climbed facing forward, since backward or sideways they are particularly uncomfortable. The natural attitude consists of standing, arms hanging without effort, head held high although not so much that the eyes stop seeing the steps immediately above the one being stepped on, and breathing slowly and regularly. To climb a staircase, one begins by lifting that part of the body located on the right below, wrapped almost always in leather or suede, and which, except for exceptions, fits exactly on the step. Once said part, which for brevity we will call the foot, is placed on the first step, the equivalent part on the left is picked up (also called the foot, but which should not be confused with the aforementioned foot), and bringing it to the height of the foot, it is made to follow until placing it on the second step, with which the foot will rest on this one, and the foot will rest on the first. (The first steps are always the most difficult, until the necessary coordination is acquired. The coincidence of name between the foot and the foot makes the explanation difficult. Take special care not to lift the foot and the foot at the same time).
Having arrived in this way at the second step, it is enough to repeat the movements alternately until finding the end of the staircase. One exits it easily, with a slight tap of the heel that fixes it in its place, from which it will not move until the moment of descent.

END*

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test02.title: Test #02 SOLE Voltage
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test02.summary: This document aims to set out the protocol for conducting Test 02 of the Solutions Guide, based on the lessons and findings from Test 01, carried out on 03.02.2024.
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test02.content:
This document aims to set out the protocol for conducting Test 02 of the Solutions Guide, based on the lessons and findings from Test 01, carried out on 03.02.2024.

What did we learn from Test 01?


Focus the writing of the solutions on improving clarity, language, and the order of instructions.
It is important that the writing of the solution makes participants feel supported through every step.
It is fundamental to understand that well-written steps depend on the strategic use of images, diagrams, or photos to provide key, relevant information.
It is important to focus efforts on improving: 1. the images that accompany each instruction; 2. the order, clarity, and organization of the instructions.
It is fundamental to have an initial section with the safety conditions that must be ensured before performing the test.
Before starting the solutions (for the Guide), perhaps suggest that people be in a comfortable, quiet, and safe space.
Participants said that the solution for the can antenna motivated them more than it challenged them, while the homemade antenna solution felt more like a challenge/frustration than motivation. We need to review how to manage frustration.
The tone of the guide should be one of companionship and compassion; a tone that makes it clear that the solutions are not for experts, and that anyone interested can do it. This tone is currently unclear. The ethical and political commitment of the guide should be clear in this tone. There is no clear communicative commitment.
It is worth reviewing which typography, font size, and layout facilitated reading. It would be worth testing with people who have difficulty reading on a computer. Also, test layouts with column distribution.


Progress: solutions must make participants feel they are moving forward. Participants must know where they are in the test and how much is left.
Companionship: solutions must be written in such a way that participants feel supported through a colloquial and approachable tone.
Strategy:
Confirmation: solutions must reassure participants that they are on the right track and that their progress is indeed correct.

Typology of images to be used for the tests

Result images: show the final result of the step or the solution being performed. These images allow participants to contrast the progress they are making with what the test asks of them.
Process images: show the steps necessary to reach a result or a specific step.
Context images: show the solutions with people in specific contexts.

Participant profiles
The following profiles can overlap. For example, there are people who may have very little knowledge about how the internet works, but may be very interested in learning for the test.













Interest: people interested in learning how to carry out a solution.Need: people who need the solutions to solve concrete problems.Knowledge: people who know quite a bit about how the internet works, or any of the pillars of the guide: electricity, space, convening people, space management, or connectivity.Skills: people who have soft skills and/or motor skills to carry out the solutions.
2. Objectives of Test 02:

Evaluate the progress made in the solutions based on the lessons from Test 01.
Verify the changes produced in participants by the audio-reading format for the solutions.
Receive feedback on the solutions regarding “how to convene your community” and find the differences and similarities with the “the internet signal is bad” tests:

3. Questions to formulate Test 02:

Participant profiles: Based on the lessons and objectives, who and how many people should be part of the test? How do we divide the test for the profiles of interest, need, knowledge, and skills?
Test format: Should we carry out the solution virtually and remotely? What is the reason we should do it this way? Does remote mean doing the test with a synchronous observer or, on the contrary, giving a time of a week and a half (for example) to carry out the test?
Care: What considerations and care should we have for the people who will perform these tests?
Expectations: What do we expect from the people who will perform the test?
Feedback/evaluation: How will we receive the feedback/evaluation from the participants?
Roles: What roles within the SOLE team are necessary to carry out this test?

4. Proposal for Test 02 (answers to the questions in point 3):

Participant profiles: Test 02 will be carried out by participants remotely, virtually.

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test03.content:
Common Ground Workshop
Title: Creating devices to reflect on our technological autonomy
Facilitators: Nicolás Gaitán, Manuela Cordoba, and Mateo Acosta, SOLE Colombia Foundation
Duration: 90 minutes
Description: First, we’ll set up some analog data visualization devices designed to spark reflection and dialogue among participants. After this initial warm-up, we’ll encourage participants to create their own devices with their own big questions to challenge the rest of the group.
Objective
To inspire the creation of reflective devices for managing data related to technological autonomy.
Time
1:30 h
Stages

Devices on autonomy, an inspiration (30 min)

Arrival at the space and interaction with the example devices. We will install 5 different devices that allow participants to reflect on their differences… Additionally, there will be a spot with reference materials for inspiration and others that are more thought-provoking.
Introduce the photo-taking process.

Device 1 - Colored stones: screen time


Question:
How much time do others spend looking at screens?
How much time do you spend looking at screens per day?
Materials: colored stones, spoon, canvas with a circular drawing, baskets to hold the stones.


Device 2 - Decision tree: Sharing and privilege

Ideally, everyone should interact in a group with this device. At the end, each person who follows a path should place a dot.
jamboard.google.com/d/1Y34vGSI9O59fpOe5OWD6ck5qWBsgEy-hZfoSQ56dwbI/viewer


Device 3 - Technological privilege ladder

Take a step if your power doesn’t go out often.
Take a step forward if you don’t usually have trouble accessing the internet.
Take a step forward if you haven’t felt worried about the amount of data (GB) you consume on the internet.
Take a step forward if you have a postpaid internet plan.
Take a step forward if you have ever bought a cell phone for more than 300 USD.
Take a step forward if you have never had to fix an internet problem on your own.
Take a step forward if you have more computers than the number of people in your house.
Take a step forward if you pay for more than 2 internet services (e.g., Netflix, Spotify, Google Drive, iCloud, Mubi, meditation apps, ChatGPT, etc.).
Take a step if you don’t usually spend time in public recreational and cultural spaces.

Materials: Masking tape, printout with the script of the questions.


Device 4 - Ribbons: a call to autonomous action


How much of a “tinkerer” (cacharrero) do you consider yourself?
How curious are you about how the gadgets you use in your daily life work?
Materials: Colored ribbons, 3 large sheets of poster board.


Device 5 - LEGO data; Awareness-information

If one LEGO brick represents 10 GB, place your thoughts in relation to the following questions:

How many GB of internet do you think you consume per month?
How many GB of internet do you think you need?

One person consumes more than 500 GB per month.

www.populoos.es/blog/cuantos-GB-consume-persona-mes/
[www.highspeedinternet.com/es/recursos/cuantos-datos-de-internet-necesitas#:~:text=El%20usuario%20promedio%20de%20internet,un%20informe%20reciente%20de%20OpenVault](www.highspeedinternet.com/es/recursos/cuantos-datos-de-internet-necesitas#:~:text=El usuario promedio de internet,un informe reciente de OpenVault).

Most people need 600 GB per month.
20230606_SOLE+WLH_Prst_Taller de Inspiración SOLE

Reference library

We will leave a section where people can go to consult other ways of presenting data.

Presentation, workshop overview, and reflection on data (15 minutes)

We present SOLE and Voltaje, and the tensions that emerge in our projects regarding data management. Finally, we move with the group of participants to reflect on their answers in the 4 devices.
Reflections
a. Device 1 - Colored stones: screen time.
The importance of “tinkering” (cacharrería) for the Latin American context, and how these methods allow for an approach to knowledge and local ways of learning.
b. Device 2 - Decision tree: Sharing and privilege
The paradoxes that distance our beliefs from our practices, and the mechanisms to mobilize them.
c. Device 3 - Privilege ladder: We are positioned from different places and histories, which enables or hinders our journey on this earth.
d. Device 4 - Ribbons: Estimating my internet spending
Real estimates of the cost of each type of consumption and a national comparison of the prices charged.
e. Device 5 - LEGO data; Awareness-information
Changing habits regarding access to information online and offline, new logics of cultural consumption.
General: Reflection, dialogue, and questioning VS extraction.

Designing your own devices (30 minutes)



Two truths and a lie regarding technology (10 minutes)
People will say two truths and one lie regarding technology, and the others will have to guess which one is the lie.


Device design (20 minutes)


Design a quick device to question, reflect, and dialogue about the use of technology both in your personal life and in the organizations where you work. Think of questions that the rest of the participants can answer and that can generate great conversations and new questions on the subject.

Materials: Table with possible materials for designing the devices, adhesive tape, newsprint, post-its, markers, colored pencils, colored stones, ribbons, yarn, sheets of paper, adhesive tape, adhesive dots, lentils.


Interaction with the devices (15 minutes)


Quick presentation of the created devices and the defined questions.
Invitation for participants to interact with these devices throughout the day.
We close with a general reflection and a thank you.

Resource economy
The particularity of a reflective question VS an extractive one
The power of visualization in questioning our habits, beliefs, expectations, etc.

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test04.content:
PURPOSE
Clarify user contributions to SOLE Voltaje.
Questions
Who wants to contribute?
Why do they want to contribute?
How is the contribution currently produced?
What obstacles (technical and non-technical) do users encounter when trying to contribute?
What non-technical changes can be introduced to encourage contribution?
The day after, how does participant contribution become a daily habit?
What elements are relevant/important for group interaction with SOLE Voltaje?
Moments
The hands-on one: Tinkering station and SOLE as practice
DESCRIPTION

What are we going to do?: Clarify user contribution through active participation in tinkering workshops and alternative SOLE practices (different from the usual practice under ideal conditions).
How are we going to do it?: Through tinkering activities and alternative SOLEs where participants can test this Station according to their motivation.
Why?: If people experience a creative tinkering workshop and alternative SOLEing, they can live and imagine use cases for their own challenges or personal/organizational projects and give us feedback regarding the event’s purpose questions.

DESCRIPTION
How do we realize that we are not alone in this tinkering business? How do we accompany and support each other in exploring solutions to improve our experience of using the Internet in a group?
The WhatsApp chat is a place for people who are having connectivity challenges or who are building Voltaje solutions to:

find a community that helps them get through the specific difficulties they have
be able to share/receive new solutions that are not in Voltaje
share/receive how in other places they are using solutions that may or may not be in Voltaje (for example, “5 tricks for…” or other content that we can find on the internet and see how people react) - watch out at the end, the invitation is to use the internet in a group
share/receive interesting information about connectivity challenges and solutions in the world, discoveries, work in other places, initiatives…
provide support to those who venture to explore the Voltaje space, and the test, and find themselves lost - helper?

The purpose of the activity is to observe how people participating in the challenges interact with this channel, analyze if it is important and useful for them, and receive feedback on the interaction that takes place that day to make the constructions and/or modifications required to fulfill its purpose, and provide support among all to the people who interact with Voltaje and the test.”
PHASES
Purpose:
Experience using the WhatsApp chat to share and discuss connectivity solutions. Each challenge lasts 30 minutes and the challenges can take place at the same time as participants interact with the rest of the installation activities. There is a group that starts at this station and is in charge of starting challenge 1; after 30 minutes, we notify the next group to start challenge 2 (the same is repeated with 3).
Activities:
The presentation of each challenge is done by Bel through the WhatsApp group

Challenge 1 (30 minutes): The group in charge of the challenge must decide among all the presentation entries which connectivity challenge they think is the coolest. The discussion happens live (between the people interacting in this group) and in the chat, with the people who are not at the location. People who are at other stations can also participate in the discussion, but those who facilitate or lead this challenge are those in the group that starts. In the chat, it must be clear which connectivity challenge they choose to solve.
Challenge 2 (30 minutes): The group that is left in charge of Challenge 2 must find the solution for the challenge proposed in the first challenge, consulting the SOLE Voltaje guide and what they have experienced in the rest of the space. The discussion must be reflected in the chat and the decision of which solution is the most appropriate must be clear to all members of the chat. They can request opinions and experiences from all members. The tinkerers in the chat can stimulate the discussion and can also encourage the exploration of the space in the workshop, or experimentation in the other stations.
Challenge 3 (30 minutes): the group in charge picks up the baton from the previous group (must understand it by reading the chat) and selects the interactions in the chat that they found especially useful or interesting. Then, they must analyze how the chat structure (such as message organization, type of responses, use of multimedia) contributed to the understanding and resolution of the problem.”

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-tests.content:
The Voltaje tests have been our way of exploring, testing, and pushing the limits of the solutions and devices we’ve built. It’s all about sparking that “tinkerer spirit” and encouraging a hands-on approach to technology and connectivity—one that helps us create spaces for autonomous, community-led learning.
Thanks to everyone who’s jumped in and participated with us in these tests, we’ve been able to keep finding new ways to stretch the blanket of the internet to more places and communities. Plus, it’s helped us get a much clearer picture of what we’re really doing here at Voltaje.

en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.title: What's the Internet all about?
en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.summary: The Internet is like a big, cozy blanket of solidarity that hooks the whole world together.
en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
When you think about the Internet, what’s the first thing that pops into your head?
If we think of libraries as repositories of human knowledge written in books, and today’s computers hold that information—plus a whole lot more—stored as zeros and ones in their memory, then we could imagine the Internet as the sum of all the information created and saved on every computer on the planet. These computers are connected through a network of cables and wireless signals, all swapping information back and forth.
The Internet is way more than just that, but in a nutshell: it’s a huge, decentralized network of computers talking to each other.
There are other communication networks in the world, like the postal service, telephone lines, radio, or television. A big difference between those and the Internet is that on the Internet, folks can communicate both ways and swap digital information super fast—at the speed of light!
