en/inspire/insp-who-is-solecolombia.content:
At SOLE Colombia, we’re tinkering away at a fairer, brighter future together, one Big Question at a time.
We spark curiosity in groups of folks, turning internet-ready spaces into Self-Organized Learning Environments (SOLEs). It’s all about recognizing our own power and helping our lives and communities really flourish.
We’re shaking up the status quo by building communities that learn beyond borders and differences, bridging the gap between people and ideas to create a more vibrant, shared world.
Let’s change the world together!

en/new-here.title: New here
en/new-here.summary: New here Welcome to SOLE Voltaje! An initiative by SOLE Colombia dedicated to improving access to knowledge through community-based solutions for using the Internet as a group.
en/new-here.content:
New here
Welcome to SOLE Voltaje! An initiative by SOLE Colombia dedicated to improving access to knowledge through community-based solutions for using the Internet as a group. There are three steps to start using SOLE Voltaje:

Get inspired: Explore our big questions, videos, and stories from the communities we’ve worked with.
Solve: Find a solution to help boost connectivity in your place, your community, or your region. Solutions are organized into categories: signal, electricity, devices, people, and space—because using the Internet as a group takes more than just a connection.
Got questions?: Share what you learn, drop us a line with your questions, join our “tinkerer’s” WhatsApp group, and help build this movement for a more inclusive Internet.

You’ll also find an experience to learn what the Internet is and how it works, plus an invitation to help us spread the blanket of solidarity so others can get connected too: SOLE Voltaje Disconnected.
Our Tinkerer’s Ethos

  
  

  📄 See video summary (Accessibility)
  
    This video complements the welcome to SOLE Voltaje by explaining our "Tinkerer's Ethos," a fundamental pillar of the initiative. Through this resource, you'll get to know the philosophy behind our community solutions for accessing knowledge.
  



SOLE Colombia, 2024

Have you ever wondered how the Internet actually gets to your house? Why do we pay so much to get connected, or what would it be like to live disconnected? Getting online might seem like magic, but it’s really just information traveling the world through servers—physical places that make it possible for you to read this right now.
For many, the “connected” world remains a mystery, either because they don’t have access or because they don’t know how it works. But here, we like to question everything. We don’t just go along with the mystery; this is a safe space to explore. Together, we can understand, question, and reinvent the future of the Internet.
SOLE Voltaje is that constant tension between what we already know and what’s left to discover, between the need to be connected and the desire for freedom and technological autonomy. Here, we develop tools, provocative ideas, inspiration, and spaces for collective learning that drive the use of the Internet as a group to answer Big Questions. We believe in another possible future for network connection: one that is open, secure, and where we can all decide how we want to be connected—connected humanly.
Everything you find here is the fruit of collaboration and the know-how of “tinkerers” (cacharreros in Colombia)—people who don’t accept “it doesn’t work” as an answer, people ready to solve problems, to take apart what’s broken until it works again. We want more people around the world to get excited about building the Internet with their own hands. You, too, can be an active tinkerer of the network!
To change the world together
The goal of SOLE Voltaje is to enable people or organizations working with those who have no or limited Internet access to improve their situation in a self-managed way, as far as their own resources allow.
These resources include the amount of money they can dedicate to improving their situation, the time they have to self-learn, implement, and test solutions, the number of people who could join them on their journey, and the level of complexity of the solutions they can develop.
Over time, we hope that people in rural areas and digitally excluded communities can use and link various solutions together to finally have a permanent community space with connectivity and devices to learn, dialogue, and create flourishing communities using the Internet.
There is also a pedagogical purpose behind this guide: to invite people to use technology, in a broad sense, to learn.
We would like to re-engage current users and invite new ones to get curious about the Internet and how it works, and how they can use it as a group to learn what they need or are interested in. That’s why, within the solutions, there is also a glossary of terms that teaches users technical and non-technical concepts so they can become active “tinkerers” of the Internet.
What is SOLE Colombia?
SOLE Colombia is a non-profit organization whose purpose is to create an equitable and beautiful future together, one Big Question at a time.
We ignite the curiosity of groups of people, transforming spaces enabled for the Internet into Self-Organized Learning Environments (SOLE), to recognize our power and allow our lives and communities to flourish.
We shake up the status quo by creating networks of communities that learn beyond borders and differences, building bridges between people and ideas toward a more vibrant shared world.
Did you get started?
If you want to know more about our organization and how we are changing the world, visit our website here.
We aren’t big fans of social media, but we do share some of the things we do here:

en/nuevo-aqui.title: New here: how to work on SOLE Voltaje
en/nuevo-aqui.summary: If you’ve arrived at SOLE Voltaje to write, review, or help organize content, take a breath. You don’t have to understand the whole system at once.
en/nuevo-aqui.content:
If you’ve arrived at SOLE Voltaje to write, review, or help organize content, take a breath. You don’t have to understand the whole system at once. This garden is tended step by step, just like when you’re setting up an antenna, organizing a workshop, or testing if a signal is improving.
The idea of this page is to show you the easiest path to get started without moving pieces that are already working.

What is this place?
SOLE Voltaje is a digital garden of practical knowledge. Here, we gather solutions, stories, concepts, and resources so that more communities can understand, share, and improve their relationship with the internet.
The content lives primarily in Spanish and is then translated into English and Portuguese with the help of AI. That’s why, whenever you want to create or fix something, start in content/es/.

What is this guide for?
It serves three purposes:

Knowing where to write.
Understanding which commands to use.
Avoiding the duplication of documents, databases, or files that were only temporary.

The most important rule is this: if something is already working, understand it first before you touch it.

Where do we work?
These are the main folders:

content/es/solve/: step-by-step solutions.
content/es/inspire/: stories, questions, and inspirations.
content/es/glossary/: concepts explained in simple language.
content/es/disconnected/: resources for working offline.
content/assets/: images, icons, and support files.
docs/: documentation for those maintaining the project.
scripts/: automations for translation, images, links, and metadata.

The content/en/ and content/pt/ folders are generated translations. They are not the usual place to write new content.

How do I see the site while I work?
From the Dev Container, run:
npm run dev
Then open:
http://localhost:8080
When you save changes, the site rebuilds so you can check how it looks.

How is the content updated?
For simple text changes:

Edit the file in content/es/.
Check that the tone is clear and friendly.
Run npm run dev to see it.
If you added images or made significant changes, run npm run content or npm run pipeline.

To sync metadata from the editorial databases:
npm run sync
To translate:
npm run translate

Where are the databases?
The main source is in Google Sheets. Only the current TSV copies are kept in the repository root:

solutions_status.tsv
inspire_status.tsv
concepts_status.tsv
disconnected_status.tsv
glossary_tags.tsv

If you see files like *_frontmatter.tsv, *_current_snapshot.tsv, old logs, or CSVs exported from tests, they are likely temporary artifacts. They shouldn’t remain as living documentation.

How to write with the Voltaje tone?
Write as if you were accompanying someone who wants to solve something with their own hands.
Better:

Let’s test if this solution helps you improve the signal before buying something more expensive.

Worse:

The user shall execute the wireless connectivity validation procedure.

Here, we prefer clarity, patience, and examples. Solutions aren’t just instructions; they are an invitation to tinker without fear.

What shouldn’t you touch at first?

quartz/, if you aren’t changing the site itself.
.github/workflows/, if you aren’t adjusting deployments.
package-lock.json, if you didn’t install dependencies.
Translations in content/en/ and content/pt/, unless doing a specific review.
Generated or temporary files.


Where to go next?

To create solutions: go to Soluciona →
To get inspired with stories and questions: go to Inspírate →
To understand technical concepts: go to the Conceptorio →
To learn about internal editorial rules, check content/CLAUDE.md in the repository.

en/solve/solv-agree-with-neighbors.title: How to agree with a neighbor on sharing internet?
en/solve/solv-agree-with-neighbors.summary: Set up community agreements to share internet signal from a house or shop.
en/solve/solv-agree-with-neighbors.content:
Hi. I’m Sanjay, and over the last few years, I’ve been working with communities in remote rural areas where the Internet is scarce. Together, we’ve figured out ways to extend the reach of available connections through neighborly agreements. In this specific solution, we’ll learn about the kinds of agreements you can make so that neighbors who have connectivity can share it with others at certain times and through different methods.
Reading this guide will take you about 5 minutes, and we’ve organized it into 5 key steps. Don’t be scared if some terms sound technical at first; the best way to do this is to read these recommendations as a group and take your time. At SOLE Voltaje, we want you to feel capable of handling your own technology.

What is agreeing with a neighbor to share Internet access?
In many remote places where people don’t have cell service (mobile coverage), we’ve found a person or a place that pays for an Internet service, and it turns out to be the only—or one of the few—ways to get online in that community. For example, the local shop that sells PINs to connect to satellite internet, or the neighbor who pays for their own home connection. Usually, this service is too expensive for most people.
This signal could be used communally by offering other community members access to the Internet if you propose an agreement with this neighbor that allows access under certain conditions.

What is it for?
This solution will help you establish an agreement for communal Internet use based on available connections. For now, we’ve identified the following:
Shop with Internet
Usually, there’s a shop in the community or village that sells groceries and offers internet service so people can connect with their phones for a set time using connection PINs WiFi Signal →—temporary passwords—or another password-controlled access system. The shop owner pays their monthly service fee, and any difference generated by selling the service gives them a profit.
Neighbor with Internet
There are people or groups who have the ability to pay for an Internet service in their homes or headquarters. However, they aren’t willing to share their WiFi → password because they don’t want freeloaders connected to their network, which would slow down their speed or eat up their data plan. This is the main reason for getting services that have access barriers like passwords.
This way, when an agreement is made with a neighbor, the community gets Internet access at specific times and at a lower cost than what it would cost each member to get their own service. On the other hand, the neighbor gets a contribution from the community to help pay for their service. Together, neighbor and community can make the most of the contracted Internet service.

Do I really need this?
In many parts of the world, getting Internet connectivity isn’t easy, whether due to a lack of signal, high prices, or both. This solution might be the only way for communities to get more members online.
At SOLE Voltaje, we encourage people to use the internet in groups because it’s cheaper, safer, and more fun—whether for learning, starting a business, or just hanging out. For example, so kids can do school homework or take online courses, to look for information relevant to a productive project, for health, or to sell products online; to download a movie, or to have a karaoke session so everyone can enjoy it together.
Food for thought: before proposing an agreement, ask yourself if there’s a public or community space that already has a signal that isn’t being put to good use.

Options to consider
There are two main ways we’ve explored for these agreements:

Communal connectivity time bank: This is an agreement to use the Internet connection for limited periods (e.g., 30 minutes, 1 hour, 4 hours a day) at the specific location where the signal is available (shop or outside the neighbor’s house), for a fraction of the total cost. For this, you need to define the uses and the value of the “bank” along with the type of Internet service the neighbor has.

Uses of the bank: Education (homework, courses), Health (paperwork, appointments), Recreation (movie club, dance), Productive (online sales).
Value of the bank: It could be a fixed monthly fee per family, rotating who is in charge of contributing each month, or contributing on-demand (whenever it’s needed).


Bank + Install a community router: This is an agreement that includes buying and connecting a community Router → to the neighbor’s Modem. This allows the community to connect to its own device rather than directly to the neighbor’s, which provides more privacy and range.

How to do it?
Below, I’ll share the steps that I’ve seen work best when we sit down to talk with neighbors:

Step 1 → Determine where there is internet in the community

The first thing is to map the area. Ask with curiosity: Which neighbors have an antenna? Who has a data plan they don’t finish by the end of the month? What kind of internet is it (satellite, radio link, or cellular)? This helps us know who we can talk to first.

Step 2 → Define the place to use the communal internet

The best place to connect isn’t always the neighbor’s living room (sometimes we want privacy, or they do too!). Decide if the internet will be used in the same shop/house or if it’s better to take it to a nearby community space (like the community hall) using a long cable or a Router →.

Step 3 → Establish minimum ground rules

Before asking for the password, agree among yourselves: What are we going to use it for? Who has priority (e.g., kids studying)? How much is each of us going to contribute? Having this clear prevents the neighbor from feeling like we’re “asking for a favor” and helps them see it more as a fair collaboration.

Step 4 → Let’s make a deal!

Sit down with the signal owner. Explain that the community wants to contribute so the internet isn’t so expensive for them and so everyone benefits. Define if you’ll use a Time bank or if you’ll install a Router so the signal reaches further.

Tip: Be transparent about how many people will connect so the neighbor doesn’t get scared thinking the internet is going to get slow.


Step 5 → Test and adjust periodically

What we agree on today might not work in a month. Meet up every so often to see if the money is enough, if the internet is sufficient, and if the neighbor feels comfortable with the agreement.

Encouragement: The best agreements aren’t the ones on paper, but the ones based on trust and mutual respect.


Don’t get fooled

“Unlimited internet” isn’t always infinite: Many companies say it’s unlimited, but after a certain amount of data is downloaded, the speed gets very slow. Ask the neighbor if their plan has a “fair usage policy.”
Sharing the password without a router is a risk: If you give your home password to everyone, someone could get into your equipment’s settings. It’s better to use a secondary router for the community.
Salespeople who promise magic: Don’t believe anyone who tells you that with a verbal agreement “everything is fixed.” Make sure the technical equipment (the modem) can handle several people at once.


How much is enough?

For homework and paperwork: You don’t need the most expensive speed. A basic 5 or 10 Mbps connection is enough for several kids to look for information at the same time.
For video and movies: Here you do need more power. If the neighbor’s plan is very small, it’s better to download the movies at night (when no one is using the internet) to watch them together later.

Sharing equipment: The internet is better if there are big screens: How to share available computers? →
The physical space: To avoid being out in the elements: How to get a community hall or any community space to use the internet in a group? →

en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.title: How to team up with others to boost your call?
en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.summary: Other folks can help your message travel a lot further.
en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.content:
Hi, I’m Belén. I don’t know much about tech, but I love people, and building relationships with them is something I’m pretty good at. I arrived at SOLE some time ago and I’ve learned a lot about the power of people and what we can achieve when we come together.

What does it mean to partner with places that bring people together?
There are many people and organizations that can help your message travel further and clearer, and who can turn your projects into a path for transformation in your community. Knowing how to reach them and grab their attention is a way to join forces and achieve great things.

What is this for?
Often, you want to count on your community to do things or learn together, but you run into trouble finding new people to join the movement, or you end up doing everything with the same old crowd.
With these recommendations, you’ll know how to approach others so they can support the call to action in your community.

What do you need?

Courage
Curiosity and the ability to listen
Something to take notes with


How to do it?

Step 1 → Define the purpose of your call

The first thing is always the “why” behind what you’re going to do. If you intend to partner with others, you need to be clear about the purpose of what you’ll be doing with them. Only then can you focus your search for those who can help you spread the word.
For example, if you’re looking for people to build an antenna, would it be better to look for them at a hardware store, during the workday, or at the exit of a preschool? Maybe a place where people go to find materials to build things or tinker (or cacharrear) is better. The hardware store owner might be a better ally than the school teachers for a call to build an antenna.
Even though you shouldn’t underestimate the talent in your community, you can prioritize the people and places you want to reach with a ‘why’ that is crystal clear.
If you can, define your proposal in detail: Is it one event, or a series of events? What do you need to have, buy, or equip your purpose with? Do you need more people, or are you doing it alone?


Step 2 → Locate the connectors

Look around you: in your neighborhood, in your community, in your town… you might even have allies in your own home!
Recognizing people and organizations with the ability to bring others together, and partnering with them, is a strategic move to get what we want.
Think about people and places where there’s a flow of people, people who talk to the community, think about those who organize events. These types of actors will be relevant for spreading the word… keep your purpose in mind so you can better see who has contact with the people you want to reach.
It’s worth asking ourselves how we can build networks to successfully call people to our activities. If you work on sharpening your skills to join forces with others, you’ll start to see how it flows better each time.

Photo: SOLE Colombia


Step 3 → Read the interests of those who connect others

Just as you want to organize a specific event, for example, hosting a SOLE, other people also have specific interests in the activities they want to promote.
Think about what catches the attention of each of these actors and how you can address both their interests and yours: including the other person in a negotiated agenda can win you a long-term ally, not just a one-time collaborator.
For example, if your interest is to create the habit of doing SOLE in your community, you could partner with the Local Action Board (JAL). Understanding how to use the Internet in a group to learn things together can meet the JAL’s goals related to planning and executing community development projects, or guaranteeing digital rights for the community. It’s a nice way to open the conversation about the activity you want to organize and how the JAL can support the call for your event.


Step 4 → Choose who you want to work with

Now that you’ve recognized the strategic actors to help you spread the word, and you know how to align their goals with yours, choose the one you feel most comfortable working with for each of your objectives.

Photo: SOLE Colombia


Step 5 → Work on the invitation and the message

Lay out your ideas and prioritize them. Developing each of your ideas deeply and finding the best way to present them to your ally is a way to practice your pitch and how the information can best reach them.
You can make a script of the possible questions and answers that might come up in the conversation. Put yourself in all possible scenarios, keep in mind the objections and problems your ally might have regarding your proposal. Having most scenarios covered, with a possible answer or alternative solution, will make your proposal look strong and solid.
Proposing a meeting to show your ideas with order and calm is an excellent way to guarantee the attention of your potential ally. Agree with the person or people who can give a ‘yes’ to your proposal, be punctual for that appointment, and prepare the meeting well.
Work on the order in which you’re going to present the information: a careful and orderly speech will let your interlocutor know that you are clear about what you want to do and will give them confidence in counting on you.
Don’t forget to make it very clear:

what you are inviting your ally to
what you will do and what you need from your ally
when you need it
for how long
who will be involved
how communication will work between you
how you will tell them what you’ve achieved thanks to the relationship that unites you




Step 6 → Find out how to make your proposal

Some allies might be available to you anytime, anywhere. Others have a more formal way of working or need to make decisions by consensus. Others even need you to send a written proposal before you can talk to anyone.
Approach the person, organization, business, or any other ally and find out the best way to present your proposal. Follow the instructions and organize your time so you can respond punctually to their requirements.


Step 7 → Present your proposal and listen

It’s time to show everything you’ve worked on! Trust yourself and the rigor with which you’ve prepared your proposal. We are sure that at this moment, with all the information you have, you will find the words to tell a good story that hooks your ally into doing things together.
Once you’ve made your point, listen carefully to your potential ally. There might be information you haven’t considered, so take note of the points that are weak or need expanding.
There might also be a moment of negotiation: you and your ally should have a scenario where both can win. Open your eyes and ears to anything that might have value for their purpose and strive to create a solid relationship.


Step 8 → Formalize the commitments

The moment your potential ally has everything clear, and you do too, it’s time to agree and clarify the next steps!
Put in writing what each person commits to and what the next steps are; it’s always better so nothing gets forgotten.
Thank the people who have attended to you; starting to work together is just the beginning, and celebrating that you’ve reached an agreement is a way to honor this new relationship.


How do you know if this solution works?
You’ll know you’ve succeeded in contacting places that connect people the moment you start speaking the same language and find common ground in the conversation.
For example, when someone who can bring others together pays attention to the proposal you’re making and wants you to meet their manager, or a colleague who can help you gather people. Or also, when you find yourself adapting what you’re going to say to the interest of the person who is listening to you, creating a space where the ideas start to belong to both of you.
If you exercise your listening skills, very soon you’ll be recognizing people with the ability to connect others and looking to get them interested.
If your purpose is to do a SOLE, you can start thinking about your Self-Organized Learning Environment as a place where several allies can start fulfilling their purposes thanks to your space, or, conversely, you can think of your ally’s space as a SOLE and benefit the people your ally connects so they can learn to use the Internet in a group to live better together.
You can SOLE any activity or space!

Other possible Internets
These recommendations are simple and focused. When you go looking for allies, a large part will depend on your communication skills.
Remember that you won’t always manage to convince everyone to work with you; the important thing is to do it many times: ‘practice makes perfect.’ And, at the same time, listen to your intuition to start creating a ‘radar’ in yourself that warns you of people who can be your allies… stay alert!

en/solve/solv-bandwidth.title: How to squeeze the most out of my bandwidth?
en/solve/solv-bandwidth.summary: Handy tips to get your connection running smooth.
en/solve/solv-bandwidth.content:
Make the most of your Internet service
Hi, I’m Manu. I’m no tech wizard, but I know how frustrating it is when a movie freezes or a video call drops out. So, after doing a bit of tinkering, I found some tricks to improve your home connection that I want to share with you.

What does it mean to make the most of your bandwidth?
Getting the most out of your internet service is all about using the settings and tools you have on hand to smooth out your online experience—whether that’s speed, security, or just being smart about your data.

Why does it matter?
Did you know that in the internet world, two terms get mixed up all the time? I’m talking about bandwidth and speed. Let’s break them down, and I’ll give you some tips to squeeze every bit of performance out of the internet plan you’re paying for at home.
Bandwidth and speed: what’s the deal?
Imagine bandwidth is like a giant delivery truck; it can carry a whole bunch of packages (data) at once. The bigger the truck, the more packages it can haul. But here’s the kicker: speed is how long it takes that truck to get to its destination. So, even if you have a massive truck (high bandwidth), if it’s crawling along, those packages are going to be left waiting!
In short: High bandwidth lets you move a lot of data at once, but if the speed is low, that data takes forever to arrive. And that’s exactly what drives us crazy when we’re trying to watch a video or hop on a video call!

What do you need?

A WiFi internet service at home.
A bit of patience and curiosity.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Use a network cable

If you can, plug your computer directly into the router using an Ethernet cable. This is like switching from a delivery truck to a high-speed train. The difference is night and day! A wired connection will give you the best speed and stability.

Photo taken from Pexels, (2024).


Step 2 → Connect to 5GHz if you’re using Wi-Fi


Screenshot taken by Manuela Córdoba, (2024).
If you can’t use a cable, your next best bet is to connect to your router’s 5GHz band. Think of this like getting into the fast lane on the highway: less traffic, more speed. Just keep in mind it works best when you’re close to the router.


Step 3 → Don’t forget about 2.4GHz

If you’re a bit far from the router and notice the connection getting sluggish, switch over to the 2.4GHz band. Even though it’s a bit slower than 5GHz, it’s often more reliable. Imagine it like a country road that’s always open, even if it’s not the fastest route.

Photo taken from Google Photos, (2024).


Step 4 → Adjust your Wi-Fi channel

Sometimes the connection feels slow because there are too many people in your neighborhood using the same Wi-Fi channel. Changing the channel can make your connection faster and smoother. It’s like moving your party to a spot where there’s less noise.
Go to Improve your router’s signal to follow the step-by-step guide.


Step 5 → Keep your router in shape

Finally, make sure your router is well-placed and up to date. Put it in a well-ventilated spot, away from other gadgets that might cause interference. A well-cared-for router is the secret to a solid connection.

Photo taken by Manuela Córdoba, (2024).

How do you know if this is working?
If you’ve checked your speed, your network settings, and your data usage on your devices, and they match up with what your service provider promised, you can rest easy knowing you’re getting the most out of your internet service.
By following these steps, you won’t just understand bandwidth and speed better—you’ll also be able to optimize your connection and enjoy your online time without the headaches.

Other internet possibilities
To make sure you’re really getting the most out of your service, besides checking speed and bandwidth, try running tests at different times of the day. Sometimes speeds can dip depending on how busy the network is overall.
You can also keep an eye on your data usage—check which apps and programs are eating up your data and set some limits to keep your consumption in check.

en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.title: How to generate electricity using a bicycle?
en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.summary: Get some juice flowing by building a bike-generator.
en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás. I’m what you might call a “tinkerer” or a cacharrero. I’m an engineer, and I’m fascinated by how things work. I enjoy taking gadgets apart and putting them back together just to see what makes them tick, and I also love figuring out how we can make the most of the resources we have in our community.

What is a bike generator?
A bike generator is a system that converts the mechanical energy from a bicycle into electrical energy. Basically, it turns your pedaling motion into electricity, which lets you power all sorts of things, like charging your electronics or even running lighting systems. (Source: Ecologismos)

What is it for?
This solution is a step-by-step guide on how to buy and assemble a power system using a bicycle. We’ve calculated it so that a laptop and a router can run for 3 hours, which is about how long a SOLE session usually lasts.

What do you need?

Money to buy batteries, cables, a power inverter, and a charge controller.
Energy to pedal.
An old bicycle.
Patience and plenty of enthusiasm to put the system together.
A stand to keep the bike stationary.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Calculate your energy needs

Figure out how much power you actually need. In this case, we need to power a laptop and a router for 3 hours. This will determine the capacity your system needs and how long you’ll have to pedal to generate the juice.

A laptop consumes 120W/h
A router consumes 15W/h

Now, let’s calculate the total energy load. You can find this info on the back of your devices or on their power bricks. For a SOLE session, which lasts 3 hours, for example:

Laptop: 120W/h x 3 hours = 360W
router: 15W/h x 3 hours = 45W

Adding those up gives us 405W over 3 hours. If we divide 405W / 3h, we get 135 W/h.
The bike machine can generate up to 200 watts/hour at a moderate pedaling speed, and up to 400 watts/hour at a high speed.



Step 2 → Estimate the equipment specs

Remember, to build any power generation system, you’ll need these components:
An electricity generator
This is any device capable of capturing and transforming some form of energy (mechanical, solar, thermal, hydraulic, chemical) into electrical energy. In this case, it’s the bicycle combined with an electric motor and a stationary stand.



A charge controller
Its job is to regulate the flow of energy from the motor to the batteries, controlling both the current and the voltage.

A battery
It stores the generated energy as chemical energy and releases it later as controlled direct current (DC).

A power inverter
This converts the direct current (DC) coming out of the battery into alternating current (AC) so we can plug in our devices.

Solar cable and accessories
You need electrical cable that’s sturdy enough to carry the electricity we’re generating.



Step 3 → Estimate the battery you need

We talked about an energy consumption of 405W over 3 hours, or 135 W/h. Beyond the total daily consumption, we need to consider the depth of discharge and efficiency.



Step 4 → Estimate the controller you need

For this, we have to calculate the input and output current for the controller.





Step 5 → Estimate the inverter you need

Since we’re using low-consumption equipment, we’ll use a modified sine wave inverter. The calculation is done by oversizing our total consumption by 25%.


Step 6 → Choose the right cable

Usually, solar cables are sized using the AWG (American Wire Gauge) standard.



Step 7 → Find a supplier

Look for an electrical supply shop and get quotes for this equipment. Compare costs between different suppliers and buy based on trust, warranty, and price.


How to use it?
Precautions

Heads up: Only connect one pole at a time so you don’t get zapped. It’s a good idea to work with rubber gloves.

Connecting the circuit
The motor has a negative and a positive pole. Connect the cables coming from the motor to the controller, and from there to the battery.





How do you know if this solution works?
With this setup, you’ll have enough electricity to power your SOLE. If you can turn on your computer and router just by pedaling, it works!

Other possible Internets
This solution gives you energy independence. Imagine a community network where every family contributes a little bit of power with their own bike.

en/solve/solv-build-3Gantenna.title: Build a DIY 3G antenna
en/solve/solv-build-3Gantenna.summary: Boost signal with a homemade antenna.
en/solve/solv-build-3Gantenna.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás, and for a while now, I’ve been learning how to improve my connectivity. I’m no expert, but through internet searches, tutorials, and, above all, trial and error, I’ve learned a lot.
I’ve already tested and installed several solutions, and today, I’m sharing one of them with you: the DIY 3G antenna. Let’s get to it!

What is building a DIY 3G antenna?
Building a 3G antenna means that by gathering and assembling easily accessible materials, you can boost the strength of the 3G and 4G signal for a cell phone or a MiFi-type modem.

What is it for?
This DIY antenna will increase the ability to receive the waves that carry the 4G signal (mobile internet), thereby improving the quality of the connection from your cell phone or a shared modem (MiFi).

What do you need?


3 mm thick aluminum rod (it has to be exactly 3mm).
50 cm of plastic conduit (ideally 2cm wide).
Quick-drying epoxy glue (comes in two tubes).
10 m of coaxial cable (or the length you need for the antenna to reach the connection point).
2 clamps or vises.
2 locking pliers.
20 cm of copper wire (recommended: 1mm thick).
A ruler (even better if you have a “caliper,” which allows you to be more precise).
Hacksaw (if you can get an electric angle grinder with a thin cutting disc, you’ll save a looot of time).
Fine-tip permanent marker (e.g., Sharpie).
Pencil.
Soldering iron, solder (tin), soldering paste (flux).
Pliers and wire cutters (the latter is optional).
Metal file.
Workbench with good lighting.
Plastic ties (also known as “zip ties”).
Pole to mount the antenna (a bamboo pole as long as possible or a rigid rod of any material).
Utility knife, cutter.
Wire strippers (optional).
Cell phone or shared modem (MiFi).
Plus… good vibes.
Patience.
Lots of precision.


How to do it?

Step 0 → Follow these safety recommendations

This solution has an intermediate level of difficulty and involves using some tools that can cause accidents if you aren’t careful. That’s why it’s important to keep the following recommendations in mind:

When using any sharp object, position it so that the cutting force is directed away from your body, not toward it.
Keep pets or children away from the work area, mainly because of the risk of contact with a hot soldering iron.
Before cutting, make sure the clamps, vises, or pliers holding the material don’t allow it to move even slightly when you apply force.
When using solder and epoxy glue, protect the work surface to avoid damaging it.
Do not hoist the antenna during storms, as the antenna could act as a lightning rod, attracting a strike to your surroundings.



Step 1 → Check the materials

Before starting, check and have all the necessary items on hand. In case you don’t recognize any of the materials, you can find them in the photo where the numbered materials appear.
You can buy them at the nearest hardware store since these are common materials; it shouldn’t be too hard to find them. Perhaps the most difficult (and important) item on the list is the aluminum rod. Sometimes you can find items made with this type of rod in the metal supports sold at discount stores that carry many imported products. At SOLE Voltaje, we have used different metals: copper, welding rods, and galvanized wire. We chose to buy a 3mm steel welding rod. If you can’t find aluminum at the hardware store, you can ask for other options; the important thing is that its diameter is as close as possible to 3mm or 1/8 of an inch.
Now, organize your workspace, keep these instructions handy, and divide the tasks among the people involved in the process: someone can be in charge of measuring, others of cutting, organizing, and gluing.


Step 2 → Understand the diagram

Below, we show you the final diagram and some of the assembly parts so you have a clearer idea of the final setup.


Step 3 → Measure, cut, and mark

It’s time to start! Now we get down to business; you must cut each of the 10 elements that make up the antenna. With the help of the caliper (or ruler), you have to mark the length of each one and cut them with the hacksaw or the angle grinder. It’s recommended to cut a millimeter or half a millimeter extra and finish adjusting the length by filing the edges with the metal file. Listed below are the lengths of the 10 metal rods you need to cut; in the world of antennas, these have specific names (director, reflector, and dipole) related to the function they perform.

This is the list of necessary cuts:

Reflector: 8.0 cm
Dipole: 18 cm (This should be the length of the element; the bent rod must be exactly 7.6 cm, for now, just cut the rod to this length).
Director #1: 7.6 cm
Director #2: 7.5 cm
Director #3: 7.4 cm
Director #4: 7.4 cm
Director #5: 7.3 cm
Director #6: 7.3 cm
Director #7: 7.2 cm
Director #8: 7.2 cm

📏 Remember that 10 mm = 1 cm

It’s important to mark each of the cuts with tape, as seen in the photo, to make the next step easier.



Step 4 → Bend the dipole

The dipole is an element bent into a “C” shape. Its total length should be 7.6 cm, but the rod needs to be a bit longer (approximately 18.0 cm). Making this piece is a trial-and-error task. In my case, it helped to slowly bend the rod against a circular tube 2 cm in diameter to give it the curvature.



Step 5 → Assemble the antenna

We’re halfway through the process—don’t get discouraged, we’re almost there! Now it’s time to mount the elements onto the conduit. This can be replaced by wood or some other material you have on hand, as long as it doesn’t conduct electricity.

On the surface of the conduit, you need to mark the following distances, where each of the rod cuts made in the previous step will be placed later.

Reflector: 1.0 cm
Dipole: 5.0 cm
Director #1: 6.2 cm
Director #2: 9.2 cm
Director #3: 12.8 cm
Director #4: 17.0 cm
Director #5: 21.7 cm
Director #6: 26.7 cm
Director #7: 31.9 cm
Director #8: 37.4 cm

Once the lines are marked, you can glue each of the rods with epoxy glue onto the conduit; however, we’ve seen that this configuration is very fragile and makes our antenna not last very long. For this reason, we found a better way to attach the rods to the conduit. For this, we can use the hot soldering iron, which can easily pierce the plastic with its fine tip; so, with this tool, we are going to drill the sides until they have a large enough diameter for the rod to pass through. Take advantage of the plastic while it’s still hot right after you pierce it to pass the rod through and ensure it has the right diameter. This must be done on both sides of the conduit so the rod can go all the way through.

Once you finish the 20 holes, you should disassemble the conduit and use the metal file to remove the plastic burrs to allow the rods to enter easily.

Now, before positioning each of the rods, we must make a small cut to facilitate the entry of the dipole; for this, we must disassemble the conduit and use the hacksaw to make a vertical cut so that it crosses the

en/solve/solv-buy-cellphone.title: How to pick the right smartphone for me?
en/solve/solv-buy-cellphone.summary: A phone that actually fits what you need and what you can handle.
en/solve/solv-buy-cellphone.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás, and just like you, I’ve been learning step-by-step how to improve my connectivity to do SOLE. I’m no expert, but through online searches, tutorials, and above all, trial and error, I’ve learned a ton and built some functional solutions.
What does it mean to buy the right cell phone for you?
In this specific solution, we’ll learn how to buy a Smartphone based on your possibilities and needs. Below, you’ll find a series of information, criteria, and tips that aim to be as clear as possible so you can feel supported in making your decision. The estimated reading time is 12 minutes and it consists of 10 items, but don’t be scared—you can read these with the help of others. Remember that at SOLE Voltaje, we want to promote the collective use of the internet.

What is this for?
In this solution, you’ll find a few practical tips to help you make a much more informed decision about which cell phones are the most suitable for you.

Before we start, some ethical questions!
At SOLE Voltaje, we believe in supporting people to clarify the ethical implications of a decision by questioning the circumstances that lead you to make it. This solution starts with the assumption that you want to buy a phone—but do you really need it? It’s not always the best option for you. Sometimes you have an old phone a family member can give you, or for various reasons, you might prefer not to have a phone and it’s better for you to have a computer. If, after scanning your options, you definitely decide you need to buy a phone, you’re in the right place! Here, we’ll advise you on what to keep in mind when buying a phone.

What do you need?

Saving money for the purchase.
Internet access.
A trusted store or dealer.
Curiosity.


How to do it?

Step 0 → How do I know if I need to buy a cell phone?

One of the characteristics of our current era is the massive development of international and national markets; our phones are made in China and we can buy them in Colombia, we can go to the market and buy rice brought from Brazil. Furthermore, we find disproportionate consumption options: we can buy white rice, yellow rice, bulk rice, lemon-flavored rice, etc. There are endless options to turn us into consumers of products we often don’t need. We end up buying non-nutritious food, and we fall into yet another expense that doesn’t satisfy the main function of food: nourishing us! In the same way, we fill our homes with endless merchandise that ends up gathering dust or being thrown away because, in the end, it was useless to us. That’s why we want to promote responsible consumption. For a phone, we suggest you ask yourself the following questions to know if it’s a responsible purchase:

Do you need to buy a phone, or do you have other options to access the internet and make calls?
Can you buy another option that covers your internet connection and calls, and that could be paid for by several people?
If you buy a phone, will it really improve your quality of life, or will it make it worse? For example, will you become addicted to watching content or being on social media, or will you be more stressed every month thinking about how to pay for this new expense?
Finally, is this new purchase really a priority for you?




Step 1 → What do I need a cell phone for?

Just like a car, the phone we choose must adapt to our main needs. It doesn’t make much sense to buy a 4x4 truck if you’re only going to be driving through a city with paved avenues.
Now, think about what the most important activities will be and where you’ll spend the most time on your phone: Do you want to take lots of photos of your region? Then you should pay attention to the camera features; Are you going to be out in the middle of the countryside all day, or are you going to use your phone as a modem to share your internet with other people participating in a SOLE? A good battery would be fundamental; Do you want to use the internet to learn in a group? A large screen with good definition is important; Do you want to play a high-definition video game? You’ll need a good processor; Do you need to work with several applications at once? Look at the RAM memory; Do you need to have many applications and large files? Look at the internal storage.
Now that you’ve decided to buy a phone, I’ll give you an introduction using my own case as an example:

💡 At the beginning of 2024, I dropped my phone getting off a taxi. Because of my work and contact with family and friends, it’s important for me to have a phone. I decided long ago that I wouldn’t invest more than 1,000,000 COP in this tool. About 5 years ago, I learned about a new brand that was emerging; it had good prices and very good references from friends and users on the internet. This brand is Xiaomi. My last two phones had been from this brand, each costing around 700,000 COP.
However, I searched online for references and saw that there’s a new brand arriving that is affordable: Tecno. I looked at several references and saw that it’s currently the best-selling brand on Mercado Libre, so I looked for a phone with similar characteristics to the previous ones: 256 GB of internal memory, a decent processor, a battery of over 4000 mAh, a large screen, and at least 8 GB of RAM. These characteristics are compatible with my work and personal use; I don’t take professional photos, nor was I looking for it to play video games. Finally, I found a phone from this brand for $475,000 COP. This phone I bought was a Tecno Spark 20 Dual Sim with 256 GB. So far, I can say it’s been an excellent purchase!


Now it’s your turn to identify what you need the phone for!


Step 2 → Set a budget

Before anything else, define what your budget will be. You can calculate how many days of work you’re willing to invest in this device. Don’t go into debt for a phone; we’re often offered financing for 1 or 2 years, and the phone breaks or gets stolen before we finish paying for it.

Once you have the above clear, you’ll know which features you should pay the most attention to.


Camera
If you love taking photos, here are some aspects that are central when examining your device’s camera:


Resolution
This is what we commonly know as megapixels. Although it’s very important, it’s not everything we should look at when evaluating a camera. The more megapixels it has, the more detail you’ll see in the images. However, you should have a limit. The standard could be a 12 MP camera, because if it has good features and excellent image processing, you’ll get high-quality photos. If you start having higher resolution photos, the files will be very heavy and will fill up your phone’s internal storage quickly.




Sensor and lenses
A good cell phone camera must have a quality sensor, as well as several lenses. The latter, in fact, has already become a standard. When combined, they allow for better images. One of the most popular lenses is the wide-angle. Thanks to this, much more information is incorporated into the photographs, and it provides a visual angle of up to 120 degrees, perfect for group photos or indoors where there isn’t much space.



Aperture
The lens aperture will be fundamental for a good photo; this feature defines how much light the camera can capture. It’s identified by the letter f followed by a number, for example, f1.9 or f2.0. The lower this number, the greater the amount of light the camera will capture. For this reason, it’s important that it be low, because with more light entering, the images will have more detail.



Screen
A screen will define whether our eyes get tired faster or slower, whether we see a certain degree of detail or not, or how fast the battery will drain.

When you’re clear that your phone should be a device used in a group, as happens when we do SOLE, this feature becomes important, since it’s not that easy for several people to read on a small screen.

Screen size
The size of cell phone screens has increased over time, although for a few years now they have remained without growing much, since they lose their portability function in your pocket. We could say that most phones are between 3.5” and 6” (this measures the diagonal, that is, from one top corner to the opposite bottom corner). Really, this depends on your taste: do you want a large screen that allows you to watch a video from afar with others, or do you prefer a small one so your phone doesn’t draw as much attention?




Screen technology
Full HD technology is more recent than HD, and the number of pixels is higher compared to HD, which works with 1,280 x 720 pixels. The Full HD system gives a much more realistic look to the image. This latest technology is only arriving in the latest phones with large panels, as high resolution doesn’t make much sense on small screens.


Type of screen
There are different types of screens, but in the current market, two are the most popular: those with LCD technology, also known as inorganic, and those with OLED technologies, known as organic.


LCD: These are backlit liquid crystal screens that usually cover the entire panel. In the past, they were the most popular, but they are being produced in smaller quantities. Being backlit, they will consume more energy, but for this very reason, they look good under direct sunlight.


OLED: These screens differ from LCDs because their materials allow them to generate light by themselves when electricity is applied. This allows them to turn each pixel on or off independently, so they consume less energy. In addition, they end up being brighter and having better definition of the color black.



Internal storage
Internal storage defines the amount of files we can save on our phone; it’s like the hard drive on a computer. This will determine how many programs you can have installed at once, and whether or not you can save all kinds of files. At the moment, we recommend buying a phone with at least 64 GB of internal memory. Also, check if it has the option to accept microSD cards to expand the capacity in the future.




RAM memory
This is the phone’s temporary memory; it helps with performance and gives a clue as to how fast applications open and how fast the phone flows. We recommend a minimum of 4GB of RAM.



Processor
The processor is the brain; it’s the one that is always awake and receives instructions. The more cores the processor has, the better performance it will have, although it will also depend on the brand. Here, the best option is to look at the name of the processor used by the phone that catches your attention and do a little research on your own. Hopefully, it hasn’t been out for more than 4 years.




Battery



Compare it with another phone
Once you have some interesting options, it’s important that you compare them. You don’t have to do this manually; there are several pages that already do this automatically. Below, we leave you some:


Versus
Movilcelular
Here we compare my phone against a Motorola:

Besides the fact that the Tecno Spark 20 is better rated in its features, we can see that in the Colombian market they have the following prices:

Motorola Edge 30 Neo Dual SIM 128 GB very peri 8 GB RAM - $ 849,900 COP
Tecno Spark 20 Dual SIM 256 GB Black 8 GB RAM - $ 499,000 COP

💡 We can have a better phone saving $ 350,000 COP by taking the risk of trying an emerging brand.

Don’t get fooled
It’s important that you constantly check out emerging brands; usually, brands appear with little advertising, very good features, and a low price. However, often out of habit and experience, we keep buying the same brand as our last phone. For example, my best friend has been with the Motorola brand since college. I think that although it’s a good brand, it has very high costs, and I prefer new, cheaper brands that have good references to save some money.
Another important element has to do with the warranty. When you live in a central city, it’s easy if something happens to the phone, as there’s a branch of all available brands in case you have to use the warranty. But in less central cities, for example in Bucaramanga, the brand of my current phone, “Tecno,” doesn’t have an office, so if you live there, you’d have to send the phone to Bogotá, pay more money, and wait longer for them to return it. But possibly in that city, there are service centers for more popular brands, as is the case with Motorola.

How much is enough?
This question is hard to answer, but I think we can rephrase it like this: Does the option you chose meet the need and intention you projected at the beginning? In the previous example, I showed you how I consider that the phone I currently have was a very good option for my lifestyle. These types of reasoning are what we want you to do when making a decision about the option you are going to buy.

en/solve/solv-buy-computer.title: How to buy a computer?
en/solve/solv-buy-computer.summary: The best computer that fits our budget and needs.
en/solve/solv-buy-computer.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás, and just like you, I’ve been learning how to improve my internet connection. I’m no expert, but by digging around online, watching tutorials, and learning through trial and error, I’ve managed to boost internet quality in areas where connectivity isn’t exactly great.
What does “buying a computer” mean for you?
In this guide, I’ll help you clear up some important points so you can make the right call. We’ll break down the main features of a computer and look at some recommendations based on those specs. You’ll also be able to weigh your own needs and budget. I hope you feel supported and confident as you move forward with picking out a machine.
What’s the point of this?
Making a purchase in a field where you’re not an expert can be a real headache. That’s why we put this guide together—to walk you through the process. Ultimately, this guide is here to help you make an informed decision so you don’t waste money or end up with a computer that doesn’t actually do what you need it to.
How do I know if I really need one?
Deciding whether or not to make a purchase comes down to two fundamental questions:

Take a moment to think it over: What need is this computer actually solving? Can this need be met in another way? For example, can you do the same thing with the smartphone you already have, or maybe a tablet?
If you’ve confirmed that your need can only be solved with a computer, it’s time to look at other options before buying. For instance, can you borrow a computer from school or the library? Can you get a donated machine from a family member or a local business?

If you’ve exhausted those options and have definitely decided to buy a computer, then this guide is for you.
What are the advantages of a computer compared to a phone?
Speed and capacity are two of the biggest advantages computers have over phones. With a computer, you’ve got a keyboard and a mouse at your disposal, which lets you type and navigate menus much faster. Plus, a computer’s larger screen lets you organize your digital workspace in a way a small phone screen just can’t.
These factors don’t just save you time; they also let you multitask. On a computer, you can switch between apps more easily and even have them open side-by-side on the screen. For example, you can have one window open with your resume and another with a job search site. Or, if you’re hunting for the best deal, you can have pages for several products open at once to compare them easily.

What are my options?

Desktop Computer

This is a computer designed to stay in one spot, like a desk or a table. The hardware components are usually housed in a tower case that holds the motherboard and all the other parts.


Laptop

Often just called a laptop, this is a computer you can move or carry around with relative ease. Laptops are small, lightweight, and designed with batteries that can keep them running for a good chunk of time (usually 4 to 5 hours). Screen sizes typically range from 11 to 15 inches.


Pros and Cons









































CategoryDesktopLaptopPortabilityStays in a fixed location.Can be carried around easily.CostMore affordable.More expensive.Upgrading & CustomizationIts hardware components can be upgraded and improved easily. This makes it easy to customize to your needs.It’s getting harder to upgrade its hardware components, as most are integrated. On some, you can change the RAM and the hard drive.Power IndependenceMust always be plugged into a power outlet.Since it has a battery, it can be unplugged for a few hours, though the battery wears out over time and eventually needs replacing.Energy ConsumptionConsumes more energy.Consumes less energy since its components are more compact.SpaceTakes up more space.Takes up very little space.

What should I keep in mind to make this decision?

Step 0 → Understand hardware vs. software

It’s important to know there are two basic parts to a computer: Hardware and software:

Hardware: The physical parts that make up the computer.
Software: The programs, instructions, data, and rules that tell the computer what to do.

Below, we’ll explain the main hardware components that matter when you’re buying.













































ElementImageDescriptionProcessor (CPU)This is the brain of the machine, definitely one of the most important factors. Remember, the more powerful this is, the faster the computer will execute your commands.StorageThe hard drive determines how much storage capacity your machine has.RAM MemoryRAM temporarily stores data for the apps you’re currently running. The more RAM your computer has, the better it can run multiple programs at once.Graphics CardThe graphics card handles processing data related to images and videos displayed on the computer.PeripheralsThese are the input and output ports for other devices you’ll connect to your computer. For example: USB ports, audio jacks, HDMI connections, etc.ScreenThis is what lets you see what you’re doing on your computer.BatteryOnly applies to laptops; it determines how long you can use the device without being plugged into power.


Step 1 → Know the key criteria

Now that you know the main hardware components, let’s talk about the specs that affect performance and cost, and the questions you should ask yourself.








































ElementDetailRelevant QuestionsProcessorIf you want a fast computer that handles tasks effectively without slowing down, look at the number of cores. Also, check the frequency or clock speed. Higher is better, measured in GHz (gigahertz). So, 3GHz is much better than 2.5GHz. As for brands, here’s the advice: If you can afford it, go for Intel; if you need something cheaper, go for AMD. And if you’re really tight on cash, choose a Celeron.How many programs will you use at once? What will you use the computer for (designing, browsing, gaming)?Intel or AMD?How many cores?Storage500 GB is plenty for “normal” home use. If you like saving movies, series, etc., you might need a hard drive of 1 TB (terabyte) or more. Speed is also key. It’s measured in revolutions per minute (rpm)—higher speed means faster reading and writing of data. There are two main technologies: The traditional hard drive (HDD), which is slower but cheaper. The other is the solid-state drive (SSD), which is faster but more expensive.SSD or hard drive? How much info are you going to save? Do you want the computer to turn on quickly?RAM MemoryThe more RAM your computer has, the better it can run different programs at the same time. How much RAM you need depends 100% on how you use it. The more programs you run (like design or editing software), the more you’ll need. If you’re doing design work, gaming, or just have the budget and want a very fast computer, get 16GB. For standard tasks (writing, browsing, etc.), 8GB is enough. If you’re on a tight budget, you can settle for 4GB, but be prepared for the computer to be a bit sluggish.What programs will I use? How many GB do I need?Graphics CardThis might be important or not, depending on your use. For basic, standard tasks, any graphics card works. But if you need to do graphic design or gaming, a dedicated graphics card is ideal. Don’t overcomplicate it. For standard use, you don’t need a fancy graphics card. Any Radeon or Nvidia card will serve you well.Will I use it for gaming or design programs?Nvidia or Radeon?ScreenYou’ll be staring at this screen a lot, so it needs to be comfortable and easy on your eyes. Keep these in mind:Size: If you need to carry the device around, 14 inches is ideal. If you’re doing graphic work, you’ll need something bigger.Resolution: There’s no point in buying a big screen with bad resolution. 1080p is Full HD and is quite good. Monitors up to 23” are recommended to avoid the pixelated look that low-resolution images have.How many inches do I need? What resolution is enough for my needs?Do you need to run several programs at once while designing or watching your favorite movies?AudioThis depends on the speakers you buy for a desktop. For laptops, audio isn’t usually their strong suit, though “gamer” laptops often come with great sound.Do you need extraordinary sound for parties or movies, or do you already have great speakers you can plug in?


Step 2 → Make the decision

Now that you know the basics, it’s time to decide. We’ve put together some simple questions; depending on your answers, we’d recommend one hardware spec over another:

Criterion 0: Set a budget

Time to set a budget! You can calculate how many days of work it takes to pay for this computer. Ultimately, the decision comes down to this. This purchase can easily represent more than a month’s work, so it’s very important to be as informed as possible before deciding.

Criterion 1: Usage habits

Let’s look at the most relevant questions for defining your habits:

Do I need the computer to be portable, or will I use it in one place?
Will I use it for gaming and design programs, or just for office work?
How much information am I going to save?
Do I need to use several programs at the same time?

With these questions and your budget, you can narrow down your list of options. Choose wisely.

Don’t get fooled
It’s important to remember that when you go to a store, a salesperson usually tries to push the “star product.” However, the cost of computers from 6 months or a year ago is often significantly lower than the latest tech. Sometimes, you can find second-hand computers that have been well-cared for and get a great deal. Also, I highly recommend buying a desktop or a laptop that lets you upgrade its hardware.
The computer I’m writing this on, I bought 13 years ago. It’s had its hard drive replaced and its RAM upgraded, plus a few repairs, but it still works well and has been a great long-term investment.
Finally, remember that it’s very easy to find pages and people dedicated exclusively to reviewing and evaluating computer performance. Some sites even let you compare options. Once you’ve selected the computers on the market that fit your case, use these sites and user comments to make a more accurate decision.
One last piece of advice that never hurts: go by the reputation of the brand and the seller. In my experience, I recommend ASUS for value for money, although at SOLE, we’ve also had good luck with Lenovo.

How much is enough?
This is a tough question, but I think we can rephrase it: Does the option you chose meet the need and intention you started with? In my case, 13 years ago, I bought a computer for university, but I also wanted to play video games and download/watch a lot of movies. If I had gone for the minimum (just enough for university), I should have chosen a lightweight laptop with good battery life, a small screen, a mid-range processor, 8GB of RAM, and a generic graphics card. Instead, I did the exact opposite: I chose a big, heavy computer with poor battery life and a dedicated graphics card—what they’d call a “gamer” computer: the ASUS N53SV.
Because I didn’t think my decision through, I ended up with a computer that was too big and heavy to carry around and had terrible battery life. In the end, its main job was university work; the gaming and movies were secondary. Right now, even though I use it, I almost never move it. In practice, it ended up being a desktop computer. That’s why at SOLE Voltaje, we don’t want you to make the same mistakes I did! Always remember that often “less is more.”
With what we’ve just covered, you can’t be easily tricked anymore. It’s time to make the decision!
