en/solve/solv-pocket-wikipedia.title: How to access an encyclopedia without internet?
en/solve/solv-pocket-wikipedia.summary: Install Kiwix, a pocket Wikipedia on your Raspberry Pi.
en/solve/solv-pocket-wikipedia.content:
Hi! I’m Gabriel and I’m an artist. I love technology and I’m one of the original tinkerers at SOLE Colombia. I’m no expert, but I’ve learned through trial and error, and that’s the best way to learn!

What is the Pocket Wikipedia?
Imagine you could fit the world’s biggest library into a little box that fits in your hand. That’s Kiwix: a program that saves all of Wikipedia (text and images included) so you can look things up even if you don’t have a single bit of internet.

What’s it for?
Having a pocket Wikipedia on your Raspberry Pi lets you take knowledge anywhere: a rural school or your own home. It’s like having your own water well; the information is always there, ready for whenever someone has a Big Question.

What do you need?

Your Raspberry Pi up and running.
A computer to give it instructions.
Internet connection (only for the initial download).
Lots of patience.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Connect to your Raspberry Pi

Before we start, make sure your Pi is powered on. We’re going to talk to it from our computer using a Terminal and starting an SSH connection.



Step 2 → Download Kiwix

Kiwix is the tool in charge of searching for the information. Copy and paste this into your Terminal:
wget download.kiwix.org/release/kiwix-tools/kiwix-tools_linux-armhf.tar.gz



Step 3 → Download the content (Wikipedia)

Now let’s go get the content. We’re going to download a version of Wikipedia in Spanish.
wget download.kiwix.org/zim/wikipedia/wikipedia_es_all_mini_2022-11.zim

Hang in there: If the internet is slow, don’t despair. Once it finishes, you won’t need the internet ever again to read this!



Step 4 → Organize the files

We’re going to unzip the tools and move them to the Pi’s executable folder.
tar -zxvf kiwix-tools_linux-armhf.tar.gz
sudo mv kiwix-tools_linux-armhf-3.3.0-1/* /usr/local/bin


Step 5 → Locate the data file

The .zim file needs to go into a special folder so the program can find it quickly:
sudo mv wikipedia_es_all_mini_2022-11.zim /var/local/


Step 6 → Set up the automatic service

We’re going to create a service so Kiwix starts up on its own as soon as you plug the Pi into power.
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/kiwix.service
Paste this content inside:
[Unit]
Description=Kiwix Service
After=network.target
 
[Service]
Type=simple
User=root
Group=root
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kiwix-serve /var/local/wikipedia_es_all_mini_2022-11.zim -p 8080
Restart=always
RestartSec=3
 
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target


Step 7 → Start the service

Tell the Pi to recognize this new service and start it:
sudo systemctl enable kiwix
sudo systemctl start kiwix

You’re doing great: You’re almost finished!



Step 8 → Open your library from any device

Done! Now, from any smartphone or computer connected to the same local network as your Pi, open your browser and type: solevoltaje.local:8080.

How to know if this solution works?
If you go to that address and see the Wikipedia search bar and can browse through articles, you nailed it!

Other possible Internets
With your pocket Wikipedia, you can now organize SOLE sessions in any park or community center, regardless of whether there’s cell service.

en/solve/solv-powerbank.title: How to pick the right battery for your gear?
en/solve/solv-powerbank.summary: Learn to calculate real battery load and choose the best fit for your setup.
en/solve/solv-powerbank.content:
Hi, I’m David. I’m your guide and fellow tinkerer. I enjoy understanding devices by taking a look at how they work. I recently learned that not all batteries are created equal and that labels sometimes tell us half-truths.

What is the real capacity of a battery?
Almost all batteries claim to have a number in mAh (milliampere-hours). The problem is that during the charging process, some energy is lost as heat. That’s why the real capacity is always lower than what the box says.

Why does understanding this matter?
Understanding this helps you avoid wasting money on gear that promises the moon but delivers very little. Knowing how much real energy you have in your pocket is the difference between staying connected or being left in the dark.

How do I know if I need this?

You feel like your power bank drains way too fast.
You want to buy a battery for a laptop and aren’t sure if it will work.
Your community wants to buy a large charging station to share.






























Battery TypeIdeal UseAdvantageDisadvantageSmall Power BankPhones and tablets.Fits in your pocket.Won’t charge laptops.Power Delivery (PD) BatteryModern laptops.Packs a lot of punch (watts).You need special cables.Power StationCommunity use, lights, radio.It’s a big “well” of energy.Expensive and heavy.

How to do it?

Step 1 → Do the “toll” math

Look at the mAh number on the box. To know what you’ll actually get, multiply it by 0.7. If it says 20,000 mAh, you’ve really got about 14,000 mAh of usable power.


Step 2 → Look for the “High Power” (PD) seal

If you need to charge a laptop, look for a battery that says Power Delivery or PD and has at least 45W or 65W.

Tip: If the battery is too weak, it simply won’t charge the laptop even if it’s plugged in.



Step 3 → Get ready for the sun

If you’re going to be away from an outlet for several days, look for a battery with a solar panel input.


Step 4 → Check your cables

For heavy-duty work, use thick, original cables. A thin cable is like a clogged hose: the energy can’t flow fast enough.

Heads up: Never leave a battery charging in the sun inside a closed car. The heat can damage it or cause a fire.



Don’t get fooled
The market sometimes lies with the numbers. My recommendation is to always check reviews from other people. Don’t trust exaggerated numbers on tiny devices.

What can you achieve with this solution?
You ensure that community work doesn’t grind to a halt. Whether it’s logging data in a remote village or keeping a community radio station running, these batteries give you peace of mind.

en/solve/solv-prueba-ia.title: How to download an encyclopedia to your phone?
en/solve/solv-prueba-ia.summary: Wikipedia in your pocket for offline use.
en/solve/solv-prueba-ia.content:
Using television as a learning tool to do SOLE
What is it for?
Imagine you could turn the TV into a space for communication and learning that doesn’t just go from the channel to the audience, but where the audience helps create the content and everyone learns together. In places where the internet signal doesn’t reach, or if part of the audience can’t get online, using television can extend your reach, especially so that children and young people can explore and connect to the network.
So, if you have a mass media or community TV channel, you can generate a Self-Organized Learning Environment, or SOLE by TV. This allows people in the community—whether they have internet or not—to learn and dialogue through the television around Big Questions.
Doing a SOLE TV means creating a new type of TV content built by asking the audience to answer a Big Question and then inviting folks to send in their answers to share on a show. Having many answers lets us spark a live conversation where we’re all experts because we build knowledge together… just like the internet!
What do you need?

A television channel (mass media, community, or online).
A host.
An audience (at least 2 people).
A time slot for the TV show (you can call it SOLE TV).
Internet access and/or social media (optional).
A video recorder or cell phone (optional).
The energy of a TV host.

How to do it?
Define the Big Question and the show date

Sole Colombia
BIG QUESTION: Define a Big Question that motivates self-organized learning using the media tools you have on hand. The Big Question is what will hook the audience into participating in this SOLE TV.
LIVE SHOW DATE: Set a date so the audience can participate and watch the show; you should start calling for answers to the Big Question about 15 days in advance.
Invite the audience to answer

Sole Colombia
CALL TO ACTION: Broadcast the Big Question through messages or short promos on the channel, inviting the audience to answer via an online form, social media comments, calling the channel, or by recording answers on the street. In the invitation or online form, include the date of the live show and ask for contact info from those who respond so you can reach out to them directly. Some people might have social media like WhatsApp or Facebook to participate that way. Others could participate by calling the channel directly or showing up in person at the station. You could also collect answers on the street by recording them with video equipment or a cell phone.
Plan the live show

Pexels
SHOW SCRIPT: While you’re receiving answers to the Big Question, you can organize a simple rundown of the show and some audiovisual bumpers to accompany the live broadcast. For a 1-hour show, it’s worth thinking about the following:

How to introduce the Big Question?
Invite 2 to 5 people based on their submitted answers to participate in the live show and share their thoughts.
What other questions could deepen the learning during the live broadcast?
Select other answers to share during the broadcast.
What other methods could we use to interact with the audience?

Then, prepare a simple script for the show’s segments. Here’s a reference:

Intro bumper, welcome, introduction of guests.
Presentation of the Big Question.
First round of answers between guests and answers sent by the audience.
Invitation for the audience to participate via social media.
New questions to dig deeper.
Second round of answers between guests and answers sent by the audience.
Conclusion of the conversation, thanks, and congratulations to the participants for their autonomous learning.

Broadcast the live show

Sole Colombia SOLE TV: Broadcast a live show using the script as a guide, but allow for an unstructured conversation combined with other pre-recorded audience answers and/or social media input to solve the Big Question together. Guests can do some research beforehand. You can also invite people to the show who have knowledge about the answer to share it in the space, or people who are great conversationalists to stir up a lively discussion. The host or participants can dig deeper with new questions that pop up.
What is achieved?
In many places, there’s no internet signal, but there is television. Also, even if there is an internet signal, people might not be able to afford it. Therefore, television becomes a medium that can allow people to learn with or without the internet.
However, television is usually a one-way medium, from the broadcaster to the audience. The audience rarely gets to participate in building the learning at the station.
Successfully transforming television into a Self-Organized Learning Environment (SOLE) and a space for civic interaction allows communities that don’t have the internet (or have limited access) to learn, dialogue, and create flourishing communities using television or a combination of television and the internet.
How far can you go?
Television is a very powerful medium because many people can access it for free. Especially for many children and young people, it might be the only communication device they have access to. It will never be the same as having internet access, since the internet is the largest library in the world, which also allows you to connect with millions of people all over the planet. However, television also allows you to connect with many people; the challenge is for them to be able to dialogue with the television to learn together. This is what SOLE TV does.

en/solve/solv-purchase-temp-satellite.title: How to get a temporary satellite internet connection?
en/solve/solv-purchase-temp-satellite.summary: A code or PIN to get online via satellite.
en/solve/solv-purchase-temp-satellite.content:
A code or PIN to access satellite internet
Hi there! I’m Belén. I didn’t write this whole solution myself, but reading through it brought back memories of so many SOLE sessions that only happened thanks to this trick. Finding a spot that sells a few data chunks or minutes of satellite internet has allowed us to bring SOLE to places we never thought we’d reach.
What is getting an Internet PIN?
Accessing the internet via a satellite connection is a solid bet in places where cables or phone lines don’t reach, like rural or remote areas. In a city, it’s a decent, budget-friendly alternative to the usual setups.
In Colombia, a “satellite connection PIN” is just a code or key that unlocks internet or communication services via satellite. You might need these codes to activate a satellite internet service, like Starlink, or to set up satellite gear in areas with zero terrestrial network coverage.
This solution explains how to access satellite internet as a pay-as-you-go service, by the hour or by the day.
What’s it for?
If you only need internet for something specific, this is your go-to solution. For example, if you want to gather your community to learn together—doing a SOLE—and you need enough data to share across two or three computers so everyone can ask the web about the things they’re curious about, this is the best way to guarantee a connection.
What do you need?

An internet provider in the area.
Cash to pay for the PIN.
A device to get online.

How to do it?
Follow these steps to buy your PIN and get connected:

Step 1 → Check if this service is available in your area

First things first, you need to know if this service is actually offered in your neck of the woods. This usually exists in places where standard mobile data networks don’t reach. If they did, it would be way more practical to just top up your phone with a data package or get a postpaid plan.
In some places, internet providers resell satellite connections where cables can’t reach or where they know folks can’t sign up for standard mobile phone plans. For example, here’s a company that offers this kind of service in Barranquilla: Zonawipi


Step 2 → Weigh your options before deciding

If you found the service in your area, take a second to see if it actually makes financial sense for you. If you have to keep buying PINs and traveling to another spot just to get online every day, this might not be the most sustainable option. Maybe another solution, like pooling money for community internet, would be better.
But if it’s definitely the best way to go, then go for it!


Step 3 → Buy the PIN and start surfing

Now that you’ve decided to buy a PIN, make sure you get the most out of it. Your connection time will be limited to the areas where this network reaches. In practice, it works just like an internet café where you connect wirelessly with your own device.
Just follow the instructions on the slip where your PIN is printed. Usually, you’ll need to connect to a WiFi → network, which will automatically redirect you to a page asking for your PIN to grant you internet access. That’s it! Now get connected and enjoy!
Remember, you’ll get the most out of your internet connection if you share it with others who can’t access this resource. A great way to learn and have fun together is by doing a SOLE. SOLE is a methodology where you can solve real-life challenges through Big Questions, using the internet. Does your community want to learn how to get better yields from their crops? Do you want to know what games kids in other countries play? Do you have questions about how a specific weather phenomenon happens or how to make the most of climate changes? Do a SOLE! You can find more info at Sole Colombia.

How do you know this solution works?
This solution gets you a temporary internet connection in a specific location.
Why might this solution work?
We have to be careful to measure the bandwidth → the service offers and, in general, the quality of the service relative to the cost. This solution is meant for occasional use; if you start using it all the time, it’ll get pretty expensive, and you’d be better off signing up for a different kind of service.

Related solutions

How to share internet from my cellphone? →
Which WiFi networks are free and available for me to connect to the internet? →

en/solve/solv-radio-link.title: How to connect two sites with a radio link?
en/solve/solv-radio-link.summary: Set up a wireless internet bridge between two distant points using directional antennas.
en/solve/solv-radio-link.content:
Hi, I’m David, and this is one of those solutions I figured out after a lot of exploring, asking questions, tinkering, and wrestling with something that seemed impossible at first.
I didn’t arrive at this from a classroom. I got here by asking myself: is there a way to connect two distant places using the air as a path, without having to lay a cable? I haven’t done it yet—this guide is part of the process of preparing to try. When I started researching, there was no reliable cellular signal available, and the first answer I found was that it was impossible.
But I explored, asked around, researched, and discovered that what seemed impossible has a name and is done with two antennas, a bit of patience, and a desire to understand how information travels through the air.
They call it a radio link. And this guide is what I wish I had found from the very beginning.

What is a radio link?

A radio link is a system that connects two places using radio waves as if they were an invisible bridge in the air.
Imagine you have a very powerful flashlight and you point it directly at another person holding a mirror. The light travels from one to the other without touching anything in between. That’s what a radio link does: instead of light, it uses an internet signal; instead of flashlights, it uses special antennas.
What makes this type of connection special is that the antennas don’t transmit in all directions (like your home WiFi, which is omnidirectional), but rather they aim all their energy toward a single point, like a megaphone that directs your voice exactly where you want it to go. This allows them to reach very far, from a few hundred meters to tens of kilometers.
Technically, “radio link” is the general name. When high frequencies are used (above 1 GHz), they are also called microwave links. These are the same systems that telecommunications companies use to connect cell towers, but in smaller, more accessible versions for communities.

What is it for?
This solution is for bringing internet from a place that has a connection to another that doesn’t, when the distance between the two makes it impossible or too expensive to lay a cable.
Think of it this way: if the town center has fiber optic internet, and 8 kilometers away there is a rural community that has never had a connection, a radio link can be the bridge that joins those two spaces.
Some of the possibilities it opens up:

A single internet connection shared among several families or an entire community, reducing the cost for everyone.
Connecting the local school to the internet without paying for cable infrastructure.
Bringing a signal from a high point (an antenna, a tower, a hill) down to homes in the valley.
Connecting a community organization’s headquarters with a neighboring antenna that already has a signal.

In Colombia, communities like those in Buenos Aires (Cauca) have built community networks using exactly this principle: one point with internet access that distributes the signal via radio links until it reaches the houses.
Buenos Aires - Cauca reference

Before you start…

Heads up: this project requires working at heights and handling electrical equipment. If you are going to install antennas on roofs, poles, or towers, make sure to have someone watching from below, use non-slip footwear, safety harnesses, and height safety equipment (if you have them or can borrow them), and never work alone at heights.


Heads up: this solution has an initial cost. The most basic equipment costs between USD 25 and USD 100 depending on the distance you need to cover. Although the equipment is durable (4–8 years if well cared for), the initial outlay requires planning.


Something to think about: before buying any equipment, do a line-of-sight study (we’ll explain how later). If there is no direct line of sight between the two points, the radio link won’t work and the money will be wasted. That step is free and it’s worth doing first.


What do you need?
Electronic Equipment
The equipment comes in two identical units: one for each end of the link.




































EquipmentFor what distanceApprox. PriceFrequencyTP-Link CPE210 (x2)Up to 5 kmUSD 25–35 ea.2.4 GHzTP-Link CPE510 (x2)Up to 15 kmUSD 35–50 ea.5 GHzTP-Link CPE610 (x2)Up to 23 kmUSD 55–80 ea.5 GHzUbiquiti NanoStation 5AC (x2)Up to 15 kmUSD 80–100 ea.5 GHz

Tip: for most community projects in Colombia, the CPE510 is the best starting point. It reaches up to 15 km, works in the 5 GHz band (which has less interference than 2.4 GHz), and its price is accessible. If the distance is less than 5 km or there is a lot of vegetation in the way, the CPE210 on 2.4 GHz might work better.

Each CPE includes in its box:

The antenna (the equipment itself)
A passive PoE adapter (the “little box” that powers the antenna with electricity via the network cable)
A short network cable

Installation Materials

UTP Cat5e or Cat6 network cable — needed from the antenna to the router at each end. The recommended maximum distance is 60 meters per run. Cat6 supports speeds of up to 1 Gbps, which is convenient if you ever have a high-speed connection.
2 poles or masts — one for each end. They can be 2-inch PVC pipes, galvanized iron pipes, or even straight, sturdy wooden posts. The height depends on what is between the two points (trees, buildings, hills).
Metal clamps to fix the antenna to the pole. Usually included with the equipment.
Zip ties or plastic cable ties to secure the network cable to the pole.
Heat shrink tubing or self-fusing tape to waterproof the cable connectors outdoors.
Drill bit and wall anchors if you need to run the cable through walls.

Tools

Wrench or Allen key to tighten clamps
RJ-45 crimping tool and connectors (if you are going to make the cable ends yourself)
Multimeter (to check the cable)
Spirit level (to install the pole straight)
A computer or smartphone to access the configuration interface
Compass or a compass app on your phone

Prerequisites

Knowing how to use a computer and a web browser
Comfort with simple work at heights (installing on roofs or low poles)
Patience for alignment: it’s the most delicate step
Someone who has a cell phone at both ends to communicate during installation (or two-way radios)


How to do it?


Step 1 → Study the terrain before buying anything

Before spending a single peso, you need to know if there is line of sight between the two points: that from one end you can directly see the other without anything in the middle.
Radio waves from a point-to-point link cannot pass through hills, buildings, or dense forests. If there is an obstacle in the way, the link won’t work or will work very poorly.
How to verify line of sight:
The fastest way is to physically go to both points and look to see if you can clearly see the other from one. If you can see them, it will likely work. If you can’t see them, you need to raise the antennas.
You can also do it from home using digital tools:

Open Google Earth Pro (it’s free).
Locate both points on the map.
Use the “Elevation Profile” tool (in the Tools → Ruler menu) to draw a line between the two points and see the terrain profile. If the terrain rises in the middle, there is a problem.
You can also use HeyWhatsThat — a free web tool that shows what you can see from a point at a certain height. It works very well in the United States; in Colombia, you have to do some testing because it’s not always as accurate as it seems.

The Fresnel Zone: more than just line of sight
Here is something many people don’t know and that costs them dearly: it’s not enough for the two points to “see” each other. Radio waves don’t travel exactly in a straight line like light. They travel in a kind of ellipsoidal bubble called the Fresnel zone.
Imagine throwing a stone into the water. The point where it lands creates circular waves that expand. Something similar happens with radio waves: although the “main beam” goes from antenna to antenna, around that beam there is a spherical zone of energy that also needs to be clear.
For the link to work well, at least 60% of the radius of the first Fresnel zone must be free of obstacles. The exact formula is complicated, but the rule of thumb is:

For a 5 km link at 5 GHz, the Fresnel zone has a maximum radius of about 5–6 meters at the midpoint of the path.
For a 15–20 km link at 5 GHz, that radius goes up to about 15–17 meters.

That means if there is an 8-meter tree exactly in the middle of your 5 km link, you must raise your antennas so that the tree remains below the “cone” of the signal.

Tip: use the Fresnel zone calculator from RF Line of Sight Calculator to calculate exactly how much you need to raise your antennas.




Step 2 → Plan the height of the antennas

Once the line of sight is confirmed, decide at what height to install each antenna.
The general rule: the higher, the better, because you reduce the possibility of trees or new buildings blocking the signal in the future. But higher also means bigger, more expensive, and harder-to-install poles.
A practical height for community projects on relatively flat terrain:

For distances less than 5 km: 4–6 meters above the highest obstacle in the path.
For distances of 5–15 km: 6–10 meters or more, depending on the terrain.

If there are hills in the way, sometimes it’s better to put the antenna on the crest of the hill instead of raising it. That’s called a “repeater node” and can be cheaper than a very tall tower.

Something to think about: if you have doubts about the height, erring on the high side is less costly than redoing the installation. A taller pole is easier to get than doing everything all over again.




Step 3 → Install the poles or masts

With the heights defined, install the physical supports where the antennas will be.
Support options:

1.5–2 inch galvanized iron pole: The most durable option. Resists wind, rain, and humidity. It can be set in the ground with cement or bolted to a wall.
2-inch PVC pipe: Cheaper. Works well for heights under 4 meters. At greater heights, it can vibrate in the wind and misalign the antenna. Also, prolonged sun exposure degrades it over time and it can become brittle—if it’s going to be outdoors, consider painting or covering it.
Roof mast: A metal structure designed to be anchored to a roof without damaging it. Ideal if the installation is on a house or building.

How to fix the pole:
If it goes into the ground: dig a hole 40–60 cm deep, put the pole in, and fill with cement. Let it dry for 24 hours before mounting anything on top.
If it goes to a wall: use expansion anchors (like Fischer plugs) with stainless steel screws. Stainless steel doesn’t rust in the rain.

Heads up: if there are strong winds in your area, add guy wires (ropes or metal rods) that stabilize the pole at various angles. A fallen pole drags the antenna down and can damage it or hurt someone.




Step 4 → Mount the antenna on the pole

Each TP-Link CPE comes with a steel clamp. The process is:

Pass the clamp around the pole.
Hook the antenna onto the clamp (it enters through a slot).
Tighten the screws without tightening them all the way yet — you need to be able to rotate the antenna to align it in the next step.

The antenna has a correct orientation. The TP-Link CPE510 and CPE210 have the label facing forward (where the signal goes). The back (where the LAN port is) faces you when you are behind the pole.

Tip: before taking the antenna up the pole, connect the network cable and start it up on the ground to verify that it turns on correctly. It’s much easier to fix a technical problem down there than while climbing a pole.




Step 5 → Run the network cable from the antenna to the router

The network cable (UTP Cat5e or Cat6) is what carries both the electrical power (via PoE) and the data between the antenna and your network router.
Maximum length: 60 meters per run. If you need more distance between the antenna and the router, you must use a switch or repeater in the middle.
How to run the cable correctly:

Measure the necessary length before cutting — add an extra 20% for bends.
If the cable runs outdoors, secure it every 50 cm with zip ties or cable clips so the wind doesn’t whip it around.
At points where the cable bends (when entering a wall, for example), leave a gentle curve. Sharp bends damage the internal fibers of the cable.
Where the cable enters a building, seal the hole with silicone so water doesn’t get in.

Waterproofing the outdoor connector:
The connection between the cable and the antenna is exposed to the elements. It is one of the points that fails most often over time. Protect it like this:

Wrap the RJ-45 connector with self-fusing tape (available at any hardware store), starting from the bottom up so water runs off.
If you want more protection, add a layer of rubber tape on top.


Heads up: water entering through the connector is the number one cause of failures in radio links installed in the field. Take your time to waterproof it well. It’s worth it.




Step 6 → Connect the PoE adapter and access the configuration interface

The PoE adapter (the “little box” that comes with the CPE) has two ports:

POE: Connects to the antenna (the cable coming from above).
LAN: Connects to the computer or your network router.

It also has a power connector to plug into the electrical outlet. The antenna does NOT need direct power — it receives it through the network cable thanks to the PoE.
To access the configuration interface:

Connect the PoE adapter to the computer with a network cable in the LAN port.
Manually configure your computer’s IP address to 192.168.0.100 (subnet mask 255.255.255.0).
Open a web browser and type http://192.168.0.254 in the address bar.
The configuration panel will appear. The default username and password are admin / admin (or whatever is on the equipment label).


Tip: if the CPE doesn’t respond at that address, try 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1. If still nothing, reset the equipment to factory settings by holding down the RESET button for 10 seconds.




Step 7 → Configure the first end as an “Access Point”

The end that has the internet connection (the one connected to the main router or the provider) is configured as an Access Point (AP).
In the TP-Link CPE interface (Pharos software):

Go to the Wireless section.
In Mode, select Access Point.
Write a network name (SSID) — it can be something like community-link-AP. Give it a name you’ll recognize.
In Frequency, if you are using the CPE510, choose a channel in the 5 GHz band that is not being used by other nearby networks. If there are no other networks, any channel works.
In Security, set a strong password. This link should not be accessible to just anyone.
Save the changes and reboot the equipment.


Something to think about: the network name (SSID) of the link can be made invisible so it’s not visible from external devices. You configure this in the “Hide SSID” option. It makes the link more secure in areas with many networks.




Step 8 → Configure the second end as a “Client”

The second piece of equipment (the one at the remote point, where you want to bring the internet) is configured as a Client.
Repeat the physical connection from Step 6 with the second CPE. Then:

Access the equipment’s interface in the same way.
Go to Wireless → Mode → Client.
Click on Survey. The equipment will search for available networks.
In the list that appears, select the SSID you gave the first piece of equipment.
Enter the network password.
Save and reboot.

When both pieces of equipment are configured, one will automatically search for the other and establish the connection… as long as they are pointing at each other.

You’re doing well: if you made it this far, you have both pieces of equipment configured. What’s left is the most exciting part — and also the most delicate: aligning them.




Step 9 → Align the antennas looking for the strongest signal

This is the heart of the entire installation. A poorly aligned antenna can have a weak signal or none at all, even if the equipment is perfectly configured.
Alignment is done in two stages: first rough orientation (pointing toward the correct area) and then fine alignment (finding the exact point of maximum signal).
Key tool: The CPE client’s web interface has a section called Signal Strength or Signal Survey that shows the signal level in real-time. You can also use the tpPharOS app on your phone connected to the AP.
The value you are looking for: The RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator), measured in dBm. Reference ranges:

























RSSI ValueQuality-45 to -55 dBmExcellent. Very stable link.-55 to -65 dBmGood. Will work well for most uses.-65 to -75 dBmAcceptable. There may be drops in heavy rain.Worse than -75 dBmBad. Likely instability. You need to check alignment or height.
Step-by-step alignment process:

Communicate with the person at the other end (by cell phone, radio, or hand signals if they are visible).
Orient the client antenna looking approximately in the direction where the AP is. A compass or compass app helps.
In the web interface (or in the app), observe the RSSI value. If you don’t see a signal from the AP, move the antenna slowly in a horizontal arc until you find it.
Once you find a signal, start the fine adjustment: move the antenna very slowly to the right and left, looking for the point where the RSSI is highest (the number least negative).
Fix the antenna at that point and repeat the movement vertically (up and down) to optimize that axis as well.
When you have the maximum on both axes, fully tighten the clamp screws.
The person at the other end does exactly the same with the AP.


Keep it up: alignment can take between 20 minutes and two hours, especially if the two points are very far away or if the terrain is uneven. It’s normal. Every tenth of a dB you gain in RSSI is worth it. Don’t rush this stage.


Tip: if you have two people at each end and they can talk by cell phone, the alignment is much faster. One person moves, the other reports the value. You adjust together.




Step 10 → Verify that the link works correctly

With the antennas aligned and the equipment running, it’s time to verify that the link has the quality necessary for the use you will give it.
From the client’s web interface, go to the status section (Status or Monitor). Look for these indicators:
RSSI (signal level):
Make sure it’s in the green range: between -45 and -65 dBm. You already saw this in the previous step.
CCQ (Client Connection Quality):
It is a percentage that indicates the efficiency of the connection. A CCQ of 90% or more is excellent. Below 70%, the link is having trouble transmitting internet packets correctly.
Real Throughput:
Open a browser on a computer connected to the client and test the speed with Fast.com or Speedtest.net. The result should be close (not equal, but proportional) to the speed at the origin point.

Something to think about: if the RSSI is good but the speed is low, check if there is interference from other networks on the same channel. Channels are like traffic lanes or different colors: if many networks share the same channel, the space gets saturated and the data gets trampled. Change the channel in the AP configuration and see if it improves.

Stability test:
Leave the link running for 30 minutes and observe if the RSSI remains stable or fluctuates. A stable link should vary less than ±3 dBm. If the signal goes up and down a lot, it may indicate that there are intermittent obstacles (like trees moving in the wind) or that the alignment is not completely fixed.

You’re doing well: if the RSSI is between -45 and -65 dBm, the CCQ exceeds 90%, and the speed test gives consistent results, you have a functional radio link. That “invisible bridge” you imagined at the beginning now exists.



Recommendations
Heavy rain and thick fog can temporarily degrade the signal, especially in the 5 GHz band. It’s normal. If the link fails only during heavy downpours, consider improving the alignment or slightly increasing the transmit power in the equipment configuration. Keep in mind that increasing power consumes more electricity and can accelerate equipment wear over time.
Connectors and cables outdoors are the most vulnerable point of the installation. Check them every 6 months. Water entering through a small crack can damage the equipment in weeks. Good initial waterproofing is worth much more than repairing or replacing equipment.
If the link has to pass near trees, install the antennas with more margin than you think is necessary. Trees grow. A tree that is 4 meters tall today can be 6 meters tall in two years and start blocking the signal without you having moved.
Do not mix equipment from different brands in the same link if you can avoid it. TP-Link CPE with TP-Link CPE, Ubiquiti with Ubiquiti. Technically they can work in cross-combinations, but sometimes there are incompatibilities in proprietary protocols that reduce speed or stability.
Document everything: the direction of each antenna in degrees, the RSSI at the time of installation, the height of the mast, the length of the cable. You can do it on video, in a notebook, on a printed paper kept in a plastic bag near the equipment, or on your phone. That record will save you hours if you ever have to check or repeat the installation.

How to know if this solution works?
Technical signs of success:

RSSI between -45 and -65 dBm stably
CCQ above 90% constantly
Speed test at the remote point with reasonable results (minimum 5–10 Mbps for basic community use)
The link stays active for 24 hours without drops

Signs of community impact:

People at the remote point can make video calls or watch videos without interruptions.
Children at school can use online educational platforms.
The organization can upload photos, documents, or reports without having to travel to the town center.
Someone who previously paid for internet separately now shares it more economically with the community.


Other possible internets
A radio link is not just technology. It is a political decision by a community that says: we also have the right to connect, and we are going to build our own way of doing it.
In Mexico, indigenous communities in Oaxaca have been operating their own community telecommunications networks for years using exactly this principle. In the Colombian countryside, projects like those of Colnodo and ISOC have shown that it is possible. You don’t need to be a telecommunications company to build a data bridge between two rural communities.
You can also explore if there are telecommunications companies, cooperatives, or entities that can donate equipment or establish an alliance with your community. In Colombia, there are calls for proposals from FONTIC and international organizations that support rural connectivity projects — that can reduce the initial cost.
Once you have the link installed, also consider configuring a secure DNS server (like Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1 or Quad9’s 9.9.9.9) on your network so that browsing is safer and more private for the people who connect.
And if you found this guide useful, you can download or print it to have it available without needing to be connected when you need it most.
What would happen if the village up on the hill and the one down by the river decided to connect with each other, without depending on an operator that doesn’t reach them? What communities do you know that are at the right distance to make this a reality?

Related solutions
A radio link brings internet from one point to another, but at that remote point, you also need to distribute it. These solutions show you how to take that next step:

When the internet already reaches the remote point, this solution explains how to distribute it among several people without cables: How to share internet wirelessly?
If you want to bring internet to areas that don’t have constant electricity, the bike generator can complement your project: How to generate electricity using a bicycle?
Before installing the radio link, it is useful to know what type of signal and speed you have at the origin point: How to perform an internet quality diagnosis?
If the distance is too great for a radio link in free bands, a satellite antenna can be the alternative: How to get a satellite antenna?
So that more people connect once you have the internet at the remote point, this guide helps you organize the space: How to organize a community internet space?

en/solve/solv-raspberrypi-pocket-interne.title: How to set up a web server on a pocket computer?
en/solve/solv-raspberrypi-pocket-interne.summary: Raspberry Pi: A little pocket-sized Internet.
en/solve/solv-raspberrypi-pocket-interne.content:
Hi, I’m Gabriel. I’m an artist. Digital gadgets fascinate me. I consider myself a tinkerer, and I invite you to be one too.

What is a Raspberry Pi or a Pocket Internet?
This solution will help you create a little internet on your local network with very few resources. By installing a server, your community will be able to access content hosted right from their computers or phones.

What is it for?
It’s for having content accessible without an Internet connection. For example, if you’re going to run a SOLE session in a really remote place. Having content downloaded beforehand allows you to research and reach conclusions without depending on an external signal.

How do you know if you need it?
If your Internet connection is spotty or hard to come by, this solution lets people browse a replica of parts of the Internet. It requires a bit of a tinkering spirit and some patience.

What do you need?

Raspberry Pi
32 GB Class 10 MicroSD card
Power supply
Ethernet cable
Memory card to USB adapter.
Internet connection (for setup).
A computer.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Prepare your Raspberry Pi

The developers of Raspberry Pi have created a tool called Raspberry Pi Imager to install the operating system.


Install the Raspberry Pi Imager software on your computer.
Connect the MicroSD to your computer.
Open the program and choose the operating system to download.




Step 2 → Connect and configure your Pi

Once it’s connected to power and your local network, we need to find its IP address.


Use the command ping solevoltaje.local in your Terminal.
Connect via the SSH protocol by typing ssh solevoltaje@192.168.0.25.
Update the software: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade.


You’re doing great: The update might take a few minutes. Patience!



Step 3 → Install the web server

We’re going to install Nginx, a program that will let your Pi act as a server.

In the terminal, type: sudo apt install nginx.
Test that it works by opening solevoltaje.local in your browser.




How do you know if this solution works?
If you can see the “Welcome to nginx” page from another device on the network, your local server is up and running!

Other possible Internets
With this solution, you’ll have a portable server ready to be filled with information. Check out the related solutions to see what else you can load onto your Pi.

Related solutions

Want to share your internet wirelessly?

en/solve/solv-save-data-phone.title: How to get the most out of my mobile plan?
en/solve/solv-save-data-phone.summary: Practical hacks and tips to manage your plan and make your data last.
en/solve/solv-save-data-phone.content:
Hi! I’m Catalina. Ever had that annoying message pop up saying your data’s run out, and you’ve got no clue where it all went? I’ve learned that with a few tweaks, we can make the same plan last a whole lot longer.

What does it mean to make the most of my mobile plan?
It’s about learning to set up your phone so it only spends Internet on what you actually decide. Learning to manage your plan is all about taking control of how you use the data you’re paying for.

Why do it?
This solution lets you keep a real handle on your spending and stops you from getting disconnected halfway through the month. It gives you the freedom to use your internet for what really matters to you and your community.

What do you need?

Your Smartphone with an active plan.
A bit of patience to dig into the settings.
A tinkering spirit.


How to do it?

Heads up: For these tricks to work, it’s best to do them while you’re connected to a WiFi network so you don’t burn through your data while you’re setting up the savings.


Step 1 → Check your data usage

Go to your phone’s settings and look for “Data usage” or “Mobile network”. You’ll see which apps have been hogging your internet over the last month.



Step 2 → Set a data limit

In that same menu, look for “Data limit” or “Data warning”. Set it up so your phone gives you a nudge when you hit a recommended daily amount.



Step 3 → Turn on data saver for apps

Go into the apps you use the most (Instagram, Facebook). Look in their settings for a “Data saver” option. Turn it on so videos don’t start playing automatically.



Recommendations

Clean up your phone: Turn off automatic app updates in the official app store.
The airplane mode trick: If you’re not going to use your phone for a while, turn off mobile data.
Use WiFi: Whenever you can, download heavy files in free connection zones.


Other internet possibilities
Managing our data well is the first step toward thinking about a collective internet. When we stop being passive consumers, we start using technology for what really serves us.

en/solve/solv-second-life-computer.title: How to give an old computer a second life by installing Linux?
en/solve/solv-second-life-computer.summary: Download and install Ubuntu to make your old computer fast and useful again.
en/solve/solv-second-life-computer.content:
Hi! I’m David. One of the things that frustrates me the most is seeing a computer become unusable just because the Operating System (Windows) gets too bloated. You can take that heavy backpack off by installing a free system called Linux.


What is installing Linux Ubuntu?
It’s swapping out your computer’s main program. Ubuntu is a friendly, easy-to-use version of Linux. It replaces your old, sluggish system with a new, free, and much lighter one.

What’s it for?
It’s for bringing that dusty old computer back to life. By installing a system that demands fewer resources, the machine will boot up fast again, you’ll be able to browse the Internet without stuttering, and use free office programs.

Before you start…

Heads up: This process will erase everything on your computer and your USB Flash Drive. Make sure to back up your important files.


What do you need?

An old computer that still turns on.
An empty USB Flash Drive of at least 16GB.
Internet connection (for the initial download).
Patience.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Download the necessary files

Go to ubuntu.com and download the installer. Also, download RUFUS at rufus.ie/es/ to prep your drive.


Step 2 → Prepare the USB drive

Plug in your USB and open RUFUS. Select your USB drive and the Ubuntu file you downloaded. Click “Start”.

You’re on the right track: You’ll know it’s ready when the green bar says “READY”.



Step 3 → Boot from the USB

Turn off the PC. Plug in the USB. When you turn it on, repeatedly press the boot menu key (usually F12, F2, or Esc). Select your USB and press Enter.


Step 4 → Start the installation

Select “Try or install Ubuntu” and then choose your language. Click the “Install Ubuntu” button. Test your keyboard to make sure everything is working right.


Step 5 → Erase the disk and install

Select “Erase disk and install Ubuntu” to give the house a clean sweep.

Keep going: The system will ask for confirmation. Don’t be afraid, just click “Continue”.



Step 6 → Set up user and location

Choose your city for the time zone and create a username and password. Don’t forget it!


Step 7 → Finish and restart

Wait for it to finish copying files. When it says “Installation complete,” click “Restart now.” Remove the USB Flash Drive when the screen goes black.


How do I know if this solution worked?
When you turn on the computer, you’ll see the Ubuntu logo and quickly arrive at a functional desktop where you can browse without any hiccups.

Other possible internets
You’ll be able to set up small computer labs by recycling technology that others throw away. It’s an act of technological and community independence.

en/solve/solv-share-computers.title: How to share available computers?
en/solve/solv-share-computers.summary: Discover the power of group Internet usage.
en/solve/solv-share-computers.content:
Hi, I’m Sanjay. I’ve seen how many computers end up gathering dust in closets just because people are afraid they’ll break. With this solution, I want to show you the importance of using the Internet as a group and how to manage borrowing equipment.

What is sharing computers?
It’s about getting hands-on with devices that we all use and take care of together. It’s a shared experience that opens the door for us to walk the paths of the Internet side by side.

What’s it for?
Sharing computers is a win-win. We don’t need to spend as much on maintenance, and more people get to benefit. When we use them together, we avoid sketchy sites and get a better grasp of the information. We turn technology into a playground where everyone can join in.

What do you need?

Computers to share.
A place with electricity.
A generous spirit.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Manage the equipment

Look for computers in public libraries or schools. Often, they’re just sitting there because nobody knows how to get them running. Talk to the person in charge, tell them your goal (like setting up a SOLE), and set a date for a meetup.



Step 2 → Agree on ground rules

Get your community together and chat about shared responsibility. Ask them what kind of care they think the equipment needs. This first time is crucial so they’ll keep lending you the gear in the future.



Step 3 → Enjoy it as a group!

Head over to the library or public space with your crew. Remember to seat several people per computer (for example, 4). Enjoying it together is the secret sauce to learning.


How do you know if this solution is working?
You’ll know it’s working when you manage to get someone in charge to trust your group, and you see people learning and laughing in front of a shared screen.

Other possible Internets
This solution promotes public access. If there’s no state presence in your area, you can try raising funds (¿Cómo recolectar recursos en comunidad?) to buy your own equipment.

en/solve/solv-share-internet-cellphone.title: How to share your phone's internet?
en/solve/solv-share-internet-cellphone.summary: Set up and share your mobile data with others.
en/solve/solv-share-internet-cellphone.content:
Hi! This solution was written by Nicolás, one of the tinkerers at SOLE Colombia.
I’m Belén, and I’m reviewing it. Even though I love tinkering, sometimes it’s hard for me to understand how things work. I guess I’ve got a few years on me and everything changes so fast… when I started using computers, they were basically typewriters. But not anymore! I encourage you to lose the fear!
What is setting up a personal WiFi hotspot?
Did you know your smartphone has an almost permanent Internet connection? Usually, your cell phone plan comes with a mobile data plan that lets you access the Internet.
That connection can sometimes get slow or sluggish, and it needs a refresh. But you might also want to share it with others—want to know how? Keep reading.
What is it for?
You might want to share your mobile data Internet signal with other people. But it can also happen that, even with an Internet connection, the pages you want to open load with difficulty, or the data call connection isn’t working well.
Almost always, the best way to get everything up and running again is to restart everything from scratch.
Once you’ve restarted, you’ll be able to share your phone’s Internet signal to do a SOLE with your community!
What do you need?

A cell phone.
Enough data on your phone to share with others.
Generosity.

How to do it?

Step 1 → Restart your data connection**

Swipe down from the top of your phone to access the control panel. Once there, select the “Mobile data” option, turn it off for a few seconds, and turn it back on. Wait a moment for the phone to connect to the cellular network, and that’s it! Your connection will be fresh and working properly.

Want another trick? Turn on airplane mode; that will force all your phone’s settings related to the Internet signal to reset.



Moment 2: Set up the mobile hotspot**

Go to settings and look for “Mobile hotspot”.
In this menu, look for the option “Set up mobile hotspot”. Several details will appear; for now, we only care about setting the name of the WiFi signal you’re creating and the access password.
Once you change them, press the checkmark (or the save button) to save the new configuration.


Moment 3: Share the internet

Swipe down from the top of your phone to access the control panel; you can find the “Mobile Hotspot” option, or something similar.
Just turn it on to share the Internet signal with whoever you want.
If you want to do a SOLE, this is an excellent solution to get all the computers connected so they can do their research. You know that at SOLE Colombia, we are always thinking about how to make the most of the resources we have individually to help our communities improve their Internet experience… there’s nothing like using it as a group!

How do I know if this solution works?
With this recipe, you can reset your phone’s cellular network settings. This will improve browsing speed and connection stability. You’ll be able to share it with other phones and/or computers and search the Internet for the answers to the Big Questions that drive your SOLE.
Other possible Internets
Restarting the cellular network connection will improve your connection and you’ll be able to browse a bit faster, but the geographic area where you are must have coverage from your provider.
This recipe won’t work if the phone signal in your area isn’t good quality. Learning to share the internet will be a very important step for when you manage to get computers, as it’s easier to use the internet in a group with large screens.

en/solve/solv-share-internet-computer.title: How to share internet from your computer?
en/solve/solv-share-internet-computer.summary: Turn your computer into an internet router.
en/solve/solv-share-internet-computer.content:
Hi! I’m Catalina, welcome to this solution 👋🏽
The first version of this solution was written by a colleague, Nicolás, and I’ve added a bit to it so we can navigate it together.
This, like other solutions, is designed so that anyone can do it. I’m not a tech expert and I managed to do it! So, shall we dive in and give it a try together? Remember that if you have questions, you can join the Cacharreras Community → where we help each other solve our connectivity (and connection) issues together.
What is sharing Internet from your computer?
In short, it means setting up your computer to turn it into a router →, that is, a device capable of distributing an Internet signal to other devices. It’s similar to when you use your phone to share internet →, but with your computer.

What is it for?
Sometimes we are in places where we only have an Internet connection on one computer and we don’t know the password for the Wi-Fi → network. How do we make the most of that single connection point? With this solution, we can turn THAT computer into an access point or “hotspot” for everyone.
Another scenario, even more powerful, is one where you want to “stretch” the network. Imagine several computers connecting to each other to reach further! It would be a great network, in the literal sense of the internet, but also in the collective sense of agreeing to bring the internet to more and more people.
⚡ Keep in mind that this alternative allows you to share the Internet with up to 8 devices and is geographically limited by the range of the network generated by the computer.

What do you need?

A computer (ideally connected to the Internet via an Ethernet cable →).
Cell phones or other devices without Internet access.
Patience.


How to do it?

Step 0 → How do I know if my computer works for this solution?

Any computer works if its Internet connection is via cable, that is, not through a Wi-Fi network. Even old computers can become high-power routers by making some configurations in their operating system → but they require a wired connection.
If your computer is not connected by cable and is a recent model, it might still work: for a computer to function as a router receiving and distributing a signal via Wi-Fi, its wireless network card must have a capability called Monitor Mode. The easiest way to know if your computer has this card is the true tinkerer’s way: by testing it!
So, let’s get started! 👇🏽


Step 1 → Go to your computer’s Internet settings

⚠️⚠️ Keep in mind that Nicolás wrote this solution using an operating system quite popular in Colombia: Windows 10. If you have another operating system, your screen might look slightly different, but the idea is the same.
To start, select the Start button (the Windows symbol button). In the settings window, look for the following options: Settings > Network & Internet > Mobile hotspot (click on each option to find the next one).




Step 2 → Activate and configure the Internet zone.

When you are in the mobile hotspot window, turn on the option to share internet with other devices. In the image below 👇🏽 you can see that you can share Internet via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. Useful, right?



Step 3 → Connect other people!

You are now ready to share your Internet with others! In the “Mobile hotspot” window, you will find the network name and the password. If you want to change it, you can do so using the “Edit” button.

How do I know if this solution works?
On another device (computer, cell phone, tablet, etc.), turn on Wi-Fi network search (or Bluetooth if you chose to share via this method). If you find the network you configured on your computer, you’ve got half the job done.
Now, connect that other device to the network. If you can browse, it means you did it!

Other possible Internets
With this solution, you can provide Internet access to more devices in one place, without needing the password for the original network. If you share with other devices, more people will be able to access the Internet. This alternative allows you to share the Internet with up to 8 devices and is geographically limited by the range of the network generated by the computer.
After that, you can promote the use of the Internet as a group to learn how to solve challenges together as a community 💪🏽🛠️ .

en/solve/solv-share-internet-wirelessly.title: Want to share your Wi-Fi?
en/solve/solv-share-internet-wirelessly.summary: Set up your Raspberry Pi as a router.
en/solve/solv-share-internet-wirelessly.content:
Hi, I’m Gabriel. Digital gadgets fascinate me. I consider myself a tinkerer, and I invite you to be one too. Today, I’ll walk you through how to share your device’s signal with others.

What is sharing your Raspberry Pi’s internet?
It’s turning a credit-card-sized computer into a portable Router. By doing this, you can connect your whole community to run a SOLE (How to do a SOLE?) without needing any cables.

What’s it for?
It lets your community connect wirelessly and access the information hosted on your Raspberry Pi. If you have a wired internet connection, you can also share it via WiFi.

What do you need?

A Raspberry Pi.
An internet connection (for the initial setup).
Plenty of patience.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Connect to your Pi

Make sure your system is up and running. Connect to your Raspberry Pi via a Terminal by starting an SSH connection.


Step 2 → Update the system

Run an update to get the latest software. Type this into the terminal:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade


Step 3 → Install the necessary software

We’ll install hostapd (for the access point) and dnsmasq (for the server DNS and DHCP):
sudo apt install -y hostapd dnsmasq


Step 4 → Set up a static IP

We need to assign a fixed IP address to the wireless interface (wlan0). Edit the /etc/dhcpcd.conf file and add denyinterfaces wlan0. Then, configure the IP in /etc/network/interfaces.


Step 5 → Configure the access point

Tell hostapd how to operate (network name and password) by editing the /etc/hostapd/hostapd.conf file.

Tip: Choose a secure password that’s still easy to share with your community.



Step 6 → Start the services

Enable the services so they start automatically whenever you turn the device on:
sudo systemctl unmask hostapd
sudo systemctl enable hostapd
sudo systemctl start hostapd
Reboot the Pi with sudo reboot now.


Step 7 → Run a test

From another computer or smartphone, look for the network you created and connect to it. If you can browse or see the files on the Pi, you’ve done it!


Other possible internets
With this recipe, you can bring educational content to places where the connection isn’t always reliable. It’s your own portable community network.

en/solve/solv-sole-tv.title: How to use TV for group learning?
en/solve/solv-sole-tv.summary: Turn your community TV into a space for dialogue and learning with SOLE TV.
en/solve/solv-sole-tv.content:
Hey there! It’s such a joy to greet you all. I’ve always believed that television doesn’t have to be just a box that talks at us; it can be a window for us to listen to each other. It happened to me that while watching shows, I’d ask myself: “What if we could answer back, too?” I’ve learned that when we get together to tinker with the media we already have, magical things happen.

What is SOLE TV?
It’s a proposal to transform television into a Self-Organized Learning Environment (SOLE). It involves creating television content built by asking the audience to answer a Big Question and then sharing those answers on a live show.

What is it for?
It’s for turning television into a space for participatory communication and learning. For places where the Internet signal doesn’t reach, using community television can extend the reach of knowledge built by everyone together.

Before you start…

Heads up: Make sure you have the broadcasting permissions from the community channel, and if you’re going to record minors on the street, always ask for their parents’ consent.


What do you need?

A television channel (mass media, community, or internet-based).
A host with plenty of energy and great listening skills.
An audience willing to participate.
A fixed time slot for the show.
Internet access to receive responses (optional).


How to do it?

Step 1 → Define the Big Question and date

Establish a Big Question that sparks investigation. It should be something that invites discovery and can’t be answered with a simple “yes” or “no.” Set the date for the show at least 15 days in advance.


Step 2 → Invite the audience to participate

Broadcast the question through the channel, inviting people to respond via WhatsApp, social media, or by calling in directly. Include the date of the live show in your invitation.


Step 3 → Plan the live show

Prepare a simple script with greetings, the presentation of the question, rounds of answers from guests and the audience, and a conclusion thanking everyone for the autonomous learning.


Step 4 → Broadcast the live show

Run the show, allowing for an open conversation. You can invite people who know about the topic to stir up the discussion. The host should dig deep with new questions that pop up along the way.


Recommendations

Value every answer: It doesn’t matter if it’s short; the act of participating is what’s valuable.
Keep it flowing: If the topic stalls, toss out a “provocative question.”
Use what you’ve got: If there’s no internet for a form, use a physical ballot box in the town square.


How do you know if this solution works?
You’ll know it’s working if you get responses from people who don’t usually participate and if you see folks still discussing the question at the market or the corner store after the show.

Other possible internets
Television is a very powerful medium because so many people have free access to it. SOLE TV turns a mass medium into a bridge of solidarity and shared knowledge, creating a human network of wisdom.

en/solve/solv-spread-message.title: How to spread a message?
en/solve/solv-spread-message.summary: Reach the heart of the people moved by your message.
en/solve/solv-spread-message.content:
Hey there! Manu here. Today I want to share some powerful techniques with you to get your message out to more people and make a positive impact in your community.

What is spreading your message?
It’s making sure your call reaches as many interested people as possible. It’s about testing which medium (digital or analog) is the best fit to transmit what really matters to you.

What’s it for?
Knowing how to spread the word better will let you reach your audience more efficiently. You’ll be able to inform, inspire, and get others to appreciate the value of your initiative.

What do you need?

Paper, poster board, and markers.
A computer or smartphone with internet.
Comfortable shoes for walking the neighborhood.
Enthusiasm and authenticity.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Define your “Call to Action”

Before spreading the word, decide what you want people to do: sign up? attend a meeting? In digital spaces, you can use reactions or comments to measure the impact.


Step 2 → Identify your target audience

Think about who you want to reach before choosing the channel. If it’s young people, use WhatsApp or social media. If it’s community leaders, maybe a personal visit is more effective.


Step 3 → Choose your channels

You can use digital channels (WhatsApp, groups, polls) or analog ones (posters at the local shop, flyers handed out by hand). Getting out on the street and talking to people usually creates the most authentic connections.


Step 4 → Find allies to amplify the message

Joining forces multiplies the impact. Look for support from community radio stations, schools, or neighborhood associations. Ask them to share your call so it’s on everyone’s lips.


How do you know if this solution is working?
You’ll know it’s working if people take the action you asked them to (the “call to action”). Also, if you get positive feedback or if people you didn’t know start showing interest in your proposal.

Other Internets are possible
Communication is a living process. If something isn’t working, check if the message is clear or if the medium you chose is actually what your audience uses. Other internets are possible when we expand conversations between people.

en/solve/solv-tricks-mobile-signal.title: Three hacks to boost your mobile signal
en/solve/solv-tricks-mobile-signal.summary: With a few tweaks, you can crank up your mobile signal strength.
en/solve/solv-tricks-mobile-signal.content:
Hi! I’m Sanjay. I’m no connectivity expert, but knowing a few tricks to boost my signal has made my life a whole lot easier. Today, I’ll walk you through them so your SOLE sessions run smoother.

What does boosting your mobile signal mean?
It means that with a few physical or settings tweaks, you can crank up the signal strength your Smartphone receives, improving the quality and stability of your Internet connection.

What’s it for?
It helps keep your calls from dropping and makes web browsing faster. Here, you’ll find simple hacks to boost your connection at home and make collaborative learning a breeze.

What do you need?

Cell phone
Active mobile data connection.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Change rooms

Try different spots around your house to find the sweet spot for the signal. Keep in mind that building materials (like thick concrete) can block the waves coming from the cell tower.


Step 2 → Take off the phone case

Some poorly designed cases or covers can interfere with your phone’s internal antenna. Take it off for a moment and see if your signal bars go up.


Step 3 → Toggle Airplane Mode on and off

This trick forces your phone to search for the nearest, strongest cell tower all over again. It’s like giving your connection a quick breather and a fresh start.


How do you know if it’s working?
If you see the signal bars at the top of your screen go up, or if web pages load faster than before, then the tricks worked!

Other possible Internets
Improving your individual signal is the first step toward sharing it with others. Once you’ve got a stable signal, you can turn your phone into a hotspot so your whole community can research together.

en/solve/solv-type-internet-signal.title: How to figure out what kind of WiFi signal your router is spitting out?
en/solve/solv-type-internet-signal.summary: Get the lowdown on how the internet actually reaches your device.
en/solve/solv-type-internet-signal.content:
Hi, I’m Belén. I’m no internet expert—in fact, I’m starting to feel a bit old and there’s a lot about connectivity that goes over my head. If you feel the same way, this info will shed some light on things. If you don’t feel like me, but just want to get a better handle on the differences between signals and how they relate to how your devices work, this will clear things up for you.
What does it mean to know the type of signal your device has?
Internet signals can be classified in several ways. At SOLE Colombia, we’ve chosen this classification based on the medium through which the signals are transmitted.
For now, the existing signals are:

Wired signal, the fastest and most stable

Fiber optic: uses pulsed light to transmit data through special cables. It’s the fastest and most stable type of signal known.
Coaxial cable →: transmits data through copper cables (the same ones used for cable TV).
DSL (Digital Subscriber Line): uses phone lines to transmit data. It’s slower, but it uses a network that’s been around for a long time, so it reaches many places and doesn’t need new installation.


Wireless signal, the one that connects through the air and needs signal repeaters

Wi-Fi (Wireless Fidelity): uses radio waves, in different standards, to broadcast the signal to the devices that make up its network.
Mobile network (3G/4G/5G): uses the mobile phone signal infrastructure to provide internet access and operates on a specific wave spectrum. The difference between them is speed: 3G is the slowest and oldest, 5G is the fastest and newest. Some devices on the market weren’t built to support 5G, and it isn’t available in many places around the world because the necessary developments to detect the wave spectrum aren’t there yet. As a bit of gossip, I’ll tell you that 5G technology still causes some distrust regarding data security, and the lack of spectrum regulation limits the developments needed to incorporate it everywhere 🫢


Satellite, the one that travels through space and needs a satellite dish

GEO, or based on geostationary orbit satellites: they are very far from Earth and provide greater stability, making them ideal for remote areas. You might recognize names like Viasat and HughesNet, which are providers of this technology.
LEO, or based on low Earth orbit satellites: they are closer to Earth, between 500 and 2000 km. They are faster compared to GEO, but require more devices to cover the same area. You might recognize names of providers of this service: Starlink, OneWeb, Amazon Kuiper, and Telesat Lightspeed.
MEO, or based on medium Earth orbit satellites: they are located between LEO and GEO and are the least common. The commercialization of this type of connection has been aimed at sectors like navigation (GPS) and high-end business services, so they aren’t as visible to the average end-user.



Depending on the type of device you have, you’ll have access to different possible internet signal sources. Below you can see what type of signal each device allows:
Devices and signals:















































DeviceWiredWi-FiMobileSatelliteComputerSomeAllNoneNoneTabletNoneAllSomeNoneCell phoneNoneAllAllNoneSmart TVSomeAllNoneNoneIOT (Internet of Things)SomeAllNoneNone
What is this for?
Sometimes I get overwhelmed by error messages on electronic gadgets, and I get so frustrated when the device doesn’t respond! However, I’ve learned a lot. Among other things, that some internet signals work better than others, and also, that some devices work better than others with different signals. I hope this information helps you better understand this connectivity stuff and helps you use your electronic devices better.
What do you need?

Your device, where you want to check the type of signal you have
Curiosity

How to do it?
How to know if you have a wired signal?
Having a wired internet service guarantees that you are getting 100% of the signal your provider gives you. If you have an ethernet cable → connected to your computer, you should have a wired signal.

What to do if the connection isn’t working?

Check the lights on the Router →: look for the ones that indicate the Ethernet connection (they are usually green/orange and blink when there is activity). If they are red or not lit, check the power connection. You can restart the router and start over; it almost always works.
Verify the connection on the device: check the connection status in your equipment’s settings; it should confirm if you are connected.
Check the Ethernet cable: check if it is well connected, both at the router and your device, and that it is in good condition.
If nothing works, contact your service provider.



How to know if you have a Wi-Fi signal?
Looking at the WiFi icon 🛜 is the fastest way to check your connection: the more bars that are colored, the better your signal will be. If the icon has an alert sign, it means there is a problem or it’s unavailable. If the icon is disabled or has a line through it, it means it’s turned off and you need to turn it on.

What to do if the connection isn’t working?

Access Wi-Fi settings: from your device’s settings, you can access the available networks. If any of them appear as “connected,” you are connected to that network. If you don’t see “connected” to any of them, you might need to choose one and enter a password, or the signal might be weak. You can try turning the router off and on again, and the computer too; often that works to reset all the information and start from scratch. Putting the device in ‘airplane mode’ also helps.
Check signal strength: in the device settings, you can check how strong the signal is for each available network. Moving closer to the router or removing obstacles between you can improve the signal.
If nothing works, contact your service provider; there might be an error in the configuration.



How to know if you have a mobile signal?
Look at the top corner of your cell phone. You’ll find some mobile signal bars 📶: if you see one or more bars, the phone is receiving a signal and reading your SIM card →. You can also confirm this in your phone’s settings and check the signal strength.

What to do if the connection isn’t working?

Check that your SIM card is installed correctly: it’s through the card that your mobile connection provider authorizes you to use their network. It has happened to me that I put the SIM card → in upside down in my mobile device and there was no way to connect or make calls.
Activate mobile data: make sure ‘mobile data’ is active, as well as ‘mobile networks’.
Check signal strength: usually this information is in the ‘mobile networks’ and ‘data usage’ section, or in ‘about phone’ and ‘signal strength’, and you can find them in the device settings icon.
Verify network settings: you can check if there is any error in the network configuration; if you don’t understand much, you can call your service provider.
Consult coverage maps from your signal operator: perhaps you are in an area where there is no coverage and you will have to configure one of the other internet connection options.
If nothing works, contact your service provider; there might be an error in the configuration.



How to know if you have a satellite signal?
Installing a satellite signal means you’ve had to install a software package to be able to operate the connection with your satellite dish → 📡 If your antenna is well installed and pointing towards the satellite, the weather is good, and you don’t have clouds or a storm on the way, the router is on, and you have good visibility, you should be able to enjoy a good connection.

What to do if the connection isn’t working?

Verify the physical conditions of the satellite dish: it must be installed correctly, in a place with a clear view of the sky, without obstacles like buildings or trees around.
Verify weather conditions: the presence of clouds or an approaching storm can affect the satellite signal.
Verify the orientation of the antenna towards the satellite: for this, you will need to check the elevation (vertical) and azimuth (horizontal) angles. You will need a compass and an antenna alignment app, as well as a signal meter. You can make progressive adjustments to fine-tune the signal reception.
Verify the router connection: check that it is on, the Ethernet cable is connected correctly to the satellite modem and the router, and that the cable is in good condition.
Verify the signal on your device: some satellite internet systems have signal monitoring software that can provide valuable data to know if it is connected correctly.
Test the speed: you can do a check by consulting “Be an Internet Scientist.”
If nothing works, contact your service provider; there might be an error in the configuration.



How to know if this solution works?
I’ve learned a lot by completing this solution, and I’d love to know if, after reading it and interacting with it, you feel the same way.
I encourage you to keep tinkering, and to do it with someone else—it’s always more pleasant, fun, and loaded with new questions that can lead you to delve deeper into all these topics.
Other possible Internets
Remember that the Internet is for everyone and belongs to everyone; the more we know it, the better we’ll know how to use it… sending you a hug!
